controls.control_name: Context of the Organisation and Scope (Clauses 4.1–4.4 + Amd 1:2024)
controls.short_summary: Define context, climate relevance, interested parties, scope and ISMS processes.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 4 anchors the ISMS in the organisation's real operating environment before a single technical control is chosen. Management must identify internal and external factors affecting security outcomes—including determining whether climate change is relevant under Amendment 1:2024—catalogue interested parties and their obligations, define unambiguous scope boundaries, and map the core ISMS processes and how they interact.
controls.why_it_matters: A vague or overly narrow scope is one of the fastest ways to fail a Stage 1 certification audit or undermine customer trust in an ISO 27001 certificate. Clear context and process mapping also prevent blind spots across cloud platforms, third-party dependencies, and Australian statutory or regulatory obligations.
key_deliverables: Internal and External Context Register (including Climate Change Determination)
Interested Parties and Requirements Register
ISMS Scope Statement and Boundary Diagram
ISMS Process Interaction Map
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors first check that the written scope matches actual business operations, cloud environments, and physical sites, and that Clause 4.1 explicitly records a climate-change relevance determination. The most common trap is omitting Clause 4.4 process interactions or hiding awkward legacy systems outside scope without valid boundary justification.

questions.question: How are internal and external issues affecting the ISMS—including the mandatory Amendment 1:2024 determination of whether climate change is relevant—documented and kept current?
questions.guidance: Maintain a structured context register capturing strategic, technological, regulatory, workforce, and operational factors that can positively or negatively affect ISMS outcomes. Explicitly record a formal determination on whether climate change is a relevant issue (for instance, bushfire, flood, or extreme-heat impacts on offices, data centres, power utilities, or supply chains) even if the documented conclusion is that it is not relevant. Review the register at least annually and after major organisational shifts.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify that context issues are tailored to the organisation rather than boilerplate templates, confirm an explicit Amd 1:2024 climate-change determination exists with rationale, and check review timestamps against management review minutes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A version-controlled context register lists concrete internal and external factors linked to downstream risks and opportunities. It contains a dated, reasoned determination on climate change relevance under Clause 4.1. Review logs confirm the register is refreshed annually and whenever material business or technology changes occur.
questions.red_flags: Generic PESTLE text copied from a template with no link to the risk register. No documented determination on climate change relevance. Context analysis older than 12 months despite acquisitions, cloud migrations, or regulatory changes.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine external and internal issues relevant to ISMS purpose, or omission of the mandatory Clause 4.1 determination on whether climate change is a relevant issue under ISO/IEC 27001:2022/Amd 1:2024.

questions.question: How are relevant interested parties, their information security requirements—including any climate-related expectations—and which requirements are addressed through the ISMS identified and tracked?
questions.guidance: Build an interested parties register covering customers, regulators (such as OAIC, APRA, or ASIC where applicable), shareholders, employees, insurers, and critical cloud or managed service providers. For each party, record specific legal, regulatory, contractual, and operational security requirements, note whether any climate-related obligations apply (per the Clause 4.2 Amd 1:2024 note), and explicitly state which requirements are addressed through the ISMS.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors cross-check the register against actual customer contracts, privacy policies, and statutory obligations to confirm nothing material is missed, and verify that Clause 4.2(c) explicitly identifies which obligations are addressed by the ISMS.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A current register names each stakeholder group, cites specific contractual or statutory obligations, and maps them to ISMS controls or compliance activities. Climate-related expectations from insurers, customers, or regulators are explicitly considered and recorded. Ownership and periodic review dates are clearly assigned.
questions.red_flags: Interested parties listed as broad labels like 'customers' or 'regulators' without naming actual obligations. Missing distinction between general expectations and requirements addressed via the ISMS. No link to the legal and compliance register under Control 5.31.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to identify relevant interested parties, their information security requirements, or which of those requirements will be addressed through the ISMS as required by Clause 4.2.

questions.question: How are the ISMS scope, organisational and technical boundaries, external interfaces (such as cloud services and customer data flows), and any justified exclusions documented?
questions.guidance: Publish a concise, unambiguous Scope Statement available as documented information that names the in-scope legal entities, business units, products, physical locations, cloud platforms, and supporting delivery pipelines. Clearly document interfaces and dependencies with out-of-scope units or third parties, and substantiate any scope exclusion so it does not undermine the organisation's ability or responsibility to protect customer or regulated information.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors test whether the written scope aligns with the Statement of Applicability, network diagrams, and certificate wording, and scrutinise any exclusions to ensure shared services (such as HR, IT identity providers, or CI/CD pipelines) were not improperly carved out.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An executive-approved ISMS Scope Statement defines in-scope locations, business functions, cloud infrastructure, and data flows, supported by a clear boundary diagram. Interfaces with out-of-scope systems and third parties are documented with controls at each boundary. Any exclusion carries a credible business and risk rationale.
questions.red_flags: Scope wording that contradicts the SoA or excludes core identity, deployment, or support teams relied upon by in-scope systems. Undocumented boundary interfaces with corporate IT or cloud providers. Missing documented justification for carved-out sites or subsidiaries.
questions.nc_pattern: ISMS scope is not maintained as documented information, fails to account for interfaces and dependencies with activities performed by other organisations, or omits critical functions required to deliver in-scope security outcomes under Clause 4.3.

questions.question: How are the processes needed for the ISMS and their interactions defined, maintained, and continually improved?
questions.guidance: Document the core management and operational processes that make the ISMS function—such as context review, risk management, document control, access management, incident response, internal audit, and management review—and show how outputs from one process feed into another. Define process owners, inputs, outputs, and handover points so the ISMS operates as a cohesive management system rather than isolated spreadsheets.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors look for a process map or governance manual demonstrating Clause 4.4 compliance, then trace real transactions across processes (for example, how a security incident triggers risk reassessment, corrective action, and management review input).
questions.what_good_looks_like: An ISMS process architecture or interaction diagram clearly defines each required management system process, its accountable owner, inputs, outputs, and interfaces with other processes. Operational records demonstrate those handovers actually occur in practice rather than existing only on paper.
questions.red_flags: No documented view of ISMS processes or how they connect. Siloed security activities where incident post-mortems, audit findings, and change requests never feed back into the risk register or management review.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine the processes needed for the ISMS and their interactions in accordance with Clause 4.4 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

controls.short_summary: Demonstrate top management commitment, approve policy and assign ISMS authorities.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 5 ensures information security is owned by executive leadership rather than delegated away as an IT side project. Top management must actively champion the ISMS, approve a strategic Information Security Policy, ensure sufficient budget and skilled people are provided, and assign unambiguous roles, responsibilities, and reporting authorities across the organisation.
controls.why_it_matters: Certification auditors interview executives directly; if leadership cannot articulate security priorities, risk appetite, or resource trade-offs, the ISMS lacks real authority. Strong executive sponsorship is also essential to align security investment with business strategy and board accountability.
key_deliverables: Approved Information Security Policy
Executive Security Committee Minutes and Attendance Records
ISMS Roles, Responsibilities and Authorities Matrix (RACI)
Security Budget and Resourcing Approvals
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors test genuine leadership involvement through executive interviews, committee minutes, budget approvals, and signed policies. The classic failure is a rubber-stamped policy signed once by a CEO who never attends governance meetings or reviews ISMS performance.

questions.question: How does top management demonstrate active leadership and commitment to the ISMS, including governance participation, resourcing, and continual improvement?
questions.guidance: Capture tangible evidence of executive engagement: active participation in security steering committees and management reviews, alignment of security objectives with business strategy, documented approval of security budgets and staffing, and visible sponsorship of continual improvement initiatives. Ensure executives can explain how security requirements are embedded into core business processes.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors interview senior executives directly and cross-check their statements against board packs, committee minutes, budget sign-offs, and resource escalation decisions.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Dated governance minutes record regular executive attendance, active challenge of security metrics, and formal budget or staffing approvals. Strategic planning documents integrate information security priorities alongside commercial goals. Executives speak fluently in audit interviews about key risks and continual improvement priorities.
questions.red_flags: Executives absent from management reviews or delegating attendance entirely to junior IT staff. Unfunded remediation plans or stalled risk treatments with no executive decision. Leadership unable to describe ISMS scope or top security risks during interviews.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of objective evidence that top management demonstrates leadership and commitment to the ISMS, ensures resource availability, or directs and supports personnel as required by Clause 5.1.

questions.question: Is the Information Security Policy formally approved by top management, aligned with business strategy, communicated internally, and made available to relevant interested parties?
questions.guidance: Establish a concise, high-level Information Security Policy signed off by top management that sets strategic direction, provides a framework for setting security objectives, and commits to satisfying applicable requirements and continual improvement. Publish it to all personnel via intranet or onboarding workflows, and make an appropriate version available to customers, regulators, or partners on request.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect the policy for mandatory Clause 5.2 commitments, verify current executive approval and review dates, and sample staff to confirm they know where to find it and what it expects of them.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A current, version-controlled Information Security Policy carries dated executive approval and explicitly includes commitments to applicable requirements, security objectives, and continual improvement. Staff acknowledgements confirm internal communication, and a summary or policy pack is readily available for interested parties.
questions.red_flags: Unsigned draft policy or a policy overdue for annual review. Missing commitment to continual improvement or to establishing security objectives. Personnel unable to locate the policy during audit interviews.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a top-management-approved Information Security Policy containing the mandatory Clause 5.2 elements, or failure to communicate it within the organisation and make it available to relevant interested parties.

questions.question: How are information security roles, responsibilities, and authorities assigned and communicated, including authority to ensure ISMS conformance and report performance to top management?
questions.guidance: Define clear security accountabilities across governance, risk ownership, control operation, incident response, and internal audit using a RACI matrix, role charters, and position descriptions. Explicitly designate who holds authority to verify ISMS conformance with ISO/IEC 27001 and who reports ISMS performance directly to top management.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify that named roles—not merely generic team labels—own key ISMS clauses and risks, confirm individuals understand their assigned duties, and check that the reporting line to top management is unobstructed.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved RACI matrix and role charters assign named individuals or defined roles for ISMS conformance, risk ownership, control operation, and executive performance reporting. Position descriptions reflect these responsibilities, and updates are communicated promptly when personnel change roles.
questions.red_flags: Key ISMS duties assigned to departed employees or unassigned committees. Confusion over who has authority to accept residual risk or escalate audit nonconformities. No designated role responsible for reporting ISMS performance to top management.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure by top management to assign and communicate responsibilities and authorities for ISMS conformance and performance reporting in accordance with Clause 5.3.

controls.control_name: Planning, Risk Treatment & Planning of Changes (Clauses 6.1–6.3)
controls.short_summary: Assess risks and opportunities, maintain SoA and objectives, and plan ISMS changes.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 6 is the risk-driven engine of ISO 27001. Organisations must address both strategic ISMS risks and opportunities, run a repeatable information security risk assessment methodology, produce a Statement of Applicability covering all 93 Annex A controls alongside a signed Risk Treatment Plan, set measurable security objectives, and plan changes to the ISMS itself in a controlled way.
controls.why_it_matters: Every control decision in an ISO 27001 programme must trace back to defensible risk logic rather than guesswork or vendor sales pitches. Weak risk methodology, an incomplete SoA, or uncontrolled structural changes to the ISMS trigger major certification nonconformities.
key_deliverables: ISMS Risks and Opportunities Register
Information Security Risk Assessment Methodology and Risk Register
Statement of Applicability (all 93 Annex A controls) and Risk Treatment Plan
Information Security Objectives Plan and Tracker
ISMS Change Planning Procedure and Change Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace a vertical thread from context issues to assessed risks, chosen Annex A controls in the SoA, risk treatment actions, and risk-owner sign-offs. Frequent traps include omitting ISMS opportunities under Clause 6.1.1, unsigned residual risk acceptances, and overlooking Clause 6.3 planning of ISMS-level changes.

questions.question: How does the organisation determine and plan actions to address both ISMS risks and opportunities derived from its context and interested-party requirements (Clause 6.1.1)?
questions.guidance: Look beyond technical asset threats to evaluate management-system risks and strategic opportunities arising from Clauses 4.1 and 4.2—such as adopting automation to cut manual compliance effort, leveraging certification for enterprise sales, or mitigating key-person dependency in the security team. Document how planned actions are integrated into ISMS processes and how their effectiveness will be evaluated.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors specifically check that opportunities—not just negative risks—have been identified and acted upon, and verify traceability back to the context and interested-party registers.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintained ISMS risks and opportunities register links directly to Clause 4.1 issues and Clause 4.2 stakeholder expectations. Each entry specifies planned actions, an accountable owner, target completion dates, and how effectiveness is reviewed. Records show actions are embedded into business and security workflows.
questions.red_flags: Risk planning covers only IT vulnerabilities with zero consideration of management-system risks or strategic opportunities. Actions listed without owners, timelines, or effectiveness evaluation criteria.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine risks and opportunities arising from organisational context and interested parties, or failure to plan how to integrate and evaluate actions to address them under Clause 6.1.1.

questions.question: Is a consistent, repeatable information security risk assessment methodology defined and applied to produce a current risk register with assigned risk owners (Clause 6.1.2)?
questions.guidance: Document clear risk acceptance criteria and scoring criteria (likelihood, consequence, and inherent versus residual ratings) so different assessors reach consistent, valid, and comparable results. Apply the methodology across in-scope assets, processes, and third parties to identify confidentiality, integrity, and availability risks, assign named risk owners, and prioritise risks against acceptance thresholds.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors test whether scoring definitions are objective enough to yield repeatable results, confirm every risk has an accountable risk owner with authority to accept or treat it, and check that high risks actually align with the organisation's threat landscape.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented risk methodology defines clear likelihood and impact scales, risk acceptance thresholds, and escalation rules. The live risk register records CIA impact, inherent and residual scores, existing controls, and named risk owners for each risk. Independent reviewers can reproduce scores consistently.
questions.red_flags: Undefined or subjective 'High/Medium/Low' labels with no scoring definitions or acceptance criteria. Risk register populated with generic threats unrelated to actual systems. Missing risk owners or outdated scores left unchanged after incidents.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented risk assessment criteria capable of producing consistent, valid, and comparable results, or failure to identify, analyse, evaluate, and assign owners to information security risks under Clause 6.1.2.

questions.question: How are risk treatment options selected, mapped into a complete Statement of Applicability covering all 93 Annex A controls, tracked via a Risk Treatment Plan, and approved with signed residual risk acceptance (Clause 6.1.3)?
questions.guidance: Select risk treatment options (modify, retain, avoid, share) and determine all necessary controls before comparing them against ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A to ensure nothing essential was missed. Produce a Statement of Applicability listing all 93 Annex A controls with explicit inclusion or exclusion justifications and implementation status, maintain a funded Risk Treatment Plan, and obtain documented approval from risk owners for both the plan and residual risks.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify all 93 ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls appear in the SoA (spotting outdated 2013 control numbering immediately), challenge every exclusion justification, and check for dated risk-owner signatures approving the RTP and residual risks.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A current SoA addresses all 93 ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls with clear inclusion rationales, rigorous exclusion justifications, and accurate implementation status. A living Risk Treatment Plan assigns owners, budgets, and due dates, backed by dated approvals from risk owners accepting residual risk.
questions.red_flags: SoA referencing ISO 27001:2013's 114 controls or missing new 2022 controls (such as 5.7, 5.23, 8.28). Blanket 'not applicable' exclusions without valid justification. No documented sign-off by risk owners approving the RTP and residual risk levels.
questions.nc_pattern: Incomplete or inaccurate Statement of Applicability omitting required Annex A comparison or justifications, missing Risk Treatment Plan, or failure to obtain risk-owner approval for the treatment plan and acceptance of residual risks under Clause 6.1.3.

questions.question: Are measurable information security objectives established, documented, communicated, and supported by structured action plans specifying resources, responsibilities, timelines, and evaluation methods (Clause 6.2)?
questions.guidance: Set concrete information security objectives at relevant functions and levels that align with the Information Security Policy, risk results, and applicable obligations. For each objective, document what will be done, what resources are required, who is responsible, when it will be completed, and how results will be evaluated, then track progress regularly and communicate updates.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check that objectives are genuinely measurable (avoiding vague slogans like 'improve security') and contain all five Clause 6.2 planning elements, plus evidence of active monitoring and updates.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented security objectives specify clear targets (for example, critical vulnerability remediation SLAs or phishing reporting rates) aligned with policy and risk priorities. Each objective has an action plan detailing tasks, resources, owner, deadline, and evaluation metric, reviewed quarterly in governance forums.
questions.red_flags: Aspirational statements with no measurable target, baseline, or deadline. Objectives set once at initial certification and never updated or evaluated. Missing resource allocation or named accountability.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish documented, measurable information security objectives or omission of required planning elements (actions, resources, responsibilities, completion dates, and evaluation methods) under Clause 6.2.

questions.question: When changes to the ISMS itself are required (such as scope shifts, governance restructures, risk methodology updates, M&A, or core GRC tooling changes), how are those changes planned and executed in a controlled manner (Clause 6.3)?
questions.guidance: Distinguish Clause 6.3 (changes to the ISMS framework itself) from routine IT change management under Control 8.32. Define a lightweight ISMS change-planning process that assesses the purpose and potential consequences of structural ISMS changes, protects system integrity during transition, confirms resource availability, and updates roles, documentation, and regulatory notifications (including operational risk change assessments where applicable).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors ask for examples of recent organisational or ISMS changes—such as office moves, acquisitions, cloud platform shifts, or GRC tool migrations—and look for evidence that the transition was planned deliberately rather than patched retrospectively.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented ISMS change-planning procedure sets triggers for formal change plans, such as restructures, M&A, scope expansions, or methodology revisions. Completed change plans capture impact analysis, resource needs, role reassignments, communication steps, and post-change verification.
questions.red_flags: Conflating Clause 6.3 purely with IT ticket workflows while having no governance over scope, methodology, or leadership changes. Major organisational restructures or new product launches absorbed into the ISMS with no planned transition record.
questions.nc_pattern: Changes to the ISMS are executed in an ad-hoc manner without planned control to preserve management system integrity, contrary to Clause 6.3 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

controls.short_summary: Provide resources, competence, awareness, communication and document control.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 7 supplies the operational foundations that keep an ISMS alive: adequate budget and people, verified role competence, targeted security awareness across all personnel, structured internal and external communications, and disciplined document control—including governing external-origin documents the organisation relies upon.
controls.why_it_matters: Well-designed security policies fail when teams lack skills, time, or accurate current documentation. Auditors routinely uncover hidden nonconformities in missing competence evidence, incomplete awareness topics, or uncontrolled external standards and supplier compliance reports.
key_deliverables: Security Resourcing Plan and Role Competence Matrix
Role Competence Verification and Training Effectiveness Records
ISMS Awareness Programme and Completion Logs
Internal and External ISMS Communication Plan
Document Control Procedure and Master Document Register (including External-Origin Documents)
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify competence records for specialist security roles (including internal auditors), check that awareness explicitly covers all three Clause 7.3 items, and inspect document control logs. A frequent surprise finding is failing to identify and control external-origin documents under Clause 7.5.3.

questions.question: How are the resources needed for the ISMS provided, and how is competence determined, verified (including for new hires and role changes), developed, and evidenced (Clauses 7.1–7.2)?
questions.guidance: Demonstrate that budget, tooling, and appropriately skilled personnel are allocated to operate and improve the ISMS. Define required competence (education, training, or experience) for roles impacting security performance—such as ISMS managers, cloud engineers, incident responders, and internal auditors—verify competence at hiring or role transfer, address gaps via training or mentoring, evaluate whether those actions worked, and retain documented evidence.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect position descriptions, certifications, CVs, or skills assessments for key ISMS roles and check whether training taken to close a competence gap was subsequently evaluated for effectiveness.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved resourcing plan aligns staffing and tooling with ISMS scope, and a role competence matrix specifies required qualifications or experience for security-critical roles. Retained HR or LMS records verify competence on hire and promotion, plus documented evaluation of any upskilling completed.
questions.red_flags: Critical ISMS functions assigned to staff with no documented skills assessment or training history. Training attendance logs kept without evaluating whether competence was actually achieved. Chronic under-resourcing leaving mandatory ISMS tasks overdue.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine necessary competence for personnel affecting ISMS performance, lack of documented evidence of competence, or failure to provide resources required to maintain the ISMS under Clauses 7.1 and 7.2.

questions.question: How does the organisation ensure all personnel working under its control are aware of (a) the Information Security Policy, (b) their contribution to ISMS effectiveness and the benefits of improved performance, and (c) the implications of not conforming with ISMS requirements (Clause 7.3)?
questions.guidance: Design onboarding and recurring awareness modules so every employee and contractor under the organisation's control clearly understands all three Clause 7.3 elements—not just generic phishing tips. Explicitly explain where the policy lives, how daily behaviours strengthen security outcomes, and the operational, legal, and disciplinary consequences of policy non-conformance.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review awareness content against all three Clause 7.3 bullets, inspect completion rates for employees and contractors, and interview randomly selected staff to verify genuine comprehension.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Awareness curricula explicitly address the Information Security Policy, each person's role in ISMS effectiveness, and consequences of nonconformity. Completion records cover employees and in-scope contractors with automated escalation for overdue staff. Sampled staff articulate their security obligations accurately.
questions.red_flags: Awareness training limited to generic cyber hygiene that omits the organisation's own policy or nonconformity implications. Contractors or casual staff excluded from awareness tracking. Low completion rates with no management follow-up.
questions.nc_pattern: Personnel working under the organisation's control are unaware of the Information Security Policy, their contribution to ISMS effectiveness, or the implications of not conforming with ISMS requirements, breaching Clause 7.3.

questions.question: How are internal and external communications relevant to the ISMS planned—specifying what will be communicated, when, with whom, and how (Clause 7.4)?
questions.guidance: Maintain an ISMS communication matrix covering routine and event-driven communications, including policy rollouts, security alerts, audit schedules, management review updates, customer security enquiries, and regulatory notifications (such as OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches or APRA reporting where applicable). Follow ISO/IEC 27001:2022 wording by specifying what, when, with whom, and how communications occur.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review the communication matrix for completeness across internal and external audiences, then sample actual communications (such as staff updates, customer advisories, or incident notifications) to verify the plan is followed.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintained ISMS communication matrix defines topic, trigger or cadence, target internal or external audience, channel, and responsible owner. Supporting records—such as intranet bulletins, customer advisories, and regulatory contact protocols—confirm communications run as planned.
questions.red_flags: No structured plan for external or crisis communications. Ambiguity over who is authorised to communicate with regulators, media, or customers during a security incident. Outdated stakeholder contact lists.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine internal and external ISMS communications—covering what, when, with whom, and how to communicate—as required by Clause 7.4.

questions.question: How is documented information created, approved, version-controlled, protected, retained, and disposed of—including identifying and controlling documented information of external origin (Clause 7.5)?
questions.guidance: Implement document-control rules covering standard metadata (title, version, owner, approval date, classification), formal review and sign-off, secure storage and access permissions, change history, retention schedules, and controlled archiving or disposal. Under Clause 7.5.3, explicitly catalogue and control external-origin documents necessary for ISMS planning and operation—such as applicable legislation, ISO standards, ACSC Essential Eight guidance, customer security schedules, and third-party SOC 2 reports.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect the master document register for unapproved drafts, conflicting duplicate copies, or stale review dates, and specifically ask how external-origin documents are tracked so teams do not rely on superseded laws or standards.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A document control procedure and master register govern all ISMS policies, procedures, and records with consistent versioning, owner sign-off, access control, and retention rules. A dedicated external-origin documents register tracks applicable standards, laws, and third-party assurance artefacts with scheduled currency checks.
questions.red_flags: Multiple conflicting copies of policies circulated via email or shared drives. Documents missing version numbers, owners, or approval dates. Zero tracking or currency control over external-origin standards, contracts, or regulatory guidance.
questions.nc_pattern: Inadequate control of ISMS documented information—including unapproved revisions, lack of version/retention control, unauthorised modification risk, or failure to identify and control documented information of external origin under Clause 7.5.

controls.short_summary: Operate ISMS processes, control external providers and run risk treatments.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 8 turns planning into day-to-day execution. Organisations must run operational security processes against defined criteria, control planned and unintended changes, govern externally provided processes, products, or services, and carry out scheduled and change-triggered risk assessments alongside active risk treatment.
controls.why_it_matters: Even the cleanest risk methodology or policy suite fails certification if operational evidence shows risk assessments were skipped during major platform changes or external providers operate outside security oversight. Clause 8 is where auditors prove the ISMS actually works in daily operations.
key_deliverables: Operational Security Procedures and Process Criteria
Externally Provided Processes, Products and Services Control Register
Planned and Event-Driven Risk Assessment Records
Risk Treatment Execution Evidence and Closure Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample recent operational changes, third-party services, and completed risk treatments to verify plans are executed rather than shelved. The #1 trap is updating the risk register only once a year right before the audit while ignoring major mid-year cloud, vendor, or architectural changes.

questions.question: How are operational ISMS processes planned, implemented, and controlled—including managing planned and unintended changes and controlling externally provided processes, products, or services (Clause 8.1)?
questions.guidance: Establish clear operational criteria for key security processes, maintain documented evidence that they operate as intended, and ensure planned operational changes are reviewed for security impact while unintended changes are investigated to mitigate adverse effects. Under ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 8.1 wording, explicitly identify and control all 'externally provided processes, products, or services' relevant to the ISMS (such as SaaS platforms, managed SOCs, cloud hosts, and payroll or HR providers).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify operational criteria exist for key processes, check change tickets for security sign-off and post-incident reviews of unintended changes, and inspect contracts, SLAs, and assurance reports governing externally provided processes, products, or services.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented operating procedures define clear acceptance criteria and retain execution logs across core security workflows. Change records demonstrate pre-change risk checks and documented remediation of any unintended disruptions. An external provider register maps controls, SLAs, and periodic reviews for all externally provided processes, products, or services.
questions.red_flags: Critical operational controls relying on tribal knowledge with no documented criteria or logs. Shadow SaaS or managed service providers operating with no security oversight. Unplanned configuration drifts or emergency changes left unreviewed.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish criteria and control operational ISMS processes, failure to control planned changes or review consequences of unintended changes, or lack of control over externally provided processes, products, or services under Clause 8.1.

questions.question: What documented evidence demonstrates that information security risk assessments are performed both at planned intervals and whenever significant changes are proposed or occur (Clause 8.2)?
questions.guidance: Execute risk assessments on your defined planned cadence (typically annually or semi-annually) and establish explicit triggers for event-driven reassessments—such as launching a new customer-facing product, migrating cloud regions, onboarding a material supplier, or suffering a major security incident. Retain dated records showing methodology application, stakeholder input, and updated risk ratings.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors compare the risk register's change history against major business or technical events from the past 12 months (product releases, acquisitions, serious incidents) to verify change-triggered risk assessments actually took place.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Dated risk assessment logs and workshop minutes confirm scheduled reviews occurred on time and significant changes triggered documented reassessments before go-live. Version history clearly shows newly added, re-scored, and retired risks with rationale.
questions.red_flags: Risk register untouched for over 12 months or bulk-edited days before the certification audit. Major architectural changes, new AI integrations, or serious incidents absent from risk reassessment records.
questions.nc_pattern: Information security risk assessments are not performed at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed or occur, or documented results are not retained as required by Clause 8.2.

questions.question: What documented evidence verifies that the Risk Treatment Plan is actively implemented and that resulting risk reductions are recorded (Clause 8.3)?
questions.guidance: Track every Risk Treatment Plan action from approval through implementation to closure, capturing objective completion evidence (such as configuration outputs, policy approvals, or test reports) and re-evaluating residual risk once controls are live. Escalate overdue treatments to risk owners and management review for formal re-baselining or interim compensating controls.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample closed and in-progress items from the Risk Treatment Plan, ask for tangible proof the control was actually deployed, and check whether overdue high-risk treatments have been escalated.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A tracked Risk Treatment Plan links every treatment action to an owner, milestone, objective closure artefact, and updated residual risk rating. Overdue actions show documented management escalation and interim risk mitigation until completed.
questions.red_flags: Risk Treatment Plan items marked 'Complete' with no implementation proof. Numerous past-due treatment actions sitting unaddressed for months with no re-evaluation or executive acceptance.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to implement the information security Risk Treatment Plan or failure to retain documented information on the results of risk treatment under Clause 8.3.

controls.control_name: Performance Evaluation — Monitoring, Internal Audit & Management Review (Clauses 9.1–9.3)
controls.short_summary: Measure ISMS performance, run impartial internal audits and hold management reviews.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 9 proves whether the ISMS is genuinely delivering results rather than merely existing on paper. Organisations must measure and analyse security performance against defined metrics, execute an impartial internal audit programme covering all ISMS requirements, and hold formal executive management reviews addressing every mandatory Clause 9.3.2 input and documenting resulting decisions.
controls.why_it_matters: Without reliable metrics, independent internal audits, and substantive executive reviews, control drift goes unnoticed until a breach or external certification audit exposes it. Clause 9 is also the core assurance layer supporting board oversight and regulatory attestation.
key_deliverables: ISMS Monitoring, Measurement and KPI Framework with Analysis Reports
Internal Audit Programme, Coverage Matrix and Audit Reports
Auditor Independence and Competence Records
Management Review Agenda Packs (all Clause 9.3.2 inputs) and Signed Minutes/Decisions
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors examine internal audit independence, full clause/Annex A coverage across the audit cycle, and management review packs against every single Clause 9.3.2 sub-bullet—especially the 2022 addition 9.3.2(c) covering changes in interested-party needs and expectations. The #1 trap is treating an informal IT status meeting as a Management Review without covering all required inputs or recording formal decisions.

questions.question: How are information security performance and ISMS effectiveness monitored, measured, analysed, and evaluated using repeatable methods and retained evidence (Clause 9.1)?
questions.guidance: Define a structured monitoring and measurement register specifying what controls and processes are measured, the measurement method ensuring valid and comparable results, when monitoring and analysis occur, and who performs each step. Go beyond collecting raw dashboards: document regular analysis and evaluation of trends, SLA breaches, and control testing outcomes so findings feed directly into management review and improvement.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify all Clause 9.1(a)–(f) parameters are defined, inspect raw metric collections alongside documented analytical commentary, and check that control effectiveness—not just activity counts—is actually evaluated.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A monitoring plan maps measurable KPIs to ISMS processes alongside security objectives, defining collection formulas, frequencies, and owners. Quarterly performance reports present trend analysis, root-cause commentary on missed thresholds, and retained supporting evidence.
questions.red_flags: Metrics defined in policy but never collected, or raw dashboards exported with zero documented analysis or evaluation. Measuring only vanity counts while failing to evaluate whether security objectives and controls are effective.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to determine monitoring and measurement requirements, failure to analyse and evaluate ISMS performance and effectiveness, or lack of retained documented evidence of results under Clause 9.1.

questions.question: How is the internal audit programme planned and executed to verify ISMS conformance and effectiveness across all applicable clauses and controls using objective, impartial auditors (Clause 9.2)?
questions.guidance: Establish a risk-based internal audit programme specifying frequency, methods, responsibilities, audit criteria, and scope so every ISMS clause (4–10) and applicable Annex A control is audited across the cycle. Ensure auditors are competent and independent of the processes they examine (never auditing their own work), verify both control design and operating effectiveness in practice, report results to relevant management, and retain audit reports and workpapers.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect the multi-year audit coverage matrix, verify auditor independence and qualifications, review completed audit reports for genuine evidence-based sampling (not rubber-stamp checklists), and trace findings into the corrective action register.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A multi-year internal audit programme and coverage matrix ensure full coverage of Clauses 4–10 and applicable Annex A controls. Audit reports document scope, criteria, sampling of design and operating effectiveness, objective evidence inspected, and impartial auditor credentials, with findings formally reported to management.
questions.red_flags: Internal audit performed by the same person who wrote the policies and operates the controls. Audit report showing '100% compliant' across 93 controls completed in half a day with no evidence samples cited. Clauses 4–10 or key Annex A controls skipped entirely.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a planned internal audit programme covering ISMS requirements, lack of auditor objectivity and impartiality, failure to report results to relevant management, or failure to retain documented audit evidence under Clause 9.2.

questions.question: Are top management reviews conducted at planned intervals and structured to consider every mandatory Clause 9.3.2 input—including changes in the needs and expectations of interested parties (Clause 9.3.2(c))?
questions.guidance: Run formal Management Reviews on a defined cadence (typically semi-annually or annually) with executive participation. Structure the review pack strictly around all ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 9.3.2 inputs: (a) status of prior actions, (b) changes in external/internal issues, (c) changes in needs and expectations of interested parties relevant to the ISMS (the 2022 addition), (d) performance feedback covering nonconformities, monitoring results, audit results, and objectives, (e) interested-party feedback, (f) risk assessment results and RTP status, and (g) continual improvement opportunities.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors tick off every single Clause 9.3.2(a)–(g) input against management review packs and minutes—frequently catching legacy 2013 templates that omit Clause 9.3.2(c) changes in interested-party needs and expectations.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Scheduled management review packs systematically present substantive data against all Clause 9.3.2(a)–(g) items, explicitly covering changes in interested-party expectations (Clause 9.3.2(c)) and climate/context shifts. Executive attendance and active discussion of each agenda item are clearly evidenced.
questions.red_flags: Using an outdated ISO 27001:2013 template missing Clause 9.3.2(c). Management review held by IT managers without top management participation. Mandatory inputs skipped or summarised with empty 'no change' placeholders without review.
questions.nc_pattern: Management reviews are not conducted at planned intervals by top management, or omit one or more mandatory inputs specified in Clause 9.3.2 (including Clause 9.3.2(c) changes in interested-party needs and expectations).

questions.question: Are management review outputs—specifically decisions on continual improvement opportunities and any required changes to the ISMS—documented, assigned, and tracked to completion (Clause 9.3.3)?
questions.guidance: Retain formal Management Review minutes and decision logs recording executive conclusions on the continuing suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the ISMS. Explicitly record decisions on continual improvement initiatives, resource adjustments, scope or policy revisions, and any other changes to the ISMS, with named owners and target dates tracked at the subsequent review.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review minutes from the most recent management reviews to verify concrete decisions were recorded—not just passive slide presentations—and trace prior meeting actions to confirm follow-through.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Signed Management Review minutes record explicit executive decisions on continual improvement priorities, budget or resource changes, and required ISMS updates. Every action carries a named owner and due date, and status is formally closed out at the next review.
questions.red_flags: Slide deck presented with no minutes or documented decisions. Repeated carry-over of stalled management review actions across multiple cycles with no executive intervention.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to include decisions on continual improvement opportunities and required ISMS changes in management review outputs, or failure to retain documented information of management review results under Clause 9.3.3.

controls.short_summary: Drive continual ISMS improvement and resolve nonconformities at root cause.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clause 10 closes the management-system loop. Organisations must continually improve the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the ISMS, react promptly when nonconformities occur, uncover root causes so issues do not recur elsewhere, verify that corrective actions actually worked, and retain complete documented records.
controls.why_it_matters: Auditors do not expect perfection, but they do expect disciplined learning when controls break. Treating symptoms without root-cause analysis—or closing corrective actions without verifying effectiveness—leads to repeat audit findings, recurring incidents, and regulatory escalation.
key_deliverables: Continual Improvement Register and Roadmap
Nonconformity and Corrective Action (CAR) Register
Root Cause Analysis (RCA) Documentation
Corrective Action Effectiveness Verification Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace nonconformities from internal audits, incidents, and control failures through containment, root-cause analysis, systemic checks for similar gaps elsewhere, and independent effectiveness verification. The #1 trap is closing a finding as soon as a quick patch is applied without proving the underlying root cause was eliminated.

questions.question: How does the organisation systematically identify, prioritise, implement, and evidence continual improvement of the ISMS's suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness (Clause 10.1)?
questions.guidance: Establish structured intake channels for improvement ideas—drawing from internal audits, security incidents and lessons learned, KPI trends, threat intelligence, staff suggestions, and management reviews. Maintain a prioritised improvement backlog or roadmap, track implemented enhancements over the past 12 months, and demonstrate measurable gains in ISMS maturity or risk reduction.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors ask for concrete examples of ISMS improvements delivered over the past year (beyond merely fixing mandatory nonconformities) and verify that lessons learned from incidents and audits drive proactive change.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An active continual improvement register captures enhancement initiatives sourced from audits, incident post-mortems, KPI analysis, and threat trends. Completed improvements over the past 12 months are evidenced with clear before-and-after outcomes reported in management reviews.
questions.red_flags: ISMS operating in pure 'tick-box maintenance mode' with zero proactive improvements between audits. Incident lessons learned documented in post-mortems but never translated into control or process enhancements.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of objective evidence that the organisation continually improves the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the ISMS as required by Clause 10.1.

questions.question: When a nonconformity occurs, how does the organisation react to contain it, investigate root causes, check whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere, and implement proportionate corrective action (Clause 10.2)?
questions.guidance: Maintain a central Nonconformity and Corrective Action Register covering internal and external audit findings, control test failures, and systemic policy breaches. Require immediate containment and consequence handling, structured root-cause analysis (such as 5-Whys or fishbone analysis), an explicit check for similar weaknesses across other teams or systems, and corrective actions proportionate to impact. Where APRA CPS 234 applies, link material control weaknesses that cannot be remediated in a timely manner to the 10-business-day notification workflow (§36).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample closed and open nonconformities to check that containment is distinguished from true root-cause corrective action and verify that the organisation actually checked whether the same failure existed elsewhere.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A central nonconformity register records each issue, immediate containment taken, documented root-cause analysis, systemic extent checks across other business units or systems, and targeted corrective actions with owners and due dates. Material control weaknesses trigger timely executive and regulatory escalation where applicable.
questions.red_flags: Corrective actions limited to one-off fixes (such as deleting a single stale account) without fixing the broken offboarding workflow. Missing root-cause analysis or no evaluation of whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to react to nonconformities, failure to evaluate causes and check for similar nonconformities elsewhere, or failure to implement proportionate corrective action under Clause 10.2(a)–(c).

questions.question: How is the effectiveness of completed corrective actions verified, how are necessary changes fed back into the ISMS, and what documented evidence is retained (Clause 10.2)?
questions.guidance: Do not close a nonconformity on the day a fix is deployed. Allow an appropriate observation period or perform targeted re-testing to confirm the corrective action genuinely prevented recurrence, update affected ISMS documents, risks, or controls where needed, and retain complete records showing the nature of the nonconformity, subsequent actions taken, and verified results.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check closure dates against implementation dates to confirm genuine effectiveness verification occurred, inspect verification evidence (such as re-audit samples or monitoring logs), and verify required ISMS updates were completed.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every closed corrective action includes independent verification evidence confirming the fix operates effectively over time, dated sign-off by an appropriate reviewer, and documented updates to affected risks, policies, or procedures. Complete records of nonconformities, actions, and results are retained securely.
questions.red_flags: Nonconformities marked 'Closed' on the same day an email reminder was sent with zero verification evidence. Recurring identical audit findings year after year proving previous corrective actions were ineffective.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to review the effectiveness of corrective actions taken, failure to update the ISMS where necessary, or failure to retain documented information on nonconformities, actions, and corrective action results under Clause 10.2.

controls.short_summary: Approve, publish, acknowledge, and review security policies on a planned cycle.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish an overarching information security policy alongside topic-specific policies that translate executive intent into actionable rules for staff and relevant external parties. Management must formally approve every policy, communicate it clearly to its intended audience, and review it at planned intervals or after significant business, legal, or threat changes.
controls.why_it_matters: Policies anchor the entire ISMS by setting enforceable expectations and demonstrating leadership commitment during certification audits. Stale, unapproved, or unread policies leave staff guessing and undermine disciplinary or contractual enforcement after an incident.
key_deliverables: Executive-approved Information Security Policy
Suite of topic-specific security policies (access, acceptable use, cloud, incident, supplier)
Policy distribution and personnel acknowledgement register
Planned policy review log and version history
Risk-accepted policy exception register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors first inspect approval dates, executive sign-off, and review histories to confirm policies are living documents rather than templates downloaded before the audit. The most common trap is publishing policies on an intranet without proof that staff and contractors actually received and acknowledged them, or allowing review dates to lapse past 12 months.

questions.question: Provide the management-approved overarching information security policy and the supporting suite of topic-specific policies aligned with business and legal obligations.
questions.guidance: Confirm that an overarching policy defines strategic direction and commitment, while topic-specific policies cover risk-relevant areas such as access control, acceptable use, cloud services, cryptography, incident management, and supplier security. Check that statutory, regulatory, and contractual obligations are reflected rather than left as generic boilerplate.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify document control metadata, executive or Board-level approval signatures, effective dates, and alignment between stated policy commitments and the organisation's Statement of Applicability.
questions.what_good_looks_like: The organisation maintains a concise, executive-signed overarching policy supported by modular topic-specific policies mapped to its risk profile and legal obligations. Each document carries version history, a named policy owner, an approval record, and clear scope boundaries covering employees and relevant third parties.
questions.red_flags: Policies remain marked as draft, lack named executive approval, reference another company's name, or omit core areas required by the organisation's own risk treatment plan.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a management-approved information security policy, or omission of topic-specific policies required to support controls declared applicable in the Statement of Applicability.

questions.question: Provide evidence that information security policies are communicated to, and acknowledged by, all relevant employees and external parties.
questions.guidance: Review how policies are published (for example, HRIS, LMS, or policy portal) and how target audiences—including contractors and relevant third parties—confirm understanding on onboarding and after material updates.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent joiners, existing staff, and active contractors against acknowledgement logs to confirm completion rates and follow-up on overdue attestations.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All active employees and in-scope contractors complete timestamped policy acknowledgements at onboarding and after material revisions. Automated reminders and manager escalations track overdue acknowledgements until resolved.
questions.red_flags: Policies sit in a buried SharePoint folder with no read-receipt mechanism, acknowledgement rates are below 85% with no chase process, or contractors are excluded altogether.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to communicate established information security policies to relevant personnel and external parties or inability to demonstrate acknowledgement as required by organisational policy.

questions.question: Provide evidence of planned periodic and event-driven policy reviews, together with formal governance over policy exceptions.
questions.guidance: Verify that policies are reviewed at defined intervals (typically annually) and triggered by major business, architectural, or regulatory changes. Where temporary deviations are unavoidable, inspect the exception workflow for risk assessment, compensating controls, expiry dates, and executive sign-off.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect review meeting minutes, change logs showing substantive review (not merely changing the footer year), and the active exception register for expired or unapproved waivers.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every policy displays documented annual or event-triggered reviews approved by management, even when no text changes were needed. Policy exceptions are time-bound, backed by compensating controls, approved by an authorised risk owner, and tracked to closure before expiry.
questions.red_flags: Policies are overdue for review by more than a year, review logs show rubber-stamped dates without governance records, or informal email waivers persist indefinitely without expiry.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to review information security policies at planned intervals or following significant changes, or systemic non-adherence to stated policies through unapproved, untracked exceptions.

controls.short_summary: Define, allocate, and maintain clear accountability for security and asset ownership.
controls.plain_english_summary: Define and allocate information security roles and responsibilities across the organisation so every control, governance forum, and information asset has a named accountable owner. Responsibilities must be communicated clearly to role holders and updated whenever organisational structures or job duties change.
controls.why_it_matters: Ambiguous ownership is the fastest path to dropped alerts, unpatched systems, and stalled audit remediation. Regulators and certification auditors expect clear reporting lines from operational teams up to senior leadership and the Board.
key_deliverables: Information Security RACI or responsibility matrix
CISO or Information Security Officer charter and position description
Asset ownership register linked to accountable individuals
Onboarding role-briefing records and HR role-change update logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors cross-check the security RACI and asset owner register against real staff interviews to confirm people actually know what they own. The top trap is assigning ownership to generic team names or departed employees without updating registers after restructures.

questions.question: Provide your information security responsibility matrix (RACI), senior security leadership charter and reporting line, and documented asset owner assignments.
questions.guidance: Check that accountability spans executive oversight, day-to-day ISMS management, technical control operation, incident response, and individual asset ownership. Verify that the CISO or equivalent lead has an unambiguous reporting line and sufficient authority to escalate risk.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm there are no orphaned ISMS processes or critical assets without a named accountable person, and check whether the security reporting line creates unresolved conflicts of interest.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A current RACI matrix maps every ISMS domain to named roles, supported by an approved CISO or security lead position description showing direct executive and committee reporting lines. Critical assets and control domains carry named human owners rather than vague departmental labels.
questions.red_flags: Security duties are assumed informally by IT without documented authority, the RACI names former employees, or no single executive is accountable for ISMS performance.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to define and allocate information security roles and responsibilities in accordance with organisational needs across the ISMS scope.

questions.question: Provide evidence that information security responsibilities are communicated during onboarding and understood by role holders in practice.
questions.guidance: Review position descriptions, induction checklists, and role-specific briefings for both general staff and specialist roles (such as system administrators, asset owners, and incident leads). Confirm that awareness extends beyond generic policy links to concrete duties.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample onboarding files for recent hires and interview selected asset owners or administrators to verify they can articulate their security duties accurately.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Position descriptions and onboarding packs explicitly state role-specific security duties, and specialist owners receive targeted handover briefings. During interviews, sampled staff and asset owners clearly describe their escalation paths and approval responsibilities.
questions.red_flags: Position descriptions omit security duties entirely, or interviewed asset owners are unaware they are listed as owners in the register.
questions.nc_pattern: Allocated information security responsibilities are not communicated to or understood by the personnel expected to execute them.

questions.question: Provide evidence that security roles and asset ownership records are updated promptly when personnel change roles, transfer, or depart.
questions.guidance: Inspect how HR mover and leaver workflows notify the ISMS owner or asset managers to reassign control ownership, approval authority, and incident response duties without gaps.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check recent staff transfers and departures against the RACI, asset register, and approval workflows to verify timely handover.
questions.what_good_looks_like: HR role-change and offboarding workflows include mandatory tasks to reassign ISMS responsibilities and asset ownership before the departing owner's final day. Change logs show timely updates to the RACI, asset inventory, and incident call trees.
questions.red_flags: Departed managers still appear as system owners or incident contacts months after leaving, or reorganisations leave controls unmanaged.
questions.nc_pattern: Information security roles and responsibilities are not maintained following organisational or personnel changes, resulting in unowned controls or assets.

controls.short_summary: Separate conflicting duties or apply documented compensating controls.
controls.plain_english_summary: Separate conflicting duties and areas of responsibility so no single individual can authorise, execute, and conceal an unauthorised or erroneous change, transaction, or access grant. Where small team sizes make full separation impractical, apply documented compensating controls such as independent review, dual control, and tamper-evident audit trails.
controls.why_it_matters: Unchecked end-to-end control over production releases, user provisioning, or payment execution invites both insider fraud and high-impact human error. Auditors scrutinise segregation across DevOps pipelines, identity administration, and finance systems.
key_deliverables: Segregation of duties (SoD) conflict matrix
CI/CD branch protection and release-approval configurations
Dual-authorisation configurations for financial and privileged actions
Periodic SoD conflict review reports
Approved SoD exception register with compensating controls
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors test real system permissions and recent production changes rather than accepting policy statements at face value. The number-one trap is developers holding direct push or admin rights to production alongside pull-request approval privileges, or small teams failing to document compensating detective reviews.

questions.question: Provide your segregation of duties matrix defining incompatible roles and conflicting permissions across IT, security, change, and financial processes.
questions.guidance: Check that the matrix explicitly identifies high-risk toxic combinations, such as requesting versus approving access, developing versus deploying production code, operating systems versus auditing logs, and initiating versus releasing payments.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm the matrix reflects the organisation's actual operating systems and high-value business workflows rather than a generic finance-only template.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A risk-based SoD matrix maps incompatible duties across identity management, software delivery, infrastructure administration, security monitoring, and finance. Each conflict specifies either hard preventive separation or mandatory compensating detective controls.
questions.red_flags: No documented definition of incompatible duties exists, or the matrix omits IT administration and software release pipelines.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to identify and segregate conflicting duties and areas of responsibility relevant to the organisation's risk profile.

questions.question: Provide technical and operational evidence showing how segregation of duties is enforced in code delivery (CI/CD), privileged administration, and financial workflows.
questions.guidance: Examine repository branch protection rules requiring independent peer review, deployment pipeline approvals separated from code authors, and dual-control settings on banking or ERP payment workflows.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent production deployments and high-value transactions to verify that the initiator, approver, and executor are genuinely distinct individuals.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Source control enforces independent pull-request approval with self-approval disabled, production releases require separate release authorisation, and payment systems enforce dual-signature release. Sampled change and payment logs confirm no single user bypassed separation.
questions.red_flags: Repository administrators routinely bypass branch protection, developers deploy directly to production without peer review, or one user can create a vendor and approve payment.
questions.nc_pattern: Stated segregation rules are not enforced in critical production, access, or financial systems, enabling single-person execution of high-risk changes without compensating controls.

questions.question: Provide evidence of periodic reviews for conflicting access combinations and governance over approved segregation exceptions.
questions.guidance: Review periodic access-conflict check outputs and inspect how small teams or break-glass scenarios document risk acceptance, independent log review, and expiry dates when strict separation cannot be maintained.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that exceptions are formally approved by senior management, backed by independent audit-trail review evidence, and revisited periodically rather than left open indefinitely.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Periodic access reviews explicitly flag toxic role combinations and track remediation to completion. Where resource constraints require combined duties, documented exceptions specify compensating independent monitoring, management sign-off, and review dates.
questions.red_flags: Access reviews check single entitlements without detecting cross-role conflicts, or small-team overlaps have no independent review logs.
questions.nc_pattern: Uncontrolled segregation conflicts exist without documented risk acceptance or operating compensating controls such as independent monitoring and review.

controls.short_summary: Ensure managers actively require staff and contractors to follow security policies.
controls.plain_english_summary: Management must actively require employees and contractors to apply established information security policies, topic-specific rules, and procedures in their daily work. Leaders reinforce security culture by setting clear expectations, equipping staff with time and resources to comply, and addressing breaches consistently.
controls.why_it_matters: Even well-written security policies fail when line managers treat them as optional paperwork or model shortcuts. Auditors look for practical evidence that people leaders—not just the security team—hold their teams accountable for secure behaviour.
key_deliverables: Employment and contractor agreements mandating policy adherence
Management induction or people-leader security briefing material
Performance and accountability criteria incorporating security expectations
Records of leadership communications and supervisory reinforcement on security
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors interview operational managers outside IT to verify they actively enforce security rules with their direct reports and contractors. The most common trap is treating security enforcement as solely the CISO's job while line managers quietly approve shortcuts or ignore overdue training.

questions.question: Provide evidence of how management requires employees and contractors to apply information security policies through contractual obligations, role expectations, and performance accountability.
questions.guidance: Check employment contracts, contractor schedules, manager handbooks, and performance or disciplinary standards to confirm that adhering to security policies is an explicit condition of work for both staff and contingent workers.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect sampled employee and contractor agreements alongside manager accountability frameworks to confirm obligations are clear, enforceable, and applied consistently across all workforce types.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Employment contracts and contractor agreements contain binding clauses requiring compliance with organisational security policies. Line managers are briefed on their supervisory duties, and adherence to security expectations forms part of performance reviews and accountability processes.
questions.red_flags: Contractor statements of work omit security obligations, managers cannot explain how they enforce security rules, or repeated security shortcuts carry no management follow-through.
questions.nc_pattern: Management fails to establish enforceable mechanisms requiring employees and contractors to apply the organisation's information security policies and procedures.

questions.question: Provide evidence of active management leadership, security communications, and supervisory follow-through reinforcing policy adherence across teams.
questions.guidance: Focus on visible management sponsorship rather than technical compliance auditing (which is assessed under 5.36). Look for executive town-hall briefings, team-level security reminders, manager follow-up on overdue training or policy exceptions, and resources allocated so staff can work securely.
questions.auditor_focus: Review leadership meeting packs, staff communications, and escalation records showing managers actively support security initiatives and address non-adherence within their teams.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Senior leaders and operational managers regularly communicate security priorities through all-hands meetings, operational briefings, and targeted advisories. Managers track team completion of mandatory security tasks and take documented supervisory action when staff bypass agreed controls.
questions.red_flags: All security communications originate solely from IT with zero executive visibility, or managers routinely pressure staff to bypass security controls to hit delivery deadlines.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of objective evidence that management actively supports, communicates, and requires personnel to apply established information security policies in operational practice.

controls.short_summary: Maintain current authority contacts and statutory incident notification procedures.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish and maintain designated points of contact with relevant authorities—including regulators, law enforcement, privacy commissioners, and national computer emergency response teams (CERTs). Clear pre-agreed liaison roles and notification workflows ensure timely, accurate escalation during cyber incidents, data breaches, or material control failures.
controls.why_it_matters: Scrambling to identify reporting portals, legal counsel, and statutory deadlines during a live crisis leads to missed mandatory notification windows and regulatory penalties. Pre-established relationships also accelerate law enforcement and CERT assistance when attacks unfold.
key_deliverables: Authority contact register with designated internal liaison officers
Regulatory and authority notification matrix with statutory timeframes
Incident and material control weakness escalation procedures
Periodic register review and regulatory change monitoring logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that authority contact lists are current, accessible offline during an outage, and explicitly linked to incident response playbooks with realistic reporting clocks. The most common trap is listing outdated agency names or generic hotline numbers without naming who inside the organisation is authorised to speak to regulators.

questions.question: Provide your maintained authority contact register covering relevant regulators, law enforcement, privacy authorities, and national cyber response agencies (CERTs), together with designated internal liaison roles.
questions.guidance: Ensure the register matches the organisation's actual jurisdictions and industry sectors (such as financial, privacy, health, or critical infrastructure regulators, police cybercrime units, and national CERTs). Confirm that authorised internal spokespersons and backup contacts are named and that contact details are periodically verified.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the register for completeness, last-verified dates, named internal escalation owners, and evidence of ongoing relationship maintenance or regulatory engagement where applicable.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An up-to-date, offline-accessible authority contact register lists every applicable regulator, law enforcement body, privacy commissioner, and national cyber agency with verified reporting channels and hours of operation. Named internal liaison officers and deputies hold clear authority to communicate externally.
questions.red_flags: Contact lists contain defunct agency names, broken portal links, no named internal spokesperson, or have not been checked for over 12 months.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish and maintain appropriate contacts with relevant authorities applicable to the organisation's legal, regulatory, and operational context.

questions.question: Provide documented procedures and decision thresholds for notifying relevant authorities of reportable security incidents, data breaches, or material control weaknesses.
questions.guidance: Check that notification procedures specify materiality triggers, internal legal and executive sign-off gates, statutory reporting clocks across applicable jurisdictions, and required notification templates. Where sector prudential rules apply, verify that both incident and material control weakness reporting pathways are clearly defined.
questions.auditor_focus: Trace how an operational incident or audit-identified material weakness escalates from technical triage to legal assessment and formal authority submission within statutory deadlines.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented notification playbooks map each applicable statutory regime to concrete materiality criteria, countdown clocks, pre-drafted notification templates, and executive sign-off steps. Both security incidents and unremediated material control weaknesses follow clear, tested escalation paths.
questions.red_flags: Incident playbooks mention 'notify regulators if required' without defining thresholds, timeframes, or decision makers, or omit material control weakness reporting where statutorily required.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined procedures to determine when and how relevant authorities must be notified of security incidents or statutory reportable events.
