questions.question: Provide evidence of how changes to legal, regulatory, and authority reporting obligations are monitored and incorporated into authority contact records and notification procedures.
questions.guidance: Review horizon-scanning mechanisms (such as legal counsel updates, regulatory bulletins, or compliance registers) that capture new reporting thresholds, updated portals, or emerging statutory obligations and trigger updates to internal procedures.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect recent regulatory change logs or compliance committee minutes showing how updated authority guidance or statutory amendments were assessed and reflected in registers.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A named compliance or legal owner tracks regulatory updates across all operating jurisdictions and logs impact assessments quarterly. Confirmed changes flow directly into the authority contact register, incident playbooks, and legal obligations register.
questions.red_flags: Notification workflows reference repealed legislation or superseded agency reporting portals, with no process to detect statutory changes.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to keep authority contacts and statutory notification requirements current with applicable legal and regulatory changes.

controls.short_summary: Engage with security forums and specialist groups to stay ahead of emerging risks.
controls.plain_english_summary: Maintain active contact with specialist security forums, industry information sharing and analysis centres (ISACs), vendor advisory groups, and professional associations. Engaging with peer communities helps the organisation receive early warning of emerging vulnerabilities, validate good practices, and benchmark defensive maturity.
controls.why_it_matters: No internal security team sees every emerging attack pattern alone. Active peer and vendor community links shorten the window between a newly disclosed zero-day or sector campaign and practical defensive action.
key_deliverables: Register of security forums, ISACs, and professional memberships
Staff professional development and conference participation records
Log of external advisories and good practices reviewed and acted upon
Guidelines for safe external information sharing (e.g., TLP handling)
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors look for active two-way or operational use of specialist groups rather than a neglected mailing list nobody reads. The top trap is citing a single employee's unpaid personal LinkedIn group as the organisation's sole special interest group contact.

questions.question: Provide a register of the security forums, sector ISACs, vendor security groups, and professional associations the organisation engages with, along with evidence of personnel participation.
questions.guidance: Verify that selected groups are relevant to the organisation's sector and technology stack (for example, AISA, OWASP, cloud provider security communities, or sector ISACs) and that management supports staff participation through memberships, time allocation, or training budgets.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm active memberships, named internal representatives, and recent attendance or briefing records rather than dormant subscriptions.
questions.what_good_looks_like: The organisation maintains a curated register of sector ISACs, vendor security channels, and professional bodies aligned to its risk profile, with named internal liaisons. Training records, membership renewals, or meeting attendance confirm sustained staff engagement.
questions.red_flags: No formal list of specialist contacts exists, memberships lapsed years ago, or reliance rests entirely on one staff member's ad-hoc personal accounts.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish and maintain appropriate contact with special interest groups, specialist security forums, or professional associations.

questions.question: Provide evidence that advisories, lessons learned, or good practices from special interest groups are reviewed and translated into operational security improvements.
questions.guidance: Check how insights from peer groups or vendor forums feed into security meetings, patching decisions, or control refinements, and—where the organisation shares sanitised lessons back to peers—confirm clear confidentiality and Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) guardrails exist.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect concrete examples from the past 12 months where a community alert, peer briefing, or forum guidance prompted a configuration change, risk update, or staff advisory.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Security team meeting notes record peer advisories and specialist forum findings being triaged into concrete actions, including hardening updates, detection rules, or staff alerts. Any outbound sharing follows approved sanitisation and TLP rules.
questions.red_flags: Forum newsletters arrive in an unmonitored shared inbox with no triage workflow, or staff cannot cite a single operational action informed by external specialist engagement.
questions.nc_pattern: Special interest group memberships exist on paper only, with no evidence that received security information is reviewed or used to support the ISMS.

controls.short_summary: Collect, analyse, and operationalise threat intelligence across risk and defences.
controls.plain_english_summary: Collect and analyse information relating to cyber security threats to produce timely, contextualised threat intelligence tailored to the organisation's environment. Operationalise that intelligence across risk assessments, vulnerability prioritisation, detection engineering, and incident preparedness so defences adapt to real attacker behaviour.
controls.why_it_matters: Unfiltered threat feeds create alert fatigue without improving security. Actionable threat intelligence allows lean teams to prioritise the vulnerabilities and attack paths adversaries are actively exploiting right now.
key_deliverables: Threat intelligence collection and analysis procedure
Register of authoritative threat feeds (e.g., ACSC, CISA KEV, vendor PSIRTs, ISACs)
Contextualised threat advisories or periodic threat landscape briefings
Evidence linking threat intelligence to risk register updates and defensive changes
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that threat information is actually analysed for relevance to the organisation's stack and linked back to risk assessments and patching priorities. The number-one trap is forwarding raw ACSC or vendor newsletters without recording whether the organisation is exposed or what action was taken.

questions.question: Provide your documented threat intelligence process and register of authoritative threat sources (such as ACSC advisories, CISA KEV, vendor PSIRTs, and sector feeds).
questions.guidance: Confirm that collection covers strategic (sector trends), operational (active campaigns), and tactical (indicators and exploited vulnerabilities) intelligence proportionate to organisational size and risk. Verify that current authoritative sources—such as the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC)—are used rather than defunct feeds.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the list of active feeds, named owners responsible for monitoring them, and defined criteria for validating reliability and relevance.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented procedure defines how threat intelligence is gathered from vetted sources—including ACSC alerts, CISA KEV, cloud/vendor PSIRTs, and sector ISACs—with clear triage cadences and named roles. Sources are reviewed periodically to ensure coverage matches the current technology estate.
questions.red_flags: Reliance on ad-hoc social media browsing, references to retired bodies or broken RSS feeds, or no assigned owner monitoring incoming advisories.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish a systematic process to collect and analyse information relating to information security threats relevant to the organisation.

questions.question: Provide evidence showing how collected threat information is analysed against your technology stack, prioritised, and communicated to relevant technical and business stakeholders.
questions.guidance: Look for documented triage notes assessing whether an advisory applies to in-scope assets, assigned priority ratings, and targeted communications sent to engineering, SOC, or leadership teams.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent high-profile advisories (for example, critical ACSC alerts or actively exploited CVEs) and trace the analysis record, communication timestamp, and assigned remedial action.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Incoming advisories are assessed against the asset inventory within defined turnaround times to confirm exposure and impact. Actionable summaries—distinguishing executive briefs from technical remediation tickets—are distributed promptly to accountable owners.
questions.red_flags: Raw external bulletins are mass-forwarded without applicability assessment, or critical advisories sit unanalysed for weeks.
questions.nc_pattern: Collected threat data is not analysed for organisational relevance or converted into actionable intelligence for relevant stakeholders.

questions.question: Provide evidence demonstrating how analysed threat intelligence informs risk assessments, vulnerability prioritisation, and preventive or detective control updates.
questions.guidance: Trace the closed loop from threat intelligence into ISMS risk assessments, expedited patching, firewall/EDR/SIEM rule updates, or security awareness campaigns.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect risk register revision entries, management review threat briefings, or SIEM/patching tickets explicitly referencing threat intelligence findings.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Periodic risk reviews incorporate a current threat landscape summary that adjusts likelihood ratings and treatment priorities. Technical change tickets demonstrate concrete defensive updates—such as IOC blocks, detection rules, or emergency patches—driven directly by analysed intelligence.
questions.red_flags: The risk register has remained static despite major sector attacks, and no link exists between threat briefings and operational security controls.
questions.nc_pattern: Threat intelligence operates in isolation with no evidence that findings inform risk management or security control adjustments.

controls.short_summary: Embed security requirements, design review, and go-live sign-off into every project.
controls.plain_english_summary: Integrate information security into project management regardless of delivery methodology (waterfall, agile, or vendor implementation) and across business, IT, and operational change initiatives. Security risks and requirements must be identified early, validated during design and build, and formally signed off before launch.
controls.why_it_matters: Bolting security onto a new platform days before launch causes expensive rework, missed deadlines, or silent risk acceptance. Embedding security gates throughout the project lifecycle prevents unvetted systems and shadow SaaS from entering production.
key_deliverables: Project delivery methodology with embedded security gates
Project security triage and requirements checklist
Threat modelling and security architecture review records
Pre-go-live security sign-off and residual risk acceptance records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors select 2–4 recently completed projects—including non-IT business or SaaS rollouts—and trace security involvement from initiation to go-live. The classic trap is documenting a thorough project security framework that delivery teams routinely bypass to meet commercial deadlines.

questions.question: Provide your project management methodology and security intake templates demonstrating how security risks, requirements, and threat modelling are embedded from project initiation.
questions.guidance: Verify that the framework applies to both internal software builds and commercial, cloud, or organisational change projects. Check that early-stage screening determines data sensitivity, regulatory impact, and whether threat modelling or deeper architecture review is required.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect PMO templates, agile definition-of-ready criteria, and triage thresholds to confirm security is a mandatory workstream rather than an optional afterthought.
questions.what_good_looks_like: The project delivery lifecycle embeds mandatory security triage at initiation, tailored security requirement templates, and proportional threat modelling for material architectural changes. Clear escalation triggers define when security specialists must join the project team.
questions.red_flags: Security is only engaged after procurement or during final UAT, or agile and SaaS onboarding projects are excluded from project security governance.
questions.nc_pattern: Information security is not integrated into the organisation's project management framework or is omitted from material classes of projects within ISMS scope.

questions.question: Provide operating evidence of security architecture reviews and security requirement tracking across recent material projects.
questions.guidance: Select completed or in-flight projects from the past 12 months and inspect their security risk assessments, architecture review notes, and backlog/traceability records showing how identified issues were resolved.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that security findings raised during design and build were tracked to closure or formally risk-accepted rather than quietly dropped.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Sampled projects contain completed security intake forms, dated architecture or threat-model review outputs, and traceable ticket histories closing each security requirement prior to launch. Residual items carry explicit owners and target remediation dates.
questions.red_flags: Project folders lack any security review artefacts, or architecture review recommendations were logged with no evidence of resolution.
questions.nc_pattern: Defined project security assessment and tracking requirements are not executed in practice for in-scope projects.

questions.question: Provide evidence of mandatory pre-go-live security sign-off confirming required controls are verified and residual risks are formally accepted before production release.
questions.guidance: Inspect release readiness checklists, CAB or steering committee minutes, and formal sign-off records confirming security approval is required before systems go live—including clear authority for accepting any deferred items.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check recent production launches against security sign-off logs to identify any projects released without authorisation or with unapproved high-risk findings.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every sampled production launch includes a timestamped security readiness sign-off confirming testing, hardening, monitoring, and asset onboarding are complete. Any conditional go-live carries executive risk acceptance and time-bound post-launch remediation milestones.
questions.red_flags: Systems enter production without security sign-off, or go-live checklists are signed off retroactively weeks after launch.
questions.nc_pattern: Material projects or system changes are released into production without required security verification or formal acceptance of unresolved risks.

controls.control_name: Inventory of information and other associated assets
controls.short_summary: Maintain a complete, owner-assigned inventory of information, IT, and cloud assets.
controls.plain_english_summary: Develop and maintain an accurate inventory of information and other associated assets—including hardware, software, cloud subscriptions, databases, and key repositories—with a clearly assigned owner for each asset. Keep the inventory current through asset lifecycle workflows and periodic reconciliation.
controls.why_it_matters: You cannot protect, patch, classify, or recover assets you do not know exist. Incomplete asset registers routinely expose organisations to shadow SaaS breaches, orphaned cloud buckets, and audit sampling failures across nearly every other Annex A control.
key_deliverables: Master information and associated asset inventory (CMDB/register)
Cloud and SaaS application register with assigned owners
Asset criticality and lifecycle onboarding/decommissioning procedure
Annual asset inventory reconciliation and owner attestation report
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors reconcile the asset inventory against live MDM, cloud consoles, IDP app catalogues, and finance SaaS spend to spot unrecorded systems. The #1 trap is maintaining a static spreadsheet of laptops while omitting cloud workloads, SaaS applications, and primary data stores—or leaving owner fields blank.

questions.question: Provide your complete inventory of information and associated assets—including endpoints, servers, applications, data stores, and cloud/SaaS services—with assigned owners.
questions.guidance: Confirm the inventory covers information repositories as well as physical and virtual IT assets, software, and third-party SaaS platforms within ISMS scope. Each entry should identify asset type, location or environment, classification/criticality, and a named individual owner.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample live endpoints, cloud accounts, and SSO-connected SaaS tools and trace them back into the inventory to verify completeness and accurate ownership.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A consolidated register—or linked authoritative registers covering MDM, cloud inventory, SaaS catalogues, and data maps—records every in-scope asset. Each record captures a named human owner, criticality tier, and current lifecycle status.
questions.red_flags: The inventory tracks laptops only while ignoring SaaS apps and data stores, lists generic team names as owners, or includes decommissioned servers still marked active.
questions.nc_pattern: No maintained inventory of in-scope information and associated assets exists, or significant classes of operational assets (such as cloud services or key data stores) lack ownership and visibility.

questions.question: Provide the criteria used to determine asset criticality and explain how new, changed, and cloud-hosted assets are captured into the inventory.
questions.guidance: Check how criticality aligns with business impact, data sensitivity, and availability needs (feeding directly into risk and continuity planning). Confirm how procurement, change management, or automated discovery tools (such as MDM, EDR, cloud posture, or SSO telemetry) prevent shadow IT drift.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect criticality rating definitions and test how a recently onboarded laptop or SaaS tool entered the inventory; note that automated discovery is good practice for scale, not a strict ISO requirement for small estates where disciplined manual workflows operate.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Clear criticality criteria rate assets by confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact so high-criticality systems receive commensurate controls. Onboarding, procurement, and—where proportionate—automated discovery feeds keep the register synchronised with live infrastructure.
questions.red_flags: Every asset is labelled 'High' or left unrated, or new cloud resources and SaaS subscriptions are routinely spun up without entering the inventory.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of an effective lifecycle mechanism to maintain inventory accuracy as assets are acquired, changed, or retired, leading to material inventory drift.

questions.question: Provide evidence of periodic asset inventory review and reconciliation completed within the last 12 months.
questions.guidance: Inspect formal review records showing that asset owners verified their assigned assets, resolved discrepancies against live discovery or finance records, and removed retired items.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify review dates, reconciliation exception counts, and evidence that stale or orphaned entries identified during the review were actually cleaned up.
questions.what_good_looks_like: At least annually, the organisation reconciles its asset inventory against MDM, cloud consoles, IDP catalogues, and expense records, obtaining owner sign-off and resolving unowned or decommissioned entries.
questions.red_flags: The inventory spreadsheet has not been edited for over a year, or review sign-offs occurred without checking live systems.
questions.nc_pattern: Asset inventory is not periodically reviewed and maintained, resulting in materially inaccurate or outdated asset records.

controls.control_name: Acceptable use of information and other associated assets
controls.short_summary: Define, communicate, and enforce acceptable use and handling rules for assets.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish, document, and implement clear rules governing the acceptable use and secure handling of organisational information, devices, networks, and cloud services—including generative AI and personal device boundaries. Personnel and external users must acknowledge these rules, and breaches must be addressed consistently.
controls.why_it_matters: Clear acceptable use boundaries protect against data leakage to unsanctioned cloud or AI tools, misuse of corporate endpoints, and legal ambiguity when investigating misconduct. Without defined handling rules linked to classification tiers, staff improvise risky workarounds.
key_deliverables: Acceptable Use Policy (covering devices, email, web, cloud, and AI tools)
Classification-aligned information handling matrix
User acceptable-use acknowledgement logs
Records of acceptable-use monitoring and violation handling
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that acceptable use rules reflect modern workplace realities—such as remote working, cloud storage, and generative AI—and align cleanly with the classification scheme. The top trap is publishing a decade-old AUP that never addresses SaaS uploads or personal devices and has no link to enforcement records.

questions.question: Provide your documented acceptable use policy and information handling procedures aligned to your information classification levels.
questions.guidance: Verify that rules address corporate and permitted personal devices (BYOD), email and internet usage, unsanctioned SaaS/shadow IT, generative AI tools, removable media, and concrete handling requirements (storage, sharing, printing, disposal) for each classification tier.
questions.auditor_focus: Check consistency between the Acceptable Use Policy, the Classification Scheme (5.12), and Remote Working rules (6.7), confirming approval and currency.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved, plain-language Acceptable Use Policy sets clear dos and don'ts across devices, networks, cloud apps, and AI tools, paired with a quick-reference handling matrix tied directly to each information classification tier.
questions.red_flags: Acceptable use rules omit cloud storage, personal devices, or AI tools, contradict the classification policy, or provide no practical handling guidance by sensitivity level.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to identify, document, and implement rules for the acceptable use and procedures for handling information and other associated assets.

questions.question: Provide evidence of user acknowledgement, proportional monitoring of acceptable use, and consistent handling of acceptable use violations.
questions.guidance: Inspect AUP acknowledgement records alongside proportionate technical or procedural controls (such as web filtering, DLP alerts, or cloud app controls) and HR/security workflows for responding to confirmed breaches.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify acknowledgement coverage across staff and contractors, confirm monitoring aligns with privacy/employment notice obligations, and inspect anonymised violation or incident records (or confirmed zero-breach logs).
questions.what_good_looks_like: Personnel acknowledge the Acceptable Use Policy at onboarding and upon material updates. Proportionate controls (such as web filtering or DLP policies) flag high-risk misuse, and confirmed breaches follow a documented escalation and disciplinary workflow.
questions.red_flags: Users never sign or acknowledge acceptable use rules, monitoring alerts are ignored, or confirmed misuse is handled inconsistently without documentation.
questions.nc_pattern: Acceptable use rules are not communicated to users or are not enforced when known policy violations occur.

controls.short_summary: Track, verify, and reclaim physical and digital assets on offboarding.
controls.plain_english_summary: Require employees and contractors to return all organisational assets in their possession—including laptops, mobile devices, security tokens, access cards, keys, and stored corporate data—upon termination or change of employment or contract. Reconcile returned items against the asset register and apply immediate technical containment such as remote wipe when physical recovery is delayed or impossible.
controls.why_it_matters: Unreturned laptops, access passes, and synced files represent an immediate data exposure and physical entry risk, especially in remote or hybrid workforces. Clean offboarding reconciliation also protects the organisation against asset loss and licence waste.
key_deliverables: Offboarding and role-change asset return procedure (staff and contractors)
Asset return checklist reconciled against the asset register
Signed/logged return receipts, courier tracking, and remote-wipe records
Escalation procedure and incident records for unreturned or lost assets
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors pull a sample of recent employee and contractor leavers from HR and reconcile them directly against asset return logs and MDM device status. The #1 trap is forgetting contractors or remote workers whose laptops remain marked 'active' in MDM months after departure with no remote wipe or escalation record.

questions.question: Provide your documented asset return procedure covering employees and contractors at offboarding or role change, including in-scope asset types and escalation or remote-wipe steps for unreturned items.
questions.guidance: Verify the procedure covers physical hardware (laptops, phones, monitors, hardware tokens, swipe cards, keys), removable media, and corporate information stored on permitted personal devices (BYOD wipe/removal). Ensure contractor agreements and vendor offboarding workflows are explicitly included.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm clear ownership between HR, IT, facilities, and line managers, defined return timeframes, and mandatory technical containment (device lock, remote wipe, token revocation) if an asset is not returned on time.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented offboarding procedure applies equally to staff and contractors, listing every tracked asset class against the master inventory. Clear timelines govern courier collection for remote leavers, and overdue or unrecoverable devices trigger immediate MDM lock/remote wipe, badge deactivation, and formal incident escalation.
questions.red_flags: Asset return covers only laptops while ignoring access badges, hardware MFA keys, or BYOD corporate containers; contractors are omitted; or no remote-wipe fallback exists for non-returns.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a formal process to ensure personnel and external users return all organisational assets upon change or termination of employment or engagement.

questions.question: Provide completed asset return verification records for recent employee and contractor departures, including reconciliation against the asset inventory and containment records for any unreturned devices.
questions.guidance: Review closed offboarding tickets, signed handover receipts or courier delivery confirmations, inventory status updates, and MDM wipe logs or loss incident reports for sampled leavers over the past 12 months.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check HR termination lists against IT asset return tickets to detect silent gaps—especially involuntary terminations, remote staff, and short-term contractors.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Each sampled leaver has a closed offboarding ticket reconciling every asset assigned in the register against verified return receipts, updated inventory state, and secure sanitisation prior to reuse. Any unreturned items show timely MDM wipe logs and escalated incident records.
questions.red_flags: Offboarding tickets are closed without confirming physical receipt, former employees' devices still check into MDM, or unreturned laptops have no documented follow-up.
questions.nc_pattern: Departing personnel or contractors retain organisational assets without verified return, containment (such as remote wipe), or inventory reconciliation.

controls.short_summary: Classify information by sensitivity, criticality, and legal or privacy obligations.
controls.plain_english_summary: Classify information according to the organisation's security needs based on confidentiality, integrity, availability, and relevant legal, regulatory, and privacy obligations. Keep the scheme simple enough for staff to apply reliably, assign clear classification responsibility to information owners, and review classifications as value or sensitivity changes over time.
controls.why_it_matters: Classification determines which controls—encryption, DLP, access approval, backup priority, and retention—apply to each dataset. Without clear tiers, organisations either over-protect trivial files or leave regulated personal and financial data exposed.
key_deliverables: Information Classification Policy and tier definitions
Examples table mapping business data, PII, and regulated records to tiers
Classified data repository or information asset register
Periodic classification review and reclassification records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that the classification scheme addresses integrity, availability, and privacy requirements—not just confidentiality—and that real repositories are actually classified accordingly. The #1 trap is designing an overly complex 6-tier military-style scheme that staff ignore, or omitting privacy/PII mapping.

questions.question: Provide your information classification scheme showing how confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy/legal requirements are addressed, and who is responsible for classifying information.
questions.guidance: Check that the scheme defines a practical number of tiers (commonly 3–4, such as Public, Internal, Confidential, Highly Confidential/Restricted) with concrete business examples, explicitly incorporates personal information/privacy and regulatory records, addresses integrity and availability criticality, and assigns classification accountability to information owners.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the policy for practical usability, alignment with legal/privacy obligations (such as Australian Privacy Principles or sector secrecy rules), and unambiguous owner accountability.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved 3- or 4-tier classification scheme defines clear criteria and relatable examples covering confidentiality, integrity, availability, and personal/regulated data. Information owners are formally responsible for classifying datasets at creation, with default classification rules applied when unspecified.
questions.red_flags: Classification covers confidentiality only while ignoring integrity/availability or PII, no default tier exists, or ownership for classifying information is undefined.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to establish a documented information classification scheme reflecting confidentiality, integrity, availability, and relevant interested-party or legal requirements.

questions.question: Provide evidence that key information assets and repositories are classified in practice and periodically reviewed for reclassification when sensitivity or regulatory obligations change.
questions.guidance: Inspect the information asset register, data inventory, or repository metadata to confirm classifications have been applied to core systems and data stores, and check how classifications are updated upon public release, archival, legal change, or periodic owner review.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample key repositories (such as HR, customer databases, finance folders, and source code) to confirm documented classification levels match policy definitions and show periodic owner review.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All primary data stores and document repositories carry documented classification tiers reviewed annually by asset owners. Reclassification events—such as declassifying embargoed reports upon publication or elevating datasets after adding personal data—are logged cleanly.
questions.red_flags: The classification policy exists on paper, but core databases and shared drives have never been classified or reviewed since creation.
questions.nc_pattern: Information classification scheme is not applied to organisational information assets or maintained as sensitivity and business requirements evolve.

controls.short_summary: Apply visual and metadata labels matching information classification tiers.
controls.plain_english_summary: Develop and implement practical procedures for labelling information—across electronic documents, emails, collaboration workspaces, and physical media—in alignment with the organisation's classification scheme. Consistent visual and metadata labels ensure both staff and automated protection tools recognise sensitive information before it is shared or moved.
controls.why_it_matters: Classification only prevents mistakes when users and security tools can immediately see how sensitive a file or email is. Metadata labels also enable DLP, encryption, and retention rules to fire automatically instead of relying purely on human memory.
key_deliverables: Information labelling procedure (electronic, email, and physical media)
Sensitivity label configuration (e.g., Microsoft Purview or Google Workspace labels)
Sampled labelled documents, emails, and physical media records
Staff labelling guidance and awareness training records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors ask staff to open recent confidential documents and emails live to verify that labels defined in policy actually appear in practice. The #1 trap is writing detailed labelling rules—including physical stamping—that no one follows because sensitivity labels were never enabled in the productivity suite.

questions.question: Provide your information labelling procedures and technical configuration showing how electronic files, emails, repositories, and physical media are labelled in alignment with your classification scheme.
questions.guidance: Check that labelling formats match the exact tier names in the classification policy (5.12) across electronic documents, emails, shared workspaces, and any physical printouts or removable media in scope. Document any automated or default sensitivity labelling configurations where deployed.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm alignment between policy tier names and actual system labels (e.g., Purview/Workspace/Confluence labels) and verify whether physical labelling rules are realistic for the organisation's office footprint.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Labelling procedures specify clear visual headers/footers and metadata tags matching the classification tiers for documents, emails, collaboration spaces, and physical media. Where productivity platforms support native sensitivity labels, default and mandatory labelling rules are configured and documented.
questions.red_flags: Labelling tier names differ from the classification policy, physical labelling rules contradict paperless workflows without clarification, or sensitivity labelling features sit disabled.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to develop and implement an appropriate set of procedures for information labelling aligned with the organisation's classification scheme.

questions.question: Provide operating evidence of applied labels across sampled electronic documents, emails, and applicable physical outputs, supported by staff guidance and awareness.
questions.guidance: Collect representative redacted samples of labelled confidential files, outbound emails, and—if physical media or printouts are used—physical labelling examples, alongside onboarding or refresher training showing staff know how to choose and apply labels.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect real day-to-day outputs (not solely pre-staged audit samples) and verify staff understand when to escalate or override default labels; note that automated ML-based classification is a maturity enhancement, not a mandatory ISO requirement.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Sampled documents, emails, and repositories display consistent sensitivity labels matching their content. Staff complete practical guidance on applying labels accurately during onboarding and annual refreshers.
questions.red_flags: Confidential board packs, HR spreadsheets, or client exports carry no labels at all, or interviewed staff do not know how to apply labels in their daily tools.
questions.nc_pattern: Established information labelling procedures are not followed in practice across sensitive operational documents, communications, or in-scope physical outputs.

controls.short_summary: Protect information in transit using approved channels, encryption, and agreements.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish rules, procedures, and agreements to protect information during electronic, physical, and verbal transfer within the organisation and with external parties. Define approved encrypted transfer channels by classification tier, control removable media movement, and formalise security responsibilities in external transfer agreements.
controls.why_it_matters: Data in transit—via misaddressed emails, unencrypted spreadsheets, ad-hoc file-sharing links, or lost USB drives—remains one of the leading causes of notifiable data breaches. Structured transfer rules and third-party agreements establish clear accountability across organisational boundaries.
key_deliverables: Information Transfer Policy and approved secure channel matrix
Technical controls for encrypted transfer (TLS, SFTP, secure portals, USB restrictions)
External data transfer agreements and confidentiality schedules
Sampled transfer authorisation, audit, and encryption verification logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace how sensitive files actually leave the organisation—checking email encryption, managed file transfer portals, APIs, and USB controls—rather than relying on policy prose. The #1 trap is prohibiting unencrypted email attachments in policy while finance or HR still emails unencrypted payroll or client CSVs externally.

questions.question: Provide your information transfer policy and approved secure transfer mechanisms covering electronic channels, physical transit, and removable media controls.
questions.guidance: Verify that rules specify approved mechanisms by classification level (such as enforced TLS, SFTP, encrypted portals, authenticated APIs, and tamper-evident couriers), prohibit unsanctioned consumer file-sharing tools, and either block or enforce hardware encryption and approval for removable media.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect both the policy matrix and technical configurations (email TLS enforcement, endpoint USB blocking/encryption settings, and approved MFT/portal tools).
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved Information Transfer Policy defines permitted transfer channels for each classification tier, backed by technical safeguards including enforced TLS, authenticated SFTP or secure client portals, and endpoint controls blocking unencrypted removable media.
questions.red_flags: Staff regularly use personal file-sharing sites or unencrypted USB sticks, or policy provides no guidance on secure external file exchange.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented rules and implemented controls protecting information during electronic, physical, or removable-media transfer.

questions.question: Provide evidence of executed information transfer agreements or contractual security schedules governing regular or sensitive data exchanges with external parties.
questions.guidance: Check data processing agreements, supplier schedules, or interconnection agreements defining transmission security, custody handoff, breach notification, legal jurisdiction, and return or destruction obligations.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample active external data feeds, B2B integrations, or managed service exchanges and verify signed agreements exist specifying each party's security obligations.
questions.what_good_looks_like: External parties receiving or exchanging confidential or personal information operate under executed transfer agreements or contractual data-protection schedules specifying encryption standards, custody boundaries, incident notification, and permitted use.
questions.red_flags: Recurring sensitive data extracts are sent to external partners or contractors with no written security or confidentiality terms governing the transfer.
questions.nc_pattern: Sensitive information is routinely transferred to external parties without documented agreements defining security and handling responsibilities.

questions.question: Provide operating evidence showing that confidential external information transfers use approved encrypted mechanisms with appropriate authorisation and traceability.
questions.guidance: Inspect transfer logs from SFTP/managed file transfer platforms, encrypted portal audit trails, or DLP/outbound mail records confirming confidential transfers are authorised, encrypted, and traceable.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent external transmissions of confidential or regulated datasets to confirm they followed approved channels rather than ad-hoc unencrypted email attachments.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Sampled confidential external transfers show use of approved encrypted portals, SFTP, or protected email channels with recipient verification, expiry controls on shared links, and retained audit logs.
questions.red_flags: Public anonymous sharing links remain open indefinitely, passwords for encrypted archives are sent in the same email thread, or no audit trail exists for sensitive bulk exports.
questions.nc_pattern: Confidential information is transferred externally via unapproved or unprotected channels in breach of stated information transfer rules.

controls.short_summary: Establish least-privilege, need-to-know rules governing physical and logical access.
controls.plain_english_summary: Define and implement business-driven access control rules governing physical and logical access to information and associated assets based on need-to-know and least privilege. Translate those rules into structured role- or attribute-based access models (RBAC/ABAC) so permissions are granted consistently rather than ad hoc.
controls.why_it_matters: Access control rules are the blueprint behind every permission grant; without clear least-privilege and role standards, entitlements sprawl quickly and increase the blast radius of compromised credentials. Clear rule design also separates policy intent (5.15) from identity lifecycle (5.16), credentials (5.17), and operational provisioning/reviews (5.18).
key_deliverables: Topic-specific Access Control Policy (physical and logical scope)
RBAC/ABAC role definition catalogue and permission baselines
Least-privilege and deny-by-default rule configurations
Physical-to-logical access governance alignment documentation
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that access rules enforce deny-by-default and least privilege across both logical systems and physical zones—not just one or the other. The #1 trap is relying on 'copy permissions from an existing colleague' instead of defined RBAC baselines, which silently propagates legacy over-privileged access.

questions.question: Provide your access control policy defining business-driven access rules, need-to-know, least privilege, role/attribute-based access models (RBAC/ABAC), and coordination of physical and logical access.
questions.guidance: Check that the policy establishes default-deny principles, distinguishes standard versus privileged and external access, defines who owns access rules per asset, and coordinates physical facility access rules with logical identity status.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm executive approval, alignment with asset classification (5.12) and segregation of duties (5.3), and clear linkages to operational provisioning (5.18) and physical entry (7.2).
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved Access Control Policy codifies need-to-know, least privilege, default-deny access, and structured RBAC/ABAC rules across applications, infrastructure, cloud tenants, and physical zones. Physical and logical access rules share consistent risk tiers and lifecycle governance.
questions.red_flags: Access rules default to broad 'all-staff' access, physical access rules are completely disconnected from logical access governance, or no distinction exists between standard and privileged access rules.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented business and information security rules controlling physical and logical access to information and other associated assets.

questions.question: Provide evidence that least-privilege and RBAC/ABAC access control rules are implemented as enforceable permission baselines across core systems and aligned with access monitoring.
questions.guidance: Focus on how access rules are engineered into identity provider groups, application roles, cloud IAM policies, and physical access zones—distinct from individual provisioning tickets and periodic recertifications (assessed under 5.18) or detailed log management (8.15). Check that role baselines prevent wildcard or 'clone-a-user' permission creep.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect RBAC role matrices, cloud IAM policy statements, and group permission mappings for excessive wildcards, default-allow rules, or unaligned physical/logical access groups.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Core systems enforce documented RBAC or ABAC permission sets mapped to job functions, with deny-by-default baselines and scoped cloud IAM policies. Access control decisions generate audit events routed into central monitoring (8.15), and physical zone groups mirror authorised job roles.
questions.red_flags: New users are routinely provisioned by copying an arbitrary peer's account, cloud IAM policies grant wildcard administrative access to standard roles, or shared drives are open to 'Everyone'.
questions.nc_pattern: Access control rules are not translated into enforced least-privilege permission structures, resulting in systemic over-privileged or default-open access.

controls.short_summary: Manage unique human and non-human identities across their complete lifecycle.
controls.plain_english_summary: Manage the full lifecycle of all human and non-human (service, API, and machine) identities from identity verification and unique ID issuance through role transitions to timely disablement and retirement. Prohibit casual account sharing, govern unavoidable generic or break-glass identities tightly, and regularly clear dormant accounts.
controls.why_it_matters: Unique, verified identities are the foundation of individual accountability and forensic audit trails. Orphaned contractor accounts, unmanaged service accounts, and shared logins destroy attribution and give attackers persistent footholds.
key_deliverables: Identity Lifecycle Management Procedure (joiner, mover, leaver, non-human)
Pre-creation identity verification records
Register of shared, generic, emergency, and non-human/service identities
Identity deactivation logs and dormant account cleanup reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check unique attribution (one person, one ID), service account ownership, and dormant account reports alongside leaver disablement timestamps. The #1 trap is tightly controlling employee accounts via HR-to-IDP sync while leaving third-party contractor accounts, local admin logins, or legacy service identities completely unmanaged.

questions.question: Provide your identity lifecycle management process covering pre-creation identity verification, unique ID issuance, joiner/mover/leaver identity transitions, and non-human identity governance.
questions.guidance: Verify that every human user receives a unique, non-reused identifier only after identity verification (via HR onboarding or contractor vetting), that identity attributes update cleanly on transfers or status changes, and that service/machine identities follow formal creation and expiry rules.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect identity onboarding and verification records for both employees and external users, and confirm how HR or sponsor status changes trigger identity updates across directories.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented identity lifecycle process ties unique user ID creation to verified HR or contractor sponsorship records, forbids ID reuse, and synchronises role or status transitions from an authoritative source of truth. Non-human and service identities require formal request, named human ownership, and lifecycle review.
questions.red_flags: Accounts are created on informal chat requests without identity verification, departing users' IDs are reassigned to replacements, or contractor accounts have no expiry dates or sponsors.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to manage the full lifecycle of user and non-human identities, including unique attribution and identity verification prior to account issuance.

questions.question: Provide your register and governance controls for shared, generic, break-glass, and non-human/service identities.
questions.guidance: Confirm that shared human logins are prohibited unless technically unavoidable, and that any permitted generic, emergency break-glass, or service accounts have documented justification, a named custodian, restricted interactive login, and individual attribution via PAM checkout or session logging.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the directory for uninventoried generic accounts (such as 'admin', 'support', or 'finance-shared') and verify whether interactive shared logins lack individual accountability.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An up-to-date register records every approved non-human, service, and break-glass identity with its business purpose, named human owner, and review date. Shared interactive human accounts are prohibited, and emergency break-glass accounts are vaulted with alerted checkout and individual attribution.
questions.red_flags: Multiple staff share a single generic admin or SaaS login without attribution, or dozens of legacy service accounts exist with unknown owners.
questions.nc_pattern: Uncontrolled use of shared or generic accounts that prevents individual accountability, or unowned non-human identities operating without lifecycle governance.

questions.question: Provide operating evidence of timely identity deactivation upon departure and regular detection and disablement of dormant or orphaned identities.
questions.guidance: Focus on identity state hygiene (disabling/archiving the directory identity itself and cleaning up inactive accounts after a defined threshold such as 30–90 days), complementing application-level entitlement revocation assessed under 5.18.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect automated or scheduled dormant-account reports and reconcile recent leaver lists against active directory, SSO, and standalone identity stores to catch orphaned accounts.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Directory identities are disabled automatically or within defined termination SLAs upon departure, and scheduled inactivity checks disable dormant human and contractor identities after defined thresholds (for example, 45–90 days) with documented review.
questions.red_flags: Accounts inactive for over 180 days remain enabled, or former contractors still hold active identities in standalone cloud or VPN directories.
questions.nc_pattern: Terminated or dormant identities remain active beyond stated organisational thresholds, creating unmanaged access pathways.

controls.short_summary: Govern secure issuance, enrolment, reset, and protection of credentials.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control the allocation, enrolment, reset, and protection of authentication information—including passwords, passkeys, MFA tokens, cryptographic keys, and API secrets—through formal management processes and clear user responsibilities. Ensure initial credentials are delivered securely, resets verify identity robustly, and users know how to safeguard credentials against phishing and reuse.
controls.why_it_matters: Weak credential handling—such as emailing temporary passwords in clear text, allowing helpdesk resets without identity verification, or tolerating password reuse—undermines even strong technical authentication systems. Keeping 5.17 focused on the credential and secret management lifecycle cleanly complements technical authentication enforcement in 8.5.
key_deliverables: Authentication Information and Secret Management Standard
Secure initial credential issuance and MFA/passkey enrolment procedure
Helpdesk identity-verified password and MFA reset procedure and logs
Credential hygiene and phishing-resistance user awareness records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors test the helpdesk password/MFA reset process and inspect how new hires receive initial credentials and enrol authenticators. The #1 trap is enforcing strong password policies on paper while IT still emails reusable default passwords to new starters or resets MFA over a quick unverified phone call.

questions.question: Provide your authentication information management standard covering password, passkey, MFA authenticator enrolment, API secret handling, and user responsibilities for credential protection.
questions.guidance: Confirm that requirements follow modern credential guidance (for example, long passphrases, breached-password screening, password manager usage, phishing-resistant MFA/passkey enrolment, secret vaulting for API keys, and clear user rules prohibiting sharing or reuse) without duplicating technical system-level MFA enforcement tested under 8.5.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the policy standard, authenticator enrolment lifecycle rules (including lost/replaced device handling), and evidence that staff receive practical training on safeguarding credentials.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved standard governs the full credential lifecycle across passwords, passkeys, MFA tokens, and non-human secrets. It prohibits hardcoded or shared credentials, mandates password managers or secret vaults, and defines authenticator replacement rules supported by annual staff credential-protection guidance.
questions.red_flags: Policy enforces outdated 30-day forced password rotation without complexity/breach checks, omits API keys and MFA token enrolment rules, or fails to educate users on credential phishing and reuse.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented management rules and user obligations governing the secure creation, handling, and protection of authentication information.

questions.question: Provide evidence demonstrating how initial authentication information and MFA authenticators are issued and enrolled securely for new human and service accounts.
questions.guidance: Inspect onboarding procedures and sample recent joiner tickets to confirm temporary credentials are unique, single-use, time-limited, delivered out-of-band (or via secure one-time enrolment links), and force immediate change or passkey/MFA binding on first login.
questions.auditor_focus: Check onboarding tickets and email/chat logs for signs of reusable default passwords, plaintext password emails sent alongside usernames, or unverified MFA enrolment.
questions.what_good_looks_like: New users receive time-limited, single-use enrolment links or out-of-band initial credentials that force immediate secret change and MFA/passkey binding on first sign-in. Default vendor passwords on new infrastructure and applications are changed immediately before deployment.
questions.red_flags: IT sends the same standard welcome password to every new starter in plain email, temporary passwords do not expire, or default device credentials remain unchanged.
questions.nc_pattern: Initial authentication information is distributed insecurely (such as reusable or plaintext credentials without forced change) or default authentication secrets remain active.

questions.question: Provide evidence of your identity-verified password and MFA reset process protecting credential recovery against social engineering.
questions.guidance: Review helpdesk scripts and sampled password or MFA-reset tickets to confirm strong identity verification (such as video verification with photo ID, manager callback, or out-of-band corporate verification) is mandatory and logged before any credential or authenticator is reset.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent password and MFA-reset tickets—especially for privileged users or executives—to verify that identity checks were actually performed and recorded.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Helpdesk and self-service reset workflows enforce documented identity verification—escalating to live video/ID or manager confirmation for MFA resets—with every reset logged and triggering an automatic notification to the affected user.
questions.red_flags: Helpdesk resets passwords or clears MFA tokens based on an unverified phone call or Slack message, or reset tickets contain no record of how caller identity was confirmed.
questions.nc_pattern: Credential or MFA reset processes lack reliable identity verification before issuing replacement authentication information.

controls.short_summary: Provision, review, modify, and revoke access rights with segregated owner approval.
controls.plain_english_summary: Provision, review, modify, and remove access rights to information and associated assets in accordance with the organisation's access control policy and asset-owner authorisation. Segregate access requests from approvals, adjust entitlements promptly when roles change, conduct periodic access reviews, and revoke access swiftly upon termination.
controls.why_it_matters: Access rights naturally accumulate over time as people switch teams or take on temporary projects, creating silent privilege creep and residual leaver exposure. Operational discipline across provisioning, recertification, and revocation is one of the highest-weighted sampling areas in every ISO 27001 and APRA audit.
key_deliverables: Access provisioning and modification ticket records with segregated owner approval
Periodic access rights review (recertification) reports and remediation logs
Leaver access revocation records reconciled against HR termination timestamps
Defined access revocation SLAs covering standard, privileged, and involuntary exits
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors pull three mandatory samples: recent joiners/movers (checking owner approval prior to grant), periodic access review outputs (checking stale access was actually removed), and recent leavers (comparing HR exit timestamps to revocation logs). The #1 trap is completing access reviews in a spreadsheet without ever closing the resulting removal tickets, or missing non-SSO SaaS apps on offboarding.

questions.question: Provide access provisioning and modification records demonstrating formal asset-owner approval segregated from the requester across onboarding, role transfers, and access changes.
questions.guidance: Sample recent joiner, internal transfer (mover), and ad-hoc elevation tickets to confirm that access rights are granted or adjusted only after documented approval by the relevant asset or business owner—never self-approved—and that prior-role entitlements are removed upon transfer.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify timestamps confirming approval occurred before technical provisioning, confirm requester-approver separation, and check mover tickets to verify old permissions were stripped rather than stacked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every sampled access grant or role-change ticket shows a documented business justification, segregated approval from the designated asset owner or manager prior to provisioning, and removal of superseded entitlements when personnel change roles.
questions.red_flags: Administrators grant access via verbal or chat requests without tickets, users can approve their own elevation requests, or internal movers retain access to previous departments indefinitely.
questions.nc_pattern: Access rights are provisioned or modified without documented authorisation from the designated owner or without removing redundant rights upon role change.

questions.question: Provide completed periodic access rights review (recertification) records by business or system owners, including evidence that flagged excessive or stale access was revoked.
questions.guidance: Inspect user access review cycles across critical applications, infrastructure, databases, and privileged groups (typically quarterly for privileged/high-risk access and semi-annually or annually for standard access). Confirm reviewers actively attested each user's appropriateness and that revocations were executed and verified.
questions.auditor_focus: Trace revocations flagged during the most recent review all the way to closed IT tickets and updated user lists, rather than accepting a signed review sheet alone.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Scheduled access recertifications cover all in-scope critical, privileged, and SaaS systems at defined intervals. System owners explicitly approve or revoke each entitlement, and follow-up tickets prove every rejected permission was removed promptly.
questions.red_flags: Access reviews are overdue, rubber-stamped in bulk within seconds, cover only the central directory while omitting critical SaaS or database roles, or leave flagged removals unactioned.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to review access rights at regular intervals or failure to remove unauthorised or unnecessary entitlements identified during reviews.

questions.question: Provide leaver access revocation records reconciling HR termination dates and times against actual entitlement removal across core, privileged, and standalone SaaS systems against defined SLAs.
questions.guidance: Inspect defined revocation SLAs (for example, immediate/prior to notification for involuntary exits and same-day or within 24 hours for standard departures) and sample recent employee and contractor terminations across SSO, VPN, privileged tooling, physical access, and non-SSO applications.
questions.auditor_focus: Compare independent HR leaver lists against system deactivation logs and active SaaS user tables to catch silent lags, delayed HR notifications, or missed standalone accounts.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Clear revocation SLAs differentiate involuntary and voluntary departures, supported by integrated HR-to-IT offboarding checklists covering SSO, privileged accounts, physical badges, and standalone SaaS tools. Sampled termination logs confirm timely removal with zero post-departure logins.
questions.red_flags: HR notifies IT days or weeks after a leaver's final day, contractors are missing from offboarding workflows, or terminated staff still hold active accounts in non-SSO applications.
questions.nc_pattern: Access rights of terminated employees or contractors are not revoked promptly in accordance with defined offboarding procedures and SLAs.

controls.short_summary: Manage supplier information security risks through due diligence and tiering.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish a structured risk framework to identify, assess, and treat information security risks whenever external parties access your systems, data, or premises. Before onboarding a supplier, classify their criticality, complete proportionate security due diligence, and set baseline security and regulatory expectations. This control owns the supplier risk framework and pre-engagement assessment, handing contractual terms to 5.20 and ongoing oversight to 5.22.
controls.why_it_matters: Third-party compromises remain one of the fastest paths to a major data breach or operational outage, and regulators hold the regulated entity accountable even when work is outsourced. Without documented tiering and pre-onboarding checks, critical vendors routinely enter production with unmitigated access and no risk sign-off.
key_deliverables: Supplier Information Security Risk Framework
Critical Supplier and Material Service Provider Register
Pre-Engagement Security Due Diligence Assessments
Supplier Security Tiering Matrix
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors first reconcile your supplier register against accounts payable or SSO integrations to expose shadow vendors, then sample recently onboarded high-risk suppliers for completed due diligence prior to go-live. The most common trap is treating a generic self-assessment questionnaire as sufficient assurance without verifying evidence or documenting risk acceptance.

questions.question: How is your supplier information security risk assessment and due diligence process structured before onboarding?
questions.guidance: Document the end-to-end onboarding workflow showing how procurement triggers security screening, what assessment depth applies to each risk tier, and who holds authority to approve residual risks before a contract is executed. For APRA-regulated entities, ensure due diligence explicitly evaluates the third party's security capability (CPS 234 §16), control design (CPS 234 §22), and concentration or fourth-party dependencies (CPS 230 §53).
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the documented procedure and sample 3–5 recently onboarded suppliers across risk tiers to confirm assessments were completed and signed off prior to granting data or network access.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented supplier risk framework defines clear risk tiers based on data sensitivity, system access, and operational criticality. Procurement gates prevent contract signature or technical onboarding until security due diligence is completed, evidence (such as ISO 27001 certificates or SOC 2 Type II reports) is independently reviewed, and any gaps receive formal risk acceptance.
questions.red_flags: Procurement bypasses security for urgent engagements; due diligence occurs after go-live; assessments rely solely on unverified vendor tick-box questionnaires with no supporting evidence.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a repeatable supplier security risk assessment process, or evidence that high-risk suppliers were granted access to in-scope systems without prior risk evaluation and management approval.

questions.question: Do you maintain a current supplier register with criticality tiering and assigned relationship owners?
questions.guidance: Maintain a central inventory covering every supplier that stores, processes, transmits, or can access organisational information assets, including SaaS platforms, managed service providers, and key contractors. Record risk tier, data classification handled, criticality to operations (including APRA Material Service Provider status under CPS 230 §49–51), business owner, and next review date.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check the supplier register against identity provider SSO applications, firewall/VPN connections, and finance vendor lists to test completeness and verify ownership accuracy.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A centrally maintained supplier register captures all in-scope third parties with consistent criticality ratings, data access profiles, named internal owners, and links to due diligence records. The register is reconciled periodically with procurement and IT asset records so shadow SaaS and retired vendors are promptly identified.
questions.red_flags: Multiple conflicting spreadsheets held by IT and procurement; critical SaaS tools or MSPs missing from the register; departed staff still listed as supplier owners.
questions.nc_pattern: No maintained inventory of suppliers accessing in-scope information or systems, or material omissions that leave critical third-party dependencies unassessed and unmanaged.

questions.question: How are baseline information security and applicable regulatory obligations defined for suppliers before contracting?
questions.guidance: Specify minimum security expectations by supplier tier—covering access control, encryption, incident reporting, data residency, and regulatory flow-down—so procurement and legal know what must be reflected in the agreement under 5.20. Include applicable statutory duties such as Australian Privacy Principles, CPS 234 control expectations, and CPS 230 operational resilience requirements.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that tier-specific security baselines exist and map cleanly to statutory and client obligations identified under 5.31, and confirm exceptions are risk-assessed before contracting.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A structured supplier security baseline maps risk tiers to mandatory technical, operational, and regulatory expectations before commercial negotiation begins. Legal and procurement use this baseline alongside the compliance register to flag non-negotiable statutory obligations and escalate deviations to the risk owner.
questions.red_flags: Security requirements are invented ad hoc per contract; statutory obligations such as privacy or prudential rules are not translated into supplier onboarding criteria; exceptions go undocumented.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to define information security requirements for supplier access to organisational assets, resulting in inconsistent or missing safeguards across third-party engagements.

controls.control_name: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
controls.short_summary: Embed enforceable security, audit, incident, and flow-down clauses in contracts.
controls.plain_english_summary: Translate your supplier security baseline into binding contractual commitments before a supplier handles organisational data or connects to systems. Agreements should specify data protection duties, incident notification timeframes, right-to-audit or independent assurance provisions, termination data return, and subcontractor controls. This control governs contractual terms themselves, distinct from pre-contract risk assessment (5.19) and post-signature monitoring (5.22).
controls.why_it_matters: Security expectations that sit outside the signed contract are legally unenforceable when a breach occurs or a vendor refuses to cooperate. Regulators and certification auditors routinely examine signed agreements to verify that critical obligations—especially breach notification timelines and audit rights—actually bind the supplier.
key_deliverables: Standard Information Security Schedule / Contract Clauses
Executed Supplier Agreements with Security Addenda
Contractual Security Deviation and Risk Acceptance Log
Subcontractor Approval and Flow-Down Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect signed contracts—not just unsigned templates—for a sample of critical suppliers to verify enforceable incident reporting windows, audit rights, and data handling terms. The #1 trap is maintaining polished legal templates that were never retrofitted onto legacy agreements or were quietly deleted during commercial negotiation without risk sign-off.

questions.question: Are standard information security clauses and data protection schedules incorporated into supplier agreements?
questions.guidance: Maintain approved security schedules covering asset protection, confidentiality, acceptable use, access restrictions, encryption, regulatory compliance, and secure data return or deletion upon exit. Where a tier-1 vendor insists on standard click-wrap or vendor paper, document a clause-gap review and obtain formal residual risk acceptance.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the standard security schedule and inspect signed agreements for sampled critical suppliers to confirm security obligations are binding and any material redlines were formally approved.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Legal and security maintain approved contractual security schedules tailored by risk tier, covering confidentiality, data protection, compliance, and exit obligations. Signed agreements for in-scope suppliers incorporate these terms, and any commercial redlines or vendor-paper exceptions are logged with documented risk acceptance.
questions.red_flags: Templates exist on the intranet but sampled signed contracts omit security schedules entirely; legacy critical suppliers operate on expired or informal terms with no security clauses.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope suppliers accessing or processing sensitive organisational assets without documented, agreed information security terms in their contracts.

questions.question: Do supplier agreements establish enforceable incident notification timeframes, right-to-audit clauses, and assurance obligations?
questions.guidance: Contracts should require prompt notification of security incidents affecting organisational data—fast enough to support statutory clocks such as APRA's 72-hour requirement and the OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches scheme—alongside rights to review independent assurance reports (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II) or conduct audits. For APRA Material Service Providers, agreements must include mandatory APRA access and on-site inspection rights under CPS 230 §55 and timely notification triggers under §59.
questions.auditor_focus: Check exact notification windows in sampled signed agreements (for example, 24–48 hours rather than vague 'reasonable time') and confirm contractual rights to obtain annual assurance reports or audit cooperation.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Signed agreements specify concrete incident notification timeframes aligned to organisational statutory clocks, mandate cooperation during investigations, and secure ongoing access to independent assurance reports or audit rights. Where APRA CPS 230 applies, material service provider contracts explicitly embed regulator access and information-provision clauses.
questions.red_flags: Contracts specify 'without undue delay' with no hour cap, or allow 30 days to report breaches; audit clauses are omitted or lack any alternative right to independent SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports.
questions.nc_pattern: Critical supplier agreements lack enforceable incident notification obligations or any mechanism to verify the supplier's ongoing security compliance.

questions.question: How do supplier agreements control subcontracting and enforce security flow-down to fourth parties?
questions.guidance: Require suppliers to disclose sub-processors or material subcontractors that handle organisational data or deliver critical services, obtain prior written consent or provide advance change notice with objection rights, and flow down equivalent security obligations. Ensure the primary supplier remains contractually accountable for subcontractor breaches.
questions.auditor_focus: Examine subcontracting clauses in sampled contracts and verify whether the organisation tracks disclosed sub-processors for its critical suppliers.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Supplier contracts prohibit unapproved subcontracting of in-scope services, mandate equivalent security flow-down clauses, and require advance notice of sub-processor changes. The organisation maintains visibility over material fourth parties and reviews sub-processor updates for concentration or jurisdiction risks.
questions.red_flags: Contracts allow unrestricted subcontracting without notice; no record of which sub-processors hold customer data; primary vendor disclaims liability for fourth-party failures.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to address security requirements for subcontractors within supplier agreements where third parties delegate handling of in-scope organisational information.

controls.control_name: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
controls.short_summary: Mitigate risks across ICT product sourcing, sub-tier components, and updates.
controls.plain_english_summary: Identify and manage information security risks spanning the full ICT supply chain, including hardware, commercial software, cloud infrastructure components, and upstream sub-tier suppliers. Verify the provenance and security posture of acquired ICT products and ensure supplier-delivered updates or patches are authenticated before deployment. This control focuses on technology supply chain integrity and upstream dependencies, complementing general supplier risk management (5.19) and contracting (5.20).
controls.why_it_matters: Modern compromises increasingly target upstream libraries, build pipelines, managed software updates, and sub-tier ICT components rather than an organisation's perimeter directly. Blind reliance on commercial software or unmanaged ICT chains leaves organisations unable to identify exposure rapidly when a supply chain compromise hits.
key_deliverables: ICT Supply Chain Risk Register and Dependency Map
ICT Product Security Evaluation Records
Software Update Authenticity and Integrity Verification Procedure
Supply Chain Incident Response Playbook Integration
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors look for visibility into critical ICT product dependencies and practical controls verifying the authenticity of vendor software, hardware, and updates before production rollout. A common audit pitfall—for both organisations and inexperienced assessors—is treating a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) as a blanket ISO 27001 requirement; SBOMs are valuable good practice for software vendors and high-risk products, not a universal certification mandate.

questions.question: How are ICT supply chain risks, sub-tier dependencies, and supply chain incident scenarios identified and managed?
questions.guidance: Map critical ICT components, platforms, and upstream sub-tier dependencies (such as core libraries, cloud regions, payment gateways, or managed RMM tools) to assess single-point concentration, geopolitical or provenance risk, and end-of-life exposure. Link this dependency map to incident response (5.24) so a compromise at an upstream ICT vendor can be triaged swiftly.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the ICT supply chain risk assessment and dependency records, checking that upstream technology risks feed into the ISMS risk register and incident readiness plans.
questions.what_good_looks_like: The organisation maps critical ICT products and upstream sub-tier dependencies in its risk register, evaluating concentration, lifecycle support, and provenance risks. Supply chain compromise scenarios are factored into vulnerability tracking and incident response playbooks so affected assets can be isolated rapidly.
questions.red_flags: Only tier-1 commercial vendors are tracked with zero awareness of critical upstream ICT components; end-of-life hardware or unsupported software dependencies are absent from risk assessments.
questions.nc_pattern: No systematic process to identify and manage information security risks associated with the ICT products and supply chain supporting in-scope services.

questions.question: How do you evaluate the security of ICT products and software components before adoption?
questions.guidance: Establish repeatable security checks before introducing new commercial software, hardware, or SaaS tooling—such as reviewing vendor vulnerability disclosure policies, secure development attestations, penetration test summaries, and authorised reseller provenance.
