Requesting a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is encouraged as good practice for bespoke or high-risk software vendors, but is not a mandatory ISO 27001 requirement.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent ICT product acquisitions or major component upgrades to confirm security evaluation criteria were applied and documented prior to deployment; never raise a nonconformity solely for lacking an SBOM.
questions.what_good_looks_like: ICT product acquisitions undergo documented security review covering authorised sourcing, vendor vulnerability management maturity, supported lifecycle, and independent security assurance. Where software is developed or procured for high-risk functions, component visibility (including optional SBOMs or dependency scans) supports rapid exposure assessment.
questions.red_flags: Hardware bought from unauthorised grey-market brokers; software tools deployed directly into production without any security review of vendor patching or vulnerability handling.
questions.nc_pattern: ICT products and components are routinely acquired and deployed into in-scope environments without evaluating their security posture, sourcing provenance, or ongoing supportability.

questions.question: How is the authenticity and integrity of supplier-provided software updates, patches, and firmware verified?
questions.guidance: Ensure software packages, OS patches, firmware, and third-party libraries are obtained strictly from official vendor repositories over encrypted channels, with cryptographic signature or checksum verification enforced before installation. Combine integrity verification with staged rollout or change testing (8.32) to contain potentially trojanised updates.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect patch management configurations, package manager settings, or deployment records to confirm digital signature/hash validation and controlled staging are actively enforced.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Standard operating procedures and automated tooling enforce retrieval of updates exclusively from authenticated vendor sources, verify cryptographic signatures or published hashes, and stage updates in non-production environments prior to broad release. Failed integrity checks block deployment and trigger security investigation.
questions.red_flags: Administrators download installers or firmware from unofficial mirrors; signature verification is disabled in package managers; updates auto-deploy directly to critical production servers without validation.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of controls to verify the authenticity and integrity of vendor-supplied software updates, packages, or firmware deployed to in-scope systems.

controls.control_name: Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
controls.short_summary: Monitor supplier security performance, review assurance, and control service changes.
controls.plain_english_summary: Continuously monitor and periodically review supplier service delivery to verify that security obligations remain effective after onboarding, not just at contract signature. Track SLA compliance, independent assurance renewals, supplier incidents, and material fourth-party changes, and assess security impacts whenever a supplier alters services, locations, or architecture. This control owns the post-signature operational lifecycle of supplier security.
controls.why_it_matters: A supplier that passed due diligence two years ago can suffer certificate lapses, key-staff departures, unannounced sub-processor shifts, or deteriorating patching hygiene. Without structured ongoing review and change control, silent drift erodes assurance and breaches APRA CPS 230 §58 monitoring obligations.
key_deliverables: Supplier Security Performance and SLA Monitoring Reports
Annual Supplier Reassessment Schedule and Review Records
Supplier Service Change Assessment Logs
Supplier Incident and Assurance Remediation Tracker
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that annual reviews actually took place for critical suppliers—including reading the contents and caveats of SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports rather than merely filing PDFs—and check how supplier-initiated changes are risk-assessed. The #1 trap is a static onboarding folder that has never been reviewed since the initial contract year.

questions.question: How do you monitor ongoing supplier security performance, incidents, and material fourth-party risk?
questions.guidance: Track supplier security service levels, uptime, vulnerability remediation, security incidents affecting your services, and material fourth-party changes proportionate to supplier tier. For APRA-regulated entities, explicitly embed ongoing monitoring of material service providers and their critical fourth parties under CPS 230 §58, alongside evaluating the sufficiency of third-party control testing under CPS 234 §28.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect service review minutes, supplier security scorecards, and supplier incident tracking logs to verify active operational monitoring and escalation of SLA or control breaches.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Regular service reviews track supplier security KPIs, incident notifications, and fourth-party risk indicators against contractual obligations. Deficiencies or supplier incidents trigger documented corrective action plans, management escalation, and—where unresolved—formal risk re-evaluation.
questions.red_flags: Supplier monitoring is limited to invoice payment; security incidents at critical vendors are not logged or followed up; no visibility into fourth-party changes affecting material services.
questions.nc_pattern: Complete lack of ongoing monitoring or review of security performance and incident handling for critical suppliers delivering in-scope services.

questions.question: Are critical suppliers periodically reassessed on a risk-based schedule and prior to contract renewal?
questions.guidance: Maintain a calendar of periodic reassessments (typically annual for critical/high-risk suppliers and biennial or renewal-based for lower tiers) that reviews fresh ISO 27001 certificates, SOC 2 Type II reports (including complementary user entity controls and qualified opinions), and updated risk ratings. Gate contract renewals on resolving overdue security findings.
questions.auditor_focus: Check the reassessment schedule against completed review records for sampled critical suppliers, verifying that assurance reports are current, within scope, and analysed for exceptions.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A risk-based reassessment schedule drives timely reviews of critical suppliers and gates contract renewals. Reviewers actively examine updated independent assurance reports—noting scope limitations, qualified exceptions, and customer-side controls—and track remediation of open findings.
questions.red_flags: SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates on file are expired or cover a different product/region; PDFs are archived with no evidence anyone read the exceptions; contracts auto-renew without security sign-off.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to conduct planned periodic reviews of critical suppliers' information security posture, leaving expired certifications or known deficiencies unaddressed over multiple audit cycles.

questions.question: How are changes to supplier services, hosting locations, or delivery models assessed and approved?
questions.guidance: Establish a change-review workflow covering supplier-initiated changes—such as migrations to new data centres or offshore jurisdictions, new sub-processors, architectural changes, or expanded data scope—as well as internal changes in how the organisation uses the service. Link offshoring or material outsourcing changes to APRA notification requirements (CPS 230 §59).
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent supplier service changes, scope expansions, or vendor mergers/migrations to confirm security impact assessment and approval occurred before cutover.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Material changes to supplier services, hosting regions, or integrations pass through formal change management and security impact assessment before taking effect. Updated risks are reflected in the supplier register, contracts are varied where needed, and statutory notifications are triggered when offshoring or material scope shifts occur.
questions.red_flags: Suppliers relocate data offshore or expand system privileges without security review; scope creep turns a low-risk tool into a core business platform with no risk re-tiering.
questions.nc_pattern: Material changes to critical supplier services or data-processing scope are implemented without security risk reassessment or controlled approval.

controls.control_name: Information security for use of cloud services
controls.short_summary: Govern cloud acquisition, shared responsibility, configuration posture, and exit.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish end-to-end governance over the acquisition, use, ongoing management, and exit of cloud services (IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS). Clearly delineate shared security responsibilities with each cloud service provider, enforce secure cloud configurations and data protection on the customer side, and maintain tested exit plans for orderly transition and data deletion. Cloud governance relies on independent CSP assurance for underlying infrastructure while holding the organisation strictly accountable for tenant configuration and identity controls.
controls.why_it_matters: Misconfigured cloud storage, over-privileged identities, and unmonitored SaaS tenants are among the leading causes of preventable data exposure. Equally, failing to plan for cloud exit creates severe operational lock-in and can leave sensitive customer data stranded or unverified upon contract termination.
key_deliverables: Cloud Security Policy and Evaluation Criteria
Cloud Shared Responsibility Matrix per Major CSP
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) and Configuration Baselines
Documented Cloud Exit and Data Deletion Plan
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that you understand and enforce your side of the shared responsibility model, monitor cloud configuration drift, review CSP independent assurance (ISO 27001, SOC 2, or IRAP), and have a realistic exit plan. Do not confuse customer and CSP duties—demanding customer-led penetration testing of a hyperscaler's underlying multi-tenant hypervisor is an industry anti-pattern, not an ISO 27001 requirement.

questions.question: How are cloud services evaluated prior to acquisition, and is a shared responsibility matrix documented and validated against CSP assurance?
questions.guidance: Define cloud acquisition criteria covering data sovereignty (e.g., Australian hosting regions), security features, encryption support, regulatory compliance, and independent CSP assurance (such as ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, SOC 2 Type II, or IRAP assessments). Document a concrete shared responsibility matrix for each major cloud platform mapping who owns IAM, network controls, patching, logging, backup, and incident response.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect cloud onboarding records, current CSP assurance review notes (including Complementary User Entity Controls), and the documented shared responsibility matrix for each primary IaaS/PaaS/SaaS platform.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Cloud services are approved against documented security and data-residency criteria before adoption, backed by reviewed CSP independent assurance reports. A tailored shared responsibility matrix for each major provider explicitly assigns customer-side operational duties to named internal teams, closing responsibility gaps.
questions.red_flags: Generic vendor marketing diagrams cited in place of an internal responsibility assignment; business units adopt SaaS platforms without security review; CSP assurance reports are unread or expired.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined security acquisition criteria or undocumented allocation of information security roles and responsibilities between the organisation and its cloud service providers.

questions.question: How are cloud tenant configurations, data protection controls, and ongoing security posture managed and monitored?
questions.guidance: Enforce hardened cloud baselines (such as CIS Benchmarks), least-privilege IAM, MFA, encryption at rest and in transit, private networking or tenant segmentation, and continuous posture monitoring (CSPM or periodic configuration audits). Rely on CSP independent assurance (SOC 2, ISO 27001, IRAP) for underlying hypervisor/multi-tenant isolation—customer-side testing should focus on your own tenant isolation, IAM boundaries, and application security rather than attempting multi-tenant hypervisor penetration testing. Include ongoing CSP and fourth-party monitoring under CPS 230 §58.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect cloud configuration baselines, encryption and public-access block settings, CSPM/audit alerts, and remediation evidence; verify tenant-level segmentation without falsely demanding CSP hypervisor pen-testing.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Customer-managed cloud environments follow documented configuration baselines with automated drift detection, enforced encryption, strict IAM and network boundaries, and central security logging. Posture findings are triaged promptly, and underlying platform isolation is validated through periodic review of the CSP's independent assurance reports.
questions.red_flags: Publicly exposed storage buckets or unencrypted cloud databases; root/global admin accounts lacking phishing-resistant MFA; no alerting on high-severity cloud configuration drift.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to configure, protect, or monitor customer-managed cloud environments in line with organisational security requirements, resulting in unmitigated exposure of in-scope data or administrative planes.

questions.question: Do you maintain a documented cloud exit strategy covering orderly transition, data extraction, and verifiable deletion?
questions.guidance: Maintain practical exit plans for critical cloud services addressing both planned migration and stressed exit (such as CSP insolvency or severe service failure). Specify data export formats, cryptographic key revocation, access de-provisioning, contractual transition assistance, and obtaining written confirmation of data sanitisation from the outgoing provider.
questions.auditor_focus: Review documented exit plans for critical cloud platforms against contractual termination terms and, where cloud services have been retired, inspect evidence of data return, access revocation, and deletion confirmation.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Critical cloud services have realistic, periodically reviewed exit plans detailing data portability, target transition timelines, key and credential revocation, and contractual assistance rights. When a cloud service is decommissioned, data extraction and provider deletion certificates are captured as formal closure records.
questions.red_flags: No exit plan exists for core cloud platforms; proprietary lock-in prevents feasible data export; retired SaaS subscriptions leave historical organisational data unpurged in vendor tenants.
questions.nc_pattern: No defined process or plan for managing the secure termination and exit of critical cloud services, including data retrieval, access revocation, and secure disposal.

controls.control_name: Information security incident management planning and preparation
controls.short_summary: Prepare incident response plans, roles, notification clocks, and regular exercises.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish and maintain the governance, plans, roles, communication paths, and readiness exercises required to respond swiftly and consistently to information security incidents. Define severity classification, escalation authorities, executive and legal coordination, and statutory notification triggers before a crisis hits. This control covers preparation and capability readiness, distinct from event triage (5.25), active response execution (5.26), and post-incident learning (5.27).
controls.why_it_matters: Improvising roles, legal escalation, and regulatory timelines during an active ransomware or data breach event wastes critical containment hours and frequently triggers statutory breaches. Both ISO 27001 auditors and APRA expect tested, actionable response plans with rehearsed 72-hour notification pathways.
key_deliverables: Information Security Incident Response Plan (IRP)
Incident Severity Classification and Escalation Matrix
Statutory Notification Playbook (APRA / OAIC NDB / ACSC)
Incident Response Exercise and Tabletop Test Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that the incident response plan names current roles and out-of-band contact paths, embeds concrete statutory notification clocks, and has been tested recently with documented improvements. The #1 trap is a generic boilerplate plan sitting unopened on SharePoint with outdated staff names and no test evidence in the past 12 months.

questions.question: Do you maintain a documented incident response plan with clear severity classification and assigned response roles?
questions.guidance: Maintain an accessible, version-controlled Incident Response Plan (IRP) stored both online and offline/out-of-band. Define clear severity levels, named primary and backup response roles (incident commander, technical lead, legal, communications, executive sponsor), internal reporting channels, and interfaces with external retainers or MSPs.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the current IRP for completeness, document control, accurate contact rosters, and clear severity definitions, and confirm key personnel know where to access it if corporate IT is unavailable.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved, up-to-date IRP clearly sets out incident lifecycle phases, objective severity tiers, named roles with deputy cover, and out-of-band communications. Copies are accessible offline so responders can execute immediately even during a total identity or network outage.
questions.red_flags: IRP lists former employees or generic mailboxes only; plan is stored solely on an intranet vulnerable to ransomware; roles overlap ambiguously with no single incident commander.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented incident management procedures, defined response responsibilities, or consistent incident classification criteria across the ISMS scope.

questions.question: Does incident planning embed statutory regulatory notification workflows and executive, legal, and communications coordination?
questions.guidance: Map every applicable statutory and contractual reporting obligation into the IRP, including exact clocks, decision-makers, and pre-drafted templates: APRA CPS 234 §35 (72-hour material information security incident notification, including regulator-notified triggers), APRA CPS 230 §32 (72-hour operational risk incident notification), OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) assessment and reporting, ACSC/SOCI reporting where applicable, and customer notification clauses. Clarify how legal privilege, executive briefings, and external communications are coordinated.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect notification matrices and escalation paths to verify statutory clocks are accurate, legal and executive sign-off authorities are explicit, and templates/contacts are ready for immediate use.
questions.what_good_looks_like: The IRP includes a maintained notification matrix mapping every statutory trigger (including 72-hour APRA clocks alongside OAIC NDB thresholds) to accountable approvers and regulator contact channels. Legal, executive, and communications leads operate under defined coordination protocols backed by pre-approved holding templates.
questions.red_flags: IRP omits APRA 72-hour or OAIC NDB notification procedures; legal and communications are engaged only after public disclosure; no clarity on who can authorise external notifications.
questions.nc_pattern: Incident planning fails to address mandatory legal, regulatory, or contractual notification requirements and executive escalation channels relevant to the organisation's operating context.

questions.question: Are incident response plans and mechanisms regularly tested and updated to maintain operational readiness?
questions.guidance: Run realistic exercises—such as executive tabletop simulations, technical breach drills, or joint exercises with key MSPs—at planned intervals (at least annually for APRA-regulated entities under CPS 234 §26) and after major organisational or architectural changes. Capture exercise outcomes and feed gaps into corrective actions and plan revisions.
questions.auditor_focus: Review exercise reports, attendance lists, scenario notes, and resulting IRP updates from the past 12 months to verify testing was substantive rather than a tick-box walkthrough.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Annual (or more frequent) realistic incident exercises involve both technical responders and executive decision-makers, testing escalation, containment, and statutory notification timelines. Post-exercise reports record concrete gaps, assign remediation owners, and result in documented IRP updates.
questions.red_flags: No incident response test conducted within the past year; exercises involve IT only and exclude legal/executive notification decisions; identified gaps are never tracked to closure.
questions.nc_pattern: Incident response plans have not been reviewed or tested to verify operational readiness, or testing gaps remain systematically unaddressed.

controls.control_name: Assessment and decision on information security events
controls.short_summary: Triage security events against clear criteria and document incident decisions.
controls.plain_english_summary: Assess reported or detected information security events consistently to decide whether they represent genuine information security incidents requiring formal response. Apply clear triage rules, severity criteria, and risk-proportionate escalation timelines, and record the rationale behind each assessment decision. Coverage hours and response targets must match organisational risk and operating hours—ISO 27001 does not universally mandate a 24/7 SOC.
controls.why_it_matters: Without structured triage criteria, genuine intrusions are dismissed as routine IT tickets while noisy false positives exhaust responders. Clear decision records also provide essential audit and regulatory evidence demonstrating why an event was escalated or closed without notification.
key_deliverables: Security Event Triage and Classification Procedure
Event Severity and Escalation Criteria Matrix
Event Assessment and Incident Declaration Log
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample recent security alerts and user-reported events (such as suspected phishing or anomalous logins) to verify consistent triage against documented criteria and timely escalation. A frequent false nonconformity is penalising small or moderate-risk organisations for lacking a 24/7 SOC; ISO 27001 requires triage speed and coverage proportionate to the organisation's risk profile.

questions.question: How are security events triaged, classified by severity, and escalated within risk-proportionate timeframes?
questions.guidance: Define objective triage rules and severity criteria (considering asset criticality, data sensitivity, blast radius, and business impact) that distinguish routine alerts or false positives from formal security incidents. Set triage and escalation targets proportionate to organisational risk—whether delivered via business-hours teams with on-call alerting, an MDR/MSSP, or an internal SOC—without treating a 24/7 SOC as a universal ISO 27001 mandate.
questions.auditor_focus: Review triage procedures and escalation matrices, then test sampled alerts and service-desk tickets to confirm severity was applied consistently and escalation met risk-proportionate target timeframes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Clear triage criteria enable analysts plus service-desk staff to evaluate alerts, user reports, and vendor warnings consistently. Escalation targets align with the organisation's risk profile, on-call or MDR coverage, and statutory notification clocks, with measured adherence tracked over time.
questions.red_flags: Security alerts sit unreviewed for days with no defined owner or escalation threshold; service desk resolves suspected account compromises as standard password resets without security triage; severity ratings are applied inconsistently.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined criteria or consistent operational execution to assess security events and decide whether they must be classified and escalated as information security incidents.

questions.question: Are event assessment outcomes and incident classification decisions formally documented for auditability?
questions.guidance: Record key details for every triaged security event in a central ticketing or SIEM/SOAR register: timestamp detected, reporter or alert source, initial analysis, severity rating, rationale for declaring (or not declaring) an incident, decision-maker, and follow-up actions. Accurate timestamps also anchor statutory reporting clocks.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample both escalated incidents and closed false-positive/benign events to verify rationale, timestamps, and approver attribution are preserved and tamper-resistant.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every assessed security event produces a structured ticket or case record capturing detection time, triage evidence, severity classification, the decision to escalate or close, and the responsible analyst's identity. Records are retained securely to support post-incident review, legal defensibility, and audit verification.
questions.red_flags: Triage decisions happen informally in chat threads with no ticket trail; alerts are bulk-closed with no rationale; detection and decision timestamps are missing or overwritten.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to document event assessment outcomes and incident classification decisions, leaving no verifiable record of how security events were evaluated or resolved.

controls.short_summary: Execute containment, eradication, recovery, and notifications during incidents.
controls.plain_english_summary: Respond to confirmed information security incidents in line with documented procedures and playbooks to rapidly contain harm, eradicate root causes, restore affected services safely, and notify required stakeholders. Maintain disciplined operational logs throughout the response and verify systems are clean before returning them to normal production. This control governs active execution during a live incident.
controls.why_it_matters: Delayed or uncoordinated containment allows attackers to escalate privileges, exfiltrate data, or destroy backups, turning a manageable compromise into a business-threatening crisis. Poorly executed recovery without verified eradication also leads to repeat re-compromise.
key_deliverables: Scenario-Specific Incident Response Playbooks
Active Incident Logs and Containment Action Records
Eradication and Clean Recovery Verification Records
Stakeholder and Regulatory Incident Notification Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect real incident tickets from the audit period (or tabletop records if no major incidents occurred) to verify that teams actually followed playbooks, recorded containment actions, verified clean recovery, and met notification deadlines. The #1 trap is closing incidents immediately after a quick reimage without confirming root-cause eradication or documenting stakeholder notifications.

questions.question: Are scenario-specific playbooks and containment actions executed consistently when security incidents occur?
questions.guidance: Maintain practical playbooks for high-likelihood scenarios (such as ransomware, business email compromise, credential theft, cloud exposure, and supplier breach) detailing immediate containment steps—isolating hosts, revoking sessions/tokens, blocking indicators, and preserving volatile evidence. Log every containment action with timestamps and operators.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect playbooks and sample actual incident response records to verify containment steps were executed promptly, followed documented procedures, and preserved evidence rather than destroying it prematurely.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Actionable playbooks guide responders through immediate containment for priority threat scenarios, backed by tested technical controls such as endpoint isolation and identity session revocation. Live incident records show rapid, logged containment actions coordinated by a designated incident lead.
questions.red_flags: Only a high-level policy exists with no technical playbooks; responders lack authority or tooling to isolate compromised accounts or endpoints quickly; containment actions go unrecorded.
questions.nc_pattern: Confirmed information security incidents are handled ad hoc without following documented response procedures or without evidence of timely, controlled containment.

questions.question: How are root-cause eradication and secure system restoration verified before returning systems to normal operation?
questions.guidance: Confirm that threat actor persistence mechanisms (backdoors, rogue accounts, malicious scheduled tasks, or exploited vulnerabilities) are completely removed before rebuilding or restoring from known-good backups. Document recovery validation checks, credential resets, and management approval to exit incident mode.
questions.auditor_focus: Examine closed incident tickets for proof that root causes were eradicated, restored systems were scanned and verified clean, and heightened post-recovery monitoring was applied.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Incident records demonstrate thorough root-cause eradication—patching the entry vector, rotating affected credentials, and verifying clean rebuilds or immutable backup restores—before business sign-off restores production use. Post-recovery monitoring watches closely for signs of attacker return.
questions.red_flags: Infected machines are cleaned superficially and reconnected without credential rotation or vulnerability remediation; backups are restored over compromised environments without confirming backup cleanliness.
questions.nc_pattern: Affected systems are returned to production following an incident without verifying eradication of the compromise or documenting controlled recovery checks.

questions.question: How are internal stakeholders, affected customers, and regulators notified during active incidents?
questions.guidance: Execute timely, approved communications throughout an active incident—keeping executives, legal, IT, and affected business owners informed, while meeting statutory and contractual notification clocks such as APRA CPS 234 §35 (72 hours), APRA CPS 230 §32 (72 hours) and §42 (24-hour tolerance breach), and OAIC NDB obligations. Retain copies of all formal notices and submission timestamps.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect incident communication logs and any regulatory or customer notifications issued during the audit period (or simulated in exercises) to verify adherence to approved escalation paths and statutory timelines.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Structured status briefings keep executives aligned with response teams throughout active incidents. External notifications to regulators, customers, or partners are issued accurately within statutory and contractual timeframes, with full copies, approvals, and dispatch timestamps retained in the incident record.
questions.red_flags: Regulators or affected customers are notified late or learn of a breach externally; conflicting ad hoc emails are sent by staff without legal or executive approval; no log of external notifications sent.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to execute required internal, contractual, or statutory incident notifications in accordance with documented incident response procedures.

controls.short_summary: Conduct post-incident reviews, track fixes, and feed insights into controls.
controls.plain_english_summary: Use knowledge gained from information security incidents—and relevant near-misses or external peer incidents—to strengthen controls and reduce the likelihood or impact of future occurrences. Conduct structured post-incident reviews, identify systemic root causes, track remediation actions to verified completion, and share practical lessons across relevant teams and governance forums.
controls.why_it_matters: Organisations that rush back to business-as-usual after closing an incident routinely suffer repeat compromises through the same architectural or procedural gap. Turning incidents into measurable control improvements is also a core pillar of ISMS continual improvement and APRA CPS 234 §24.
key_deliverables: Post-Incident Review (PIR) Reports
Incident Corrective Action and Remediation Register
Periodic Incident Trend Analysis Reports
Security Awareness and Control Update Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace closed high-severity incidents through to completed post-incident reviews and verify that resulting remediation tasks were genuinely implemented and closed—not merely listed in a slide deck. The #1 trap is writing thoughtful post-mortems whose recommended control changes are never transferred into the corrective action register or risk assessment.

questions.question: Are structured post-incident reviews conducted and resulting corrective actions tracked to verified completion?
questions.guidance: Define clear thresholds for mandatory post-incident reviews (covering all high/critical incidents, significant near-misses, and repeat medium incidents) within a set window after closure. Analyse timeline, detection gaps, response effectiveness, and root causes, then log concrete actions with owners, due dates, and verification evidence in the corrective action or ISMS improvement register.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample closed incidents from the past 12 months to verify PIRs were completed on time, root causes were identified objectively, and every resulting action item was tracked through to closure.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Blameless, structured post-incident reviews examine detection, containment, and root causes promptly after significant incidents. Resulting control, process, and risk-register updates are entered into the central corrective action tracker with assigned owners, target dates, and independent closure verification.
questions.red_flags: PIRs are skipped once systems are restored; reports blame individual staff rather than systemic control gaps; action items remain open indefinitely with no ownership or follow-up.
questions.nc_pattern: No structured process to review information security incidents for lessons learned, or repeated failure to implement and verify corrective actions arising from past incidents.

questions.question: How are incident trends, near-misses, and external threat learnings analysed and used to strengthen controls and awareness?
questions.guidance: Aggregate incident and near-miss metrics periodically (for example, quarterly or ahead of management review) to spot recurring patterns such as phishing vectors, misconfiguration themes, or vendor failures. Incorporate relevant external sector incidents (such as ACSC advisories or peer breaches) into risk assessments, playbook refinements, and targeted staff awareness briefings.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect management review inputs, quarterly security metrics, updated playbooks or training modules, and risk register adjustments that demonstrate incident trends actively inform ISMS improvements.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Periodic trend analysis combines internal incidents, near-misses, and relevant industry breaches to highlight systemic weaknesses for leadership review. Insights directly drive updates to risk assessments, technical detection rules, operating procedures, and staff awareness materials.
questions.red_flags: Incidents are reviewed purely in isolation with no trend tracking; recurring phishing or access-control incidents never trigger awareness or control redesign; management review receives raw ticket counts with no root-cause themes.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to analyse recurring incident patterns or feed incident knowledge back into ISMS risk management, controls, and organisational awareness.

controls.short_summary: Preserve forensically sound evidence with integrity and chain of custody.
controls.plain_english_summary: Establish procedures to identify, collect, acquire, and preserve digital and physical evidence relating to information security events so it remains admissible and reliable for legal, regulatory, insurance, or disciplinary proceedings. Protect evidence integrity through cryptographic hashing, write-protected storage, and documented chain-of-custody logs, backed by trained responders or specialist forensic retainers.
controls.why_it_matters: Well-intentioned IT staff routinely destroy critical forensic artefacts by rebooting compromised hosts, overwriting logs, or copying files casually without hashing. Compromised evidence integrity can invalidate legal action, derail regulatory investigations, or undermine cyber insurance claims.
key_deliverables: Digital Evidence Collection and Preservation Procedure
Chain-of-Custody Log Templates and Completed Records
Forensic Readiness and External DFIR Retainer Details
Responder Evidence-Handling Briefing Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify documented evidence-handling procedures covering order of volatility, hashing, secure storage, and chain of custody, plus practical readiness (trained staff or a pre-arranged DFIR retainer). The #1 trap is writing a textbook forensic procedure that first-line IT admins have never seen, leading them to wipe laptops before evidence is captured.

questions.question: Do documented procedures govern evidence identification, forensically sound collection, integrity protection, and chain of custody?
questions.guidance: Specify step-by-step handling rules covering volatile data capture (memory, active sessions, cloud audit logs), read-only acquisition, cryptographic hashing (e.g., SHA-256) at collection, tamper-evident/access-controlled storage, and a formal chain-of-custody log recording every custodian transfer, date, time, and purpose. Align procedures with applicable Australian evidentiary standards.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the evidence-handling procedure and chain-of-custody template, and review any actual evidence logs from recent incidents or exercises to confirm integrity hashes and custody transfers were recorded.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Clear evidence collection procedures cover order of volatility, immutable log export, cryptographic hash generation at acquisition, encrypted access-restricted storage, and mandatory chain-of-custody logs. Procedures align with legal counsel requirements so collected artefacts withstand regulatory or courtroom scrutiny.
questions.red_flags: No chain-of-custody form exists; responders copy files onto shared drives without hashing or access controls; volatile cloud or endpoint logs expire before acquisition.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented procedures to identify, collect, preserve integrity of, and maintain chain of custody for evidence related to information security events.

questions.question: Are relevant staff briefed on evidence preservation, and is access to specialist forensic capability established?
questions.guidance: Ensure IT administrators, service-desk staff, and incident responders know what not to disturb (such as avoiding premature reboots or reimaging) when potential legal or high-severity security events arise. Maintain documented access to qualified internal forensic specialists or a vetted external Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) retainer with clear activation triggers.
questions.auditor_focus: Check responder onboarding/training records for evidence-preservation guidance and verify current DFIR retainer agreements, panel arrangements, or internal specialist qualifications.
questions.what_good_looks_like: First-line IT and security responders receive practical evidence-preservation training reinforced during incident exercises. For complex or potentially litigious incidents, a pre-vetted external DFIR specialist or qualified internal forensic lead is on standby with pre-approved engagement terms and contact details.
questions.red_flags: IT support staff routinely reimage suspected compromised laptops immediately; no forensic specialist contact or retainer exists prior to an incident; retainer agreement has lapsed.
questions.nc_pattern: Personnel responsible for initial incident handling lack guidance on preserving evidence, and the organisation has no defined capability—internal or external—to perform forensically sound collection when required.

controls.short_summary: Maintain security controls, crisis exceptions, and restoration during disruptions.
controls.plain_english_summary: Plan how to maintain information security at an appropriate level during operational disruptions—such as natural disasters, cyber outages, site closures, or supplier failures—rather than letting controls collapse under crisis pressure. Align security and business continuity teams, govern any temporary security relaxations through formal exception approval, and verify full security restoration before standing down. This control owns maintaining security posture during disruption, distinct from ICT DR technical readiness (5.30).
controls.why_it_matters: Attackers actively exploit the chaos of outages, emergency workarounds, and manual fallback processes to slip past weakened authentication, unmonitored endpoints, or hastily opened firewall rules. Temporary crisis workarounds that are never logged or reversed routinely become permanent vulnerabilities.
key_deliverables: Information Security Continuity Requirements in BCPs
Crisis Security Exception and Compensating Control Log
Security–Business Continuity Joint Governance Terms
Post-Disruption Security Verification Checklist
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that business continuity plans explicitly address security controls during degraded or fallback operations—not just uptime—and check how emergency security exceptions are authorised and rolled back. The #1 trap is assuming a generic IT disaster recovery plan satisfies 5.29 when it says nothing about protecting confidentiality, access control, or manual fallback data during a crisis.

questions.question: How are information security requirements integrated into business continuity plans and coordinated across security and continuity teams?
questions.guidance: Embed explicit security controls into business continuity plans (BCPs) and crisis workflows—covering emergency access, secure alternate work locations, manual workaround data handling, physical security at fallback sites, and minimum security baselines for critical operations. Ensure information security representatives participate in BCP governance, scenario planning, and crisis management teams.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect BCP documentation and crisis team charters to verify security controls are embedded for degraded-mode operations and security leads hold defined roles in business continuity governance.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Business continuity plans explicitly specify how confidentiality, integrity, and access controls are preserved during manual fallbacks, remote surges, and alternate-site operations. Information security and business continuity teams share aligned governance, joint risk assessments, and clearly defined crisis coordination roles.
questions.red_flags: BCPs focus exclusively on facility evacuation or IT uptime with zero mention of information security; manual paper or spreadsheet fallback processes bypass access control and encryption entirely; security is absent from the crisis management team.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to plan how information security will be maintained at an appropriate level during operational disruptions.

questions.question: How are temporary security control adaptations or exceptions authorised, compensated, and tracked during crisis operations?
questions.guidance: Define a streamlined emergency change and exception process for disruptions so necessary temporary relaxations (for example, break-glass accounts, alternate remote access, or deferred non-critical checks) receive explicit authority approval, compensating controls, and a mandatory expiry trigger. Log every crisis-mode exception in a dedicated register so nothing is forgotten.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the emergency exception procedure and inspect logs from recent disruptions or crisis exercises to confirm temporary relaxations were approved, time-bound, and paired with compensating safeguards.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented emergency exception protocol specifies who may approve temporary security adaptations during a crisis, mandates compensating controls such as heightened monitoring, and records every exception with a mandatory rollback deadline. No ad hoc security bypasses occur without an audit trail.
questions.red_flags: Staff disable MFA, open wide firewall rules, or share admin passwords during outages with no approval or log; emergency workarounds remain active months after a disruption ends.
questions.nc_pattern: Uncontrolled or undocumented relaxation of information security controls during disruptions, with no governance over compensating safeguards or exception tracking.

questions.question: How is full information security verified and restored after a disruption, and validated during continuity exercises?
questions.guidance: Establish a post-disruption security sign-off checklist ensuring break-glass accounts are revoked, temporary firewall or access exceptions are reversed, offline/manual data captured during fallback is reconciled securely, and security logging/monitoring is restored. Validate these security continuity steps during annual BCP exercises (aligning with APRA CPS 230 §45).
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect post-disruption return-to-normal checklists, actual recovery sign-offs, and annual BCP exercise reports to verify security controls are actively tested and verified during continuity drills.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Returning to normal operations requires formal security verification confirming all crisis exceptions are closed, break-glass credentials rotated, fallback records secured, and monitoring fully active. Annual business continuity tests explicitly evaluate whether security controls hold up under disruption and recover cleanly.
questions.red_flags: BCP tests check application availability only and ignore security posture during failover or failback; no formal security verification is performed before closing a disruption event.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of controls to verify the restoration of information security posture following disruption or to validate security continuity during planned continuity exercises.

controls.short_summary: Align ICT continuity plans, RTO/RPO targets, and failover tests to business needs.
controls.plain_english_summary: Plan, implement, maintain, and test ICT continuity and disaster recovery capabilities based on business continuity objectives and disruption tolerance levels. Define clear Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) for critical ICT services, align architectural resilience accordingly, and validate recovery capability through scheduled failover and restoration testing. This control owns end-to-end ICT continuity readiness and testing, building upon—without duplicating—routine backup operations (8.13) and infrastructure redundancy (8.14).
controls.why_it_matters: An untested disaster recovery plan is an assumption, not a capability—and major outages routinely expose hidden dependencies, stale runbooks, or recovery times far slower than business tolerances allow. For APRA-regulated entities, CPS 230 requires Board-approved tolerance levels for critical operations and annual severe-but-plausible scenario testing.
key_deliverables: ICT Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan
Critical Operations RTO, RPO, and Tolerance Matrix
Annual ICT Continuity and Failover Testing Schedule
DR Exercise Reports and Remediation Action Tracker
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that RTO and RPO targets are derived from a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) rather than invented by IT, then demand dated test reports proving actual recovery times met those targets. The #1 trap is equating daily automated backup logs with an ICT disaster recovery test when full service failover and dependency restoration have never been timed end-to-end.

questions.question: Do you maintain a documented ICT continuity and disaster recovery plan aligned to critical operations and resilience architecture?
questions.guidance: Maintain an actionable ICT continuity plan detailing activation triggers, recovery sequence for interdependent services (identity, network, core databases, cloud regions, and material third parties), recovery runbooks, and resilience topology (such as multi-region or alternate-site capability aligned with 8.14). Ensure the plan addresses severe-but-plausible scenarios including cyber destruction and third-party outage.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the ICT continuity/DR plan for currency, clear dependency ordering, alignment with business continuity objectives, and coverage of critical cloud and third-party ICT services.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An up-to-date ICT continuity plan maps critical business operations to supporting ICT systems, external dependencies, and architectural resilience options. Step-by-step recovery runbooks establish clear activation authority, recovery sequence, and alternate-site or cloud failover procedures.
questions.red_flags: DR plan references decommissioned servers or omits critical SaaS/cloud platforms; no dependency order so applications attempt to recover before identity or network services; plan has not been updated after major architecture shifts.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a maintained ICT continuity plan aligned with the organisation's business continuity objectives and critical ICT service dependencies.

questions.question: Are Recovery Time Objectives (RTO), Recovery Point Objectives (RPO), and disruption tolerance levels formally defined and approved for critical ICT services?
questions.guidance: Derive RTOs, RPOs, and minimum service levels from a documented Business Impact Analysis (BIA) and have them signed off by business owners (and the Board where APRA CPS 230 §38 applies). Confirm that underlying technical continuity arrangements (replication, failover, and supplier SLAs) are engineered to meet those approved targets.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that documented RTO/RPO targets exist for all critical in-scope systems, trace back to business impact requirements, and match contracted supplier/cloud recovery commitments.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A formal RTO, RPO, and tolerance matrix covers every critical ICT service and underlying dependency, approved by business leadership based on Business Impact Analysis. Gaps between business tolerance targets and current technical or vendor recovery capability are explicitly logged as risks and funded for treatment.
questions.red_flags: RTO/RPO figures are chosen arbitrarily by IT without business approval; critical third-party SLA recovery times exceed internal tolerance levels with no documented mitigation; targets exist only on paper with no architectural feasibility check.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to define and agree ICT continuity objectives (such as RTO and RPO) derived from business continuity requirements for critical in-scope systems.

questions.question: Is ICT continuity readiness regularly validated through failover and recovery testing, with measured results against RTO/RPO and tracked remediation?
questions.guidance: Execute scheduled ICT continuity tests—progressing from tabletop walkthroughs to live failover and end-to-end service recovery—at planned intervals (at least annually under APRA CPS 230 §43–45) and after major architectural changes. Measure actual recovery times and data loss against target RTO/RPO, verify integrity of recovered services (coordinating with 8.13 backup testing without duplicating routine backup logs), and track failed steps to remediation.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the ICT continuity testing schedule, the most recent test report showing actual measured RTO/RPO results, and evidence that identified test failures were remediated and re-tested.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A planned ICT continuity testing programme validates end-to-end recovery of critical services at least annually under severe-but-plausible scenarios. Formal test reports record actual elapsed recovery times and data loss against approved RTO/RPO targets, log every gap or runbook failure, and verify remediation closure.
questions.red_flags: No ICT DR test performed in over 12 months; test report claims 'passed' without recording actual elapsed recovery times; routine single-file backup restores are presented as full disaster recovery validation.
questions.nc_pattern: ICT continuity plans and recovery capabilities are not tested at planned intervals against defined continuity objectives, or test failures remain unaddressed.

controls.control_name: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
controls.short_summary: Identify, maintain, and verify legal, regulatory, and contractual security duties.
controls.plain_english_summary: Identify, document, and keep up to date all legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual information security obligations relevant to the organisation and its ISMS scope. Monitor regulatory and contract changes proactively, translate requirements into concrete internal controls, and periodically verify ongoing compliance. In the Australian context, this spans obligations such as the Privacy Act 1988, APRA prudential standards (CPS 234, CPS 230), SOCI Act, Corporations Act, and key customer security schedules.
controls.why_it_matters: Missing a statutory obligation or client contractual security clause exposes the organisation to regulatory enforcement, civil penalties, and breach-of-contract claims. An outdated compliance register is also one of the quickest Stage 1 and surveillance audit nonconformities under ISO 27001.
key_deliverables: Legal, Regulatory, and Contractual Obligations Register
Regulatory Horizon-Scanning and Change Assessment Log
Customer Contractual Security Obligations Summary
Periodic Legal Compliance Verification Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that the obligations register is tailored to your actual jurisdictions, sector, and customer contracts—not a generic template—and verify how recent legal changes (such as CPS 230 commencement or Privacy Act reforms) were assessed. The #1 trap is listing Acts by name without mapping which specific obligations apply or which internal controls satisfy them.

questions.question: Do you maintain a current register mapping applicable legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual security obligations to internal controls?
questions.guidance: Maintain a comprehensive obligations register covering every jurisdiction and sector in which the organisation operates, alongside material security commitments made in customer and partner contracts. For each entry, document the obligation summary, accountable owner, mapped ISMS controls, and review frequency.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the obligations register for completeness against the organisation's industry, operating jurisdictions, and sampled customer agreements, confirming specific control mappings and named owners.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A living compliance obligations register captures all relevant Australian and international statutes, prudential standards, and material customer contractual security clauses. Each obligation is linked to an accountable owner, specific operational controls, and verification evidence.
questions.red_flags: Register lists broad legislation titles with no applicability analysis; customer contractual security commitments (such as data residency or annual pen-testing) are absent; register still cites repealed legislation.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a documented and maintained register identifying legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual information security requirements relevant to the ISMS scope.

questions.question: How are regulatory, legislative, and contractual changes monitored, assessed for impact, and embedded into the ISMS?
questions.guidance: Define a repeatable horizon-scanning process—using legal counsel updates, regulator bulletins (APRA, OAIC, ACSC, ASIC), industry associations, and contract review gates—to detect new or amended obligations early. Assess operational impact, update the obligations register, and assign implementation tasks before effective dates.
questions.auditor_focus: Look for concrete evidence of how a recent regulatory shift (such as APRA CPS 230 or Privacy Act amendments) or new customer contract schedule was assessed and translated into control updates.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Designated legal and compliance owners monitor authoritative regulatory feeds and review new customer contracts before execution. Material regulatory or contractual changes trigger documented gap assessments, register updates, and tracked implementation plans prior to enforcement deadlines.
questions.red_flags: Obligations register has not been updated in over 12 months; no defined mechanism to detect regulatory amendments; sales signs bespoke customer security addenda without informing security or compliance.
questions.nc_pattern: No active process to keep legal, regulatory, and contractual security obligations up to date or to respond to material changes affecting the ISMS.

questions.question: How is ongoing compliance with identified legal, regulatory, and contractual security obligations periodically verified?
questions.guidance: Establish scheduled compliance reviews or assurance attestations confirming that mapped controls remain effective against each statutory and contractual requirement. Report compliance status and any breaches or remediation plans to senior management and relevant governance committees.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect completed legal/regulatory compliance assessments, attestations, or internal audit reports confirming obligations are verified rather than passively catalogued.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Periodic compliance evaluations verify control effectiveness against every high-impact statutory and contractual requirement, backed by auditable evidence. Identified compliance gaps are escalated to leadership and tracked to remediation through formal corrective action.
questions.red_flags: Obligations are listed in a register but never checked for operational compliance; known contractual security commitments (such as encryption or reporting SLAs) are breached without detection.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to evaluate or verify compliance with applicable legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual information security requirements.

controls.short_summary: Protect organisational and third-party IP and govern software licences.
controls.plain_english_summary: Implement practical policies, contractual safeguards, and operational controls to protect both the organisation's own intellectual property and third-party IP, including commercial software licences and open-source components. Ensure staff understand IP ownership and usage rules, maintain accurate software licence entitlements, and prevent unlicensed or non-compliant software use.
controls.why_it_matters: Unlicensed software, breached open-source copyleft obligations, or mishandled third-party IP can trigger costly vendor licence audits, legal injunctions, or forced code rewrites. Uncontrolled software installation also creates shadow IT and unpatched security exposure.
key_deliverables: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing Policy
Software Asset and Licence Entitlement Register
Open-Source Software Usage and Licence Compliance Guidelines
Employment and Supplier IP Clauses
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check software licence reconciliation records against deployed installations, verify IP clauses in staff and contractor agreements, and look for basic open-source licence governance where software is developed in-house. The #1 trap is lacking proof of valid licences for commercial tools deployed on endpoints or ignoring open-source licence obligations in internal repositories.

questions.question: How are organisational and third-party intellectual property rights protected across policies, agreements, and staff awareness?
questions.guidance: Establish clear rules governing acceptable use of proprietary materials, third-party content, datasets, and code, reinforced through IP ownership and confidentiality clauses in employment, contractor, and supplier contracts. Make personnel aware of restrictions on copying copyrighted materials, reusing client IP, or uploading proprietary assets into unauthorised external tools.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the IP/acceptable use policy, sample employment and supplier agreements for IP protection clauses, and verify staff awareness content addresses IP obligations.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented policies alongside binding employment or supplier agreements clearly establish IP ownership, confidentiality, and third-party usage limits. Staff onboarding with periodic awareness training reinforces practical rules on copyrighted assets, client IP segregation, and unauthorised sharing.
questions.red_flags: Contractor or supplier contracts omit IP ownership or third-party IP handling clauses; no guidance on using proprietary or copyrighted content in external AI or cloud services.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented procedures and contractual or awareness measures to protect organisational and third-party intellectual property rights.

questions.question: How are commercial software licensing compliance and open-source software obligations managed and verified?
questions.guidance: Maintain an inventory of authorised commercial software paired with proof of purchase/entitlements and periodically reconcile installed seats against licensed volumes (coordinating with 5.9 and 8.19). Where the organisation builds or distributes software, define approved open-source licence types and use automated or review-gate checks to flag restrictive or incompatible licences.
questions.auditor_focus: Review software licence reconciliation records, proof of entitlement for sampled commercial applications, and—if software development is in scope—open-source licence policy and scan outputs.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintained software asset register tracks authorised commercial licences against active deployments, reconciled periodically to eliminate unlicensed installations or excess seats. Engineering teams follow clear open-source licence policies supported by automated dependency checks before release.
questions.red_flags: Installed software counts exceed purchased licences; proof of purchase cannot be produced for key tools; developers pull arbitrary open-source packages into commercial products with zero licence review.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to control or verify compliance with commercial software licences or applicable open-source intellectual property terms across in-scope assets.

controls.short_summary: Protect vital records against loss, tampering, premature disposal, and non-retrieval.
controls.plain_english_summary: Protect essential business, legal, financial, and ISMS records from loss, destruction, falsification, unauthorised access, and unauthorised release throughout their required retention lifecycle. Define clear retention schedules based on statutory and contractual obligations, maintain integrity and retrievability over time, and dispose of expired records securely when retention ends.
controls.why_it_matters: Losing statutory records—or being unable to prove their integrity and retrieve them during a regulatory inquiry, tax audit, or legal dispute—can result in severe penalties and adverse legal findings. Conversely, hoarding expired records indefinitely inflates data breach liability and violates privacy minimisation rules.
key_deliverables: Records Management Policy and Retention Schedule
Record Integrity and Access Control Configuration Evidence
Record Retrieval Verification Logs
Certificates and Logs of Secure Record Disposal
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that a retention schedule maps record classes to statutory periods, check controls preventing tampering or accidental deletion (such as immutability or WORM storage), and inspect proof of controlled disposal once retention expires. The #1 trap is publishing an ambitious retention schedule while leaving automated deletion unconfigured and historical archives unindexed.

questions.question: Do you maintain a records management policy and retention schedule aligned to statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements?
questions.guidance: Define what constitutes an official record (including ISMS audit logs, contracts, financial records, HR files, and customer records), classify record types, and specify minimum and maximum retention periods tied to obligations in 5.31 (such as Australian Corporations Act 7-year financial retention, Privacy Act minimisation, and APRA record expectations). Include legal-hold procedures that suspend routine disposal during litigation or regulatory inquiries.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the records management policy and retention schedule to confirm record categories, statutory rationale, storage locations, legal-hold triggers, and periodic review.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved records management policy with a retention schedule maps each business or ISMS record class to its legal basis, authoritative repository, retention period, and owner. Clear legal-hold procedures pause disposal whenever litigation or regulatory investigation arises.
questions.red_flags: No documented retention schedule exists; policy says 'retain as required by law' without specifying actual durations; no legal-hold mechanism to halt scheduled purges.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented retention and protection requirements for legal, statutory, regulatory, and ISMS records within scope.

questions.question: How are records protected against loss, falsification, and unauthorised access while remaining reliably retrievable?
questions.guidance: Enforce access restrictions, encryption, immutable or append-only storage (such as WORM buckets or retention locks), and backup protection to prevent accidental loss or unauthorised alteration. Confirm that archived records remain indexed, readable across software/format changes, and retrievable within reasonable timeframes when required by auditors or regulators.
questions.auditor_focus: Test record repository permissions, immutability or version-history settings, and request live retrieval of a sampled historical record (such as a prior-year contract or audit log) to confirm readability and integrity.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Authoritative record repositories enforce role-based access control, encryption, and retention locks or audit trails that prevent silent alteration or premature deletion. Periodic retrieval checks confirm archived records remain indexed, intact, and readable throughout their full retention lifecycle.
questions.red_flags: Critical records sit on uncontrolled shared folders where any user can overwrite or delete them; encrypted archives lack accessible decryption keys; staff cannot locate or open legacy archived records during audit.
questions.nc_pattern: Records are not adequately protected against loss, unauthorised modification, or premature destruction, or cannot be reliably retrieved within required retention periods.

questions.question: How are expired records disposed of securely once their retention period ends?
questions.guidance: Implement controlled disposal workflows—automated retention purges for digital repositories and certified cross-cut shredding or secure destruction for physical archives—subject to verifying no active legal hold applies. Maintain disposal logs or destruction certificates documenting what was destroyed, when, and under whose authorisation.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect retention purge configurations, physical destruction certificates, and disposal approval logs to confirm expired records are actually purged securely rather than retained indefinitely or discarded insecurely.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Expired digital and physical records undergo scheduled, authorised disposal once confirmed clear of legal holds, using verifiable sanitisation or certified shredding. Disposal logs and vendor destruction certificates provide an auditable trail proving secure end-of-life handling.
questions.red_flags: No records have ever been purged despite a published retention schedule; physical files are placed in general recycling bins; disposal occurs without verifying legal-hold clearance.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to securely dispose of expired records in accordance with retention requirements, or absence of verifiable disposal controls for sensitive records.

controls.short_summary: Protect personal information, govern PII flows, rights, and breach reporting.
controls.plain_english_summary: Identify and meet all applicable privacy and personal information protection obligations across the lifecycle of collecting, storing, using, disclosing, and deleting Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Maintain visibility over PII repositories and flows, apply proportionate technical and organisational safeguards, honour individual privacy rights, and operate a compliant privacy breach notification workflow (such as Australia's Privacy Act 1988 and Notifiable Data Breaches scheme).
controls.why_it_matters: Personal information breaches carry escalating statutory penalties under the Australian Privacy Act, mandatory public/individual notification duties, and lasting reputational harm. Without knowing where PII resides and who accesses it, organisations cannot realistically protect it or respond accurately within statutory breach windows.
key_deliverables: Privacy Policy and PII Handling Procedures
PII Processing Inventory / Data Flow Register
Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) and Rights Request Records
Privacy Breach Assessment and OAIC NDB Notification Procedure
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that you have mapped where PII actually lives across internal systems and third-party SaaS tools, applied data-minimisation and technical controls, and can demonstrate how privacy rights and NDB assessments work in practice. The #1 trap is publishing an external website privacy policy while having zero internal PII inventory or unmasked PII copied into test environments.

questions.question: Do you maintain current privacy policies, PII handling procedures, and a register of PII repositories and processing activities?
questions.guidance: Maintain both a public-facing privacy notice and internal PII handling procedures aligned with the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) and any applicable offshore regimes (such as GDPR). Document a PII inventory or data-flow map identifying categories of personal/sensitive information collected, lawful purpose, storage systems, cross-border disclosures, third-party processors, and retention periods.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the privacy policy, internal PII handling procedures, and PII processing inventory/data-flow map, checking that major HR, CRM, and third-party SaaS PII stores are accurately captured.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Clear privacy policies and internal handling rules are backed by a current PII inventory mapping every system and third party that collects, stores, or discloses personal information, including cross-border transfers. Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) are completed before launching high-risk projects involving new PII processing.
questions.red_flags: Only a generic website privacy statement exists with no internal handling procedure or PII map; cross-border SaaS disclosures are undocumented; sensitive PII is collected without a defined retention or minimisation rule.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to identify applicable privacy requirements or document how and where in-scope PII is collected, processed, stored, and shared.

questions.question: What technical and organisational safeguards protect PII, and how are individual access, correction, and deletion requests fulfilled?
questions.guidance: Apply least-privilege access, encryption in transit and at rest, data masking or pseudonymisation (especially preventing live PII in non-production environments), and secure deletion when PII is no longer required. Operate a documented workflow to verify requester identity and fulfil individual privacy rights—access, correction, opt-out, or deletion—within statutory timeframes.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify technical controls protecting sampled PII repositories (encryption, role-based access, non-prod masking) and inspect the privacy request log for timely, identity-verified fulfilment.
questions.what_good_looks_like: PII repositories enforce strict access controls, strong encryption, and masking in non-production environments, minimising unnecessary exposure. A tracked workflow authenticates requesters and completes access, correction, or deletion requests consistently within statutory deadlines.
questions.red_flags: Unmasked production customer PII is copied into development or test databases; broad staff groups can query full customer PII tables; privacy requests are handled ad hoc via email with no SLA tracking or identity verification.
questions.nc_pattern: Inadequate technical or procedural safeguards protecting PII against unauthorised access or disclosure, or inability to manage individual privacy rights required by applicable law.

questions.question: Is there a documented privacy breach assessment and statutory notification process aligned to applicable regimes such as the OAIC NDB scheme?
questions.guidance: Integrate a privacy breach workflow into the incident response plan (5.24) defining how suspected PII exposures are escalated to the Privacy Officer and legal counsel, assessed for 'serious harm' within the statutory 30-day OAIC NDB assessment window (or shorter international/contractual clocks), and notified to regulators and affected individuals.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the privacy breach response procedure, serious-harm assessment criteria, notification templates, and any completed breach assessment records (including decisions not to notify).
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented privacy breach workflow links security incident response directly to the Privacy Officer and legal team, specifying objective serious-harm assessment steps, statutory clocks (such as the OAIC NDB 30-day assessment limit), and notification templates. All suspected PII incidents—whether ultimately notifiable or not—have documented assessment records.
questions.red_flags: Security incident playbooks omit Privacy Officer escalation; staff are unaware of OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches thresholds; past PII exposures have no documented harm assessment explaining why notification was or was not made.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a defined process to assess suspected PII breaches and fulfil mandatory privacy breach notifications to regulators and affected individuals.

controls.short_summary: Conduct objective, independent reviews of ISMS adequacy and effectiveness.
controls.plain_english_summary: Arrange objective, independent reviews of the organisation's approach to managing information security—including its policies, processes, and control implementation—at planned intervals or whenever significant organisational, technical, or threat changes occur. Ensure reviewers are competent and independent of the areas they assess, and track all resulting findings through formal management review and remediation. ISO 27001 requires objective independence, not necessarily a formal Three Lines Model.
controls.why_it_matters: Teams that design and run security controls inevitably develop blind spots and confirmation bias. Independent review provides senior management and the Board with an unvarnished view of whether controls operate as intended and flags systemic weaknesses before an external auditor or attacker finds them.
key_deliverables: Independent Security Review Programme and Schedule
Reviewer Competence and Independence Confirmation Records
Independent Review and External Assessment Reports
Review Findings Remediation and Verification Tracker
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that independent reviews actually occurred at planned intervals (and after major changes), check that reviewers did not audit their own work, and trace findings to closure. Do not raise a false nonconformity simply because a smaller organisation lacks a formal Three Lines Model—competent external assessors or cross-functional internal reviewers who are independent of the audited function fully satisfy ISO 27001.

questions.question: Is there a planned independent review programme ensuring objective, competent review at scheduled intervals and upon significant change?
questions.guidance: Establish a documented review programme specifying scope, frequency (such as annual ISMS reviews and targeted control/architecture reviews), triggers for ad hoc reviews (mergers, cloud migrations, major incidents, or regulatory shifts), and criteria guaranteeing reviewer competence and objectivity. For APRA-regulated entities, ensure technical control testing uses functionally independent specialists (CPS 234 §30), testing sufficiency is reviewed annually (§31), and internal audit provides independent assurance over controls, BCP, and material outsourcing (CPS 234 §32; CPS 230 §30, §46, §60). Note: a formal Three Lines Model is good governance for larger institutions but is NOT an ISO 27001 mandatory requirement.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the review charter/schedule and reviewer credentials or engagement letters to verify independence (no self-audit of own controls) and explicit significant-change triggers; never issue an ISO 27001 NC solely for lacking a formal Three Lines structure.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented independent review programme defines planned review intervals, scope covering governance and technical controls, and clear triggers for out-of-cycle reviews after major changes. Reviewers—whether an independent internal audit function, peer specialists outside the audited team, or qualified external assessors—demonstrate both domain competence and verifiable objectivity.
questions.red_flags: The IT manager or CISO 'independently reviews' their own ISMS and signs off the report; no review schedule exists; major cloud migrations or acquisitions never trigger a targeted security review.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of planned independent reviews of information security management, or reviews conducted by personnel lacking objectivity because they manage or operate the controls being assessed.

questions.question: Are independent review findings reported to management and tracked through to verified remediation?
