questions.guidance: Retain formal reports from completed independent reviews (such as internal audits, external ISMS/CPS 234 assessments, or specialist security reviews), present outcomes to senior management and governance committees, and enter every finding into a central remediation or CAPA register with severity, root cause, owner, due date, and closure verification.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect completed independent review reports from the past 12–18 months, verify executive/management review presentation, and trace sampled high-priority findings through to verified closure evidence.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Completed independent review reports document scope, methodology, and risk-rated findings for formal presentation to executive management or the Audit and Risk Committee. Every finding is tracked in a central remediation register with accountable owners, realistic deadlines, and independent closure verification.
questions.red_flags: Independent review reports exist but findings are never entered into the corrective action register; high-risk findings are marked closed based solely on verbal assurance; overdue findings roll over repeatedly across audit cycles.
questions.nc_pattern: Independent review findings are not reported to appropriate management levels or are not systematically tracked and remediated.

controls.control_name: Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
controls.short_summary: Verify internal adherence to security policies, standards, and exceptions.
controls.plain_english_summary: Regularly review and verify that people, processes, and technical systems actually comply with the organisation's own information security policies, topic-specific rules, and technical configuration standards. Govern temporary policy exceptions through risk-assessed approvals with hard expiry dates, report compliance posture to management, and enforce consistent remediation when non-compliance occurs. This control owns operational policy and standard compliance verification across the organisation.
controls.why_it_matters: Well-written policies and hardening standards deliver zero protection if teams silently bypass them in daily operations. Structured compliance checking closes the gap between paper governance and operational reality—and catches drift long before a certification audit or breach.
key_deliverables: Policy and Technical Standard Compliance Review Records
Security Policy Exception and Risk Waiver Register
Management Security Compliance Dashboard / Reports
Non-Compliance Remediation and Escalation Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that management and control owners actively check adherence to internal policies and technical baselines—not merely wait for the annual internal audit—and inspect the exception register for expired or rubber-stamped waivers. The #1 trap is granting indefinite 'temporary' policy exceptions with no compensating controls or renewal review.

questions.question: How is ongoing compliance with internal security policies, topic-specific rules, and technical standards verified?
questions.guidance: Combine management-led operational compliance reviews with automated technical compliance checks (such as endpoint MDM compliance, cloud posture scans, CIS baseline audits, and access policy checks) on a defined cadence. Ensure managers verify adherence within their areas of responsibility and retain dated review outputs.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect completed operational compliance reviews and automated technical compliance reports (e.g., configuration baseline dashboards) to confirm internal standards are actively checked against real systems and processes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Scheduled management reviews paired with automated technical compliance checks routinely measure adherence to internal security policies across endpoints, servers, cloud tenants, and business processes. Results are documented with clear pass/fail metrics and retained as auditable compliance evidence.
questions.red_flags: Compliance with internal policies is only ever checked once a year during external ISO audits; technical standards exist on paper with no configuration compliance scanning; managers cannot show how they check team adherence.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of regular reviews or verification mechanisms to confirm operational and technical compliance with the organisation's information security policies, rules, and standards.

questions.question: How are security policy exceptions formally risk-assessed, approved, time-bound, and reviewed upon expiry?
questions.guidance: Maintain a formal exception workflow requiring documented business justification, residual risk assessment, compensating controls, approval by an authorised risk owner (not the requester), and a finite expiry date (typically 3–12 months). Track all active waivers in a central exception register and require re-approval or remediation before expiry.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the exception register to confirm every waiver has documented risk acceptance, compensating controls, appropriate seniority of approver, and no silently expired exceptions still active in production.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A central policy exception register tracks every approved deviation with business rationale, risk rating, compensating safeguards, formal risk-owner sign-off, and an automatic expiry review date. Expired waivers are escalated promptly for remediation or formal renewal.
questions.red_flags: Policy deviations are granted informally via email or chat; exceptions have no expiry dates and linger for years; technical staff self-approve their own security exemptions.
questions.nc_pattern: Ad hoc or uncontrolled bypassing of internal security policies without formal risk assessment, authorised approval, or ongoing tracking of exceptions.

questions.question: How is internal compliance status reported to management, and how are policy violations remediated?
questions.guidance: Consolidate policy compliance metrics, exception volumes, and recurring breaches into regular management and governance reporting (feeding Clause 9.3 management review). Define a consistent response workflow for policy violations—covering technical remediation, root-cause fixes, awareness reinforcement, and escalation to HR disciplinary processes (6.4) where wilful or repeated breaches occur.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect management compliance packs/minutes and sample records of non-compliance handling to verify breaches are investigated, remediated, and escalated consistently.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Regular compliance summaries give executive management clear visibility of policy adherence trends, open exceptions, and overdue remediation. Detected policy violations trigger root-cause investigation, documented corrective actions, and fair escalation under the disciplinary process when required.
questions.red_flags: Known policy breaches are ignored for senior or revenue-generating teams; management receives no visibility of compliance posture or exception backlogs; non-compliance triggers neither remediation nor corrective action.
questions.nc_pattern: Identified instances of non-compliance with internal security policies and standards are not escalated to management or addressed through timely corrective action.

controls.short_summary: Document, maintain, and share security-integrated IT operating procedures.
controls.plain_english_summary: Document and maintain clear operating procedures for critical ICT and information processing facilities so routine and high-risk tasks are performed consistently and securely, regardless of who is on shift. Embed explicit security steps into procedures, keep them version-controlled and accessible to authorised staff, and ensure operators are competent to execute them.
controls.why_it_matters: Reliance on tribal knowledge held by one or two senior engineers creates fragile operations, inconsistent security execution, and severe key-person risk during staff turnover or incidents. Outdated runbooks that no longer match production architecture also cause costly outages and misconfigurations.
key_deliverables: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Runbook Catalogue
Document Control and Periodic Review Log
Controlled Internal Knowledge Base / Procedure Repository
Operator Training and Handover Competence Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample critical operational activities—such as user onboarding/offboarding, patching, backup verification, or change deployment—and ask to see the documented SOP alongside evidence it is actually followed and current. The #1 trap is a wiki full of abandoned, unversioned notes from three years ago that contradict how engineers operate today.

questions.question: Are operating procedures documented for critical ICT and ISMS processes, with explicit security steps embedded?
questions.guidance: Maintain clear, step-by-step operating procedures (SOPs/runbooks) for recurring and security-critical operations—including system build/hardening, user provisioning and de-provisioning, backup and restore, patching, log review, change deployment, and scheduled jobs. Embed mandatory security checkpoints (such as approvals, least-privilege verification, and error/rollback handling) directly within each procedure.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the SOP catalogue and sample 3–5 critical operational procedures to confirm they are practical, match current systems, and explicitly integrate security checks and error handling.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Critical ICT and security operations are backed by structured, step-by-step runbooks that embed security prerequisites, approval gates, validation checks, and rollback steps. An engineer unfamiliar with a specific system can safely execute routine tasks without relying on undocumented tribal knowledge.
questions.red_flags: Critical processes such as offboarding, patching, or backup restoration exist solely in one administrator's head; SOPs omit security approvals or error-handling steps; runbooks describe legacy tools no longer in use.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented operating procedures for critical in-scope information processing facilities, or procedures that fail to incorporate required security controls.

questions.question: How are operating procedures kept accessible, periodically reviewed under version control, and reinforced through operator competence?
questions.guidance: Store approved operating procedures in a central, access-controlled repository (with offline availability for critical recovery runbooks), enforce version control and scheduled reviews (plus updates triggered by system changes under 8.32), and verify through onboarding, peer shadowing, or operational spot checks that personnel follow current procedures accurately.
questions.auditor_focus: Check procedure version histories, last-reviewed dates, repository access permissions, and operator onboarding or QA check records to verify runbooks remain accurate and actively used.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Operating procedures reside in a centrally controlled repository accessible to authorised operators, carrying clear owners, version histories, and scheduled review dates tied to change management. New or cross-trained staff complete documented onboarding on critical procedures, and periodic operational checks confirm procedures are followed.
questions.red_flags: Conflicting copies of runbooks circulate across personal folders and wikis; procedures have not been reviewed in years despite major platform upgrades; staff routinely deviate from written SOPs because they are obsolete.
questions.nc_pattern: Operating procedures are uncontrolled, inaccessible to relevant operators, or materially outdated relative to current production systems and operational practices.

controls.short_summary: Verify candidate suitability proportionally to role risk before granting access.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.1 requires background verification checks on prospective employees and relevant contractors before they join or receive access to organisational assets. Screening depth must be proportional to business requirements, information classification, and perceived risk, while strictly respecting Australian privacy and employment laws.
controls.why_it_matters: Unvetted hires or contractors in privileged, financial, or customer-data roles expose the organisation to insider fraud, credential misuse, and reputational damage. Equally, collecting excessive personal data without lawful consent creates Privacy Act 1988 and Fair Work compliance risks.
key_deliverables: Pre-Employment and Contractor Screening Policy
Role-Risk Screening Tier Matrix
Completed Background Verification Sign-Off Records
Contractor Screening Attestations or Agency Clauses
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample recent hires and contractors to confirm screening was completed before IT accounts were activated, not weeks afterwards. The most common trap is diligently vetting permanent employees while granting immediate system access to agency contractors or consultants with zero checks.

questions.question: How are pre-employment screening requirements defined proportionally to role sensitivity and aligned with Australian privacy and employment laws?
questions.guidance: Establish a screening policy and role-tier matrix distinguishing standard roles (identity, right-to-work, reference, and qualification checks) from elevated-risk or privileged roles (such as National Police Checks, financial probity, or directorship checks where legally justified). Document consent collection, spent-conviction compliance, adverse-finding escalation, and secure handling/disposal of screening data under the Privacy Act 1988.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify that screening tiers logically reflect access to sensitive or regulated information, check candidate consent workflows, and confirm legal proportionality.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved screening policy and role-sensitivity matrix define exact verification checks per risk tier, legal consent steps, and exception-approval thresholds. Procedures specify how adverse findings are reviewed fairly and how screening artefacts are minimised and retained lawfully.
questions.red_flags: Identical ad-hoc checks applied regardless of whether someone is a reception temp or a production cloud administrator. Collecting criminal or credit histories without documented legal justification or candidate consent.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined background verification criteria proportional to business requirements, information classification, and perceived risk, or failure to align screening with applicable laws under Control 6.1.

questions.question: What operating evidence confirms that required background checks are completed for employees and contractors before access to information assets is granted?
questions.guidance: Integrate HR screening sign-off as a mandatory gate before IT provisions corporate credentials or physical access badges. For contractors, managed service engineers, and agency staff, either execute checks directly or obtain contractual warranties and periodic verification attestations from the supplying agency before onboarding.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors pick a sample of hires and contractors from the past 6–12 months and compare background-check completion dates against Active Directory/IdP account creation timestamps.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Onboarding records show completed, dated verification sign-offs (without unnecessarily storing sensitive identity copies) preceding system access provisioning for sampled employees. Contractor onboarding files contain signed agency screening attestations or direct verification records.
questions.red_flags: New starters or contractors granted production access before checks conclude without a documented risk-approved exception. Zero verification evidence for outsourced developers or short-term contractors.
questions.nc_pattern: Personnel or contractors are routinely granted access to in-scope systems without completing required pre-employment screening or documented risk-accepted interim controls, breaching Control 6.1.

questions.question: How are re-screening and periodic verification managed when personnel transfer into higher-sensitivity roles or hold ongoing privileged responsibilities?
questions.guidance: Define when additional screening is triggered—such as internal promotion from a general business role into finance, security operations, or privileged infrastructure administration—and decide on a risk-based basis whether periodic re-screening is warranted for critical or regulated roles.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check internal transfer records into privileged groups to verify gap screening was performed before elevated permissions were granted.
questions.what_good_looks_like: HR role-change workflows automatically flag promotions into higher-tier roles so incremental checks are completed prior to privilege elevation. Where periodic re-checks are required by risk profile or customer contract, a tracked schedule confirms timely completion.
questions.red_flags: Long-tenured staff promoted into administrator or executive roles with no supplemental checks since initial junior hiring. Unmonitored contractual re-screening obligations.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to perform required supplemental screening when personnel move into roles carrying materially higher information security risk, contrary to organisational screening rules under Control 6.1.

controls.short_summary: Embed clear information security obligations into employee and contractor agreements.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.2 ensures employment contracts and contractor agreements explicitly state the information security responsibilities of both the individual and the organisation. Clear contractual terms establish binding expectations around policy compliance, confidentiality, acceptable use, intellectual property, and duties that survive termination.
controls.why_it_matters: If security duties are missing from employment or contractor agreements, enforcing disciplinary action, protecting trade secrets, or pursuing legal remedies after a breach becomes far harder. Clear contractual clauses also set unambiguous accountability from day one.
key_deliverables: Standard Employment Contract Templates (with Security Clauses)
Contractor and Third-Party Engagement Agreement Templates
Signed Agreement Repository and Onboarding Acknowledgement Logs
Policy and Terms Update Communication Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors review template contracts for security, confidentiality, and post-employment clauses, then sample signed files for both permanent staff and contractors. A frequent gap is legacy employees on decade-old contracts that predate modern security policies with no signed policy-acknowledgement addendum.

questions.question: Do employment contracts and equivalent contractor agreements clearly define ongoing and post-employment information security responsibilities for both personnel and the organisation?
questions.guidance: Include explicit clauses in permanent, casual, and contractor agreements requiring compliance with organisational information security policies, protection of confidential and personal information, lawful handling of intellectual property, return of assets, and enduring post-employment confidentiality obligations. Also outline the organisation's reciprocal obligations to provide policies and a compliant working framework.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect current HR and procurement contract templates to verify explicit security, acceptable-use, confidentiality, and post-employment clauses are present.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Current employment and contractor contract templates incorporate legally reviewed clauses covering policy adherence, confidentiality, intellectual property, disciplinary consequences, and post-termination duties. Legacy staff are bridged via documented policy-acknowledgement addenda where older templates lacked detail.
questions.red_flags: Employment letters covering only salary and leave with no mention of information security or confidentiality. Contractors engaged via purchase orders alone without binding security terms.
questions.nc_pattern: Contractual agreements with employees or contractors fail to state their and the organisation's responsibilities for information security as required by Control 6.2.

questions.question: What evidence confirms that new starters, contractors, and existing personnel formally acknowledge security terms at onboarding and whenever material obligations change?
questions.guidance: Capture signed agreements and policy acknowledgements prior to granting access during onboarding, and maintain an auditable log of notifications and re-acknowledgements whenever material policy or contractual security obligations are updated.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample recent employee and contractor files to confirm executed contracts exist, and inspect logs showing how updated security terms were communicated and acknowledged.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Signed employment and contractor agreements are securely retained for 100% of sampled personnel prior to their start date. Onboarding checklists and annual or change-driven policy-attestation logs prove security obligations are actively communicated and acknowledged.
questions.red_flags: Missing signed contracts for sampled staff or long-term contractors. Material changes to acceptable use, AI usage, or remote-working obligations rolled out without informing affected personnel.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to obtain signed agreements reflecting security obligations for personnel or contractors, or failure to communicate material changes in security responsibilities under Control 6.2.

controls.control_name: Information Security Awareness, Education and Training
controls.short_summary: Deliver ongoing, role-tailored security awareness and verify training effectiveness.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.3 requires personnel and relevant external parties to receive regular information security awareness, education, and role-specific training aligned with organisational policies and their day-to-day duties. Training must stay current with evolving threats and actually change workplace behaviour rather than acting as a once-a-year click-through chore.
controls.why_it_matters: Human error, social engineering, and misconfiguration remain leading causes of real-world data breaches. Role-tailored training equips developers, finance staff, executives, and support teams to spot threats relevant to their actual workflows before damage occurs.
key_deliverables: Security Awareness and Role-Based Training Plan
LMS Training Completion and Overdue-Escalation Reports
Role-Specific Training Records (e.g., Secure Coding, Incident Response)
Training Effectiveness Metrics and Content Review Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check completion rates for onboarding and annual refreshers, verify role-specific training for high-risk functions (such as developers or administrators), and ask how effectiveness is measured. A common trap is excluding contractors or executives from mandatory training.

questions.question: How is the information security awareness, education, and role-specific training programme structured across general staff, contractors, and specialist roles?
questions.guidance: Define a documented curriculum covering onboarding and recurring organisation-wide awareness (policies, phishing/social engineering, data classification, privacy, event reporting) alongside targeted role-based education for developers (secure coding/OWASP), system administrators, incident responders, finance/payroll staff, and executives.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify the training syllabus matches the organisation's policies and threat profile, and check that specialist technical and high-risk roles receive training tailored to their duties.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A formal training programme maps baseline awareness modules to all employees and in-scope contractors, and assigns role-specific training tracks to developers, administrators, finance teams, and leadership. Delivery cadence, onboarding deadlines, and policy alignment are clearly defined.
questions.red_flags: One-size-fits-all video with no role-specific training for engineers or privileged staff. Contractors with corporate email or system access omitted from the programme.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of a structured information security awareness, education, and training programme appropriate to organisational policies and job functions under Control 6.3.

questions.question: What operating records demonstrate timely onboarding and recurring training completion, escalation of overdue personnel, and practical security reinforcement?
questions.guidance: Maintain auditable LMS or attendance records tracking completion rates against defined deadlines (for example, within 30 days of joining and annually thereafter) with manager escalation for overdue learners. Reinforce formal training with periodic practical reminders—such as phishing awareness exercises, tabletop walkthroughs, or security advisories—noting that specific simulation tools are optional best practice rather than mandatory.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review live completion reports (checking denominators against active HR/contractor headcount), inspect follow-up on overdue staff, and review practical reinforcement activities.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Training dashboards reconcile against active HR and contractor rosters, showing high timely completion rates and documented escalation for any overdue individuals. Practical reinforcement records (such as security briefings, exercises, or simulation metrics) show active ongoing engagement.
questions.red_flags: Large backlog of overdue trainees with no manager follow-up. Completion percentages calculated only against active LMS users while omitting recently hired staff or contractors. Executives routinely exempted.
questions.nc_pattern: Personnel do not receive regular information security awareness and training in line with organisational requirements, or completion is not tracked and enforced under Control 6.3.

questions.question: How is training effectiveness evaluated and how is training content kept current with policy changes, incident lessons, and emerging threats?
questions.guidance: Assess whether training achieves behavioural outcomes—using knowledge checks, incident and near-miss reporting trends, helpdesk queries, or exercise metrics—and review training materials at least annually or after major policy updates, new technologies (such as generative AI), or notable security incidents.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors look for evidence that training content has evolved over the past year rather than repeating stale slides, and check how effectiveness results inform programme adjustments.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Annual content review logs document updates reflecting recent threats, policy revisions, and incident lessons learned. Effectiveness reports combine quiz scores, reporting-rate trends, and practical exercise outcomes to target refresher coaching where needed.
questions.red_flags: Training slides unchanged for three years and referencing retired tools or outdated policies. Zero measurement of whether personnel retained or applied training content.
questions.nc_pattern: Training content is materially outdated relative to current policies and organisational threats, or no periodic review ensures the awareness programme remains appropriate under Control 6.3.

controls.short_summary: Maintain and communicate a fair disciplinary process for security policy breaches.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.4 requires a formal, communicated disciplinary process to address deliberate or negligent breaches of information security policy by employees and equivalent contractual remedies for contractors or third parties. Actions must be fair, proportionate to severity, and compliant with Australian workplace legislation.
controls.why_it_matters: Policies without consequences quickly lose credibility, while ad-hoc or disproportionate punishment creates Fair Work legal exposure and discourages honest incident reporting. A transparent, calibrated framework deters negligence while supporting a just security culture.
key_deliverables: HR Disciplinary Policy Incorporating Information Security Breaches
Violation Severity and Proportionality Guidelines
Contractor Breach and Termination Clauses
Communication Evidence and Confidential Case-Handling Logs (or Nil-Event Record)
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify the disciplinary framework explicitly covers security breaches, is communicated to staff, and differentiates honest mistakes from wilful misconduct. Auditors respect HR confidentiality and do not demand private employee names—only confirmation the process works fairly when triggered.

questions.question: Is a formal, legally compliant disciplinary process established for information security breaches—including severity criteria and equivalent contractual sanctions for contractors?
questions.guidance: Ensure HR disciplinary procedures explicitly address information security policy violations, distinguishing inadvertent errors (addressed via coaching or retraining) from repeated negligence or intentional misconduct (escalating to warnings or termination) in alignment with the Fair Work Act 2009. Ensure supplier and contractor agreements specify equivalent remedies such as personnel removal or contract termination.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect the HR disciplinary policy and standard contractor terms to verify security breaches are explicitly in scope, severity is graded fairly, and investigation procedures require verified evidence before sanctions.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved HR disciplinary policy explicitly references information security breaches, defines graduated severity criteria and natural-justice investigation steps, and aligns with Australian workplace law. Standard contractor agreements include parallel remedies for security non-compliance.
questions.red_flags: Disciplinary policy makes no mention of information security or data breaches. Zero mechanism to remove or sanction non-compliant contractors. Punitive rules that fail to distinguish honest mistakes reported promptly from deliberate violations.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a formalised disciplinary process addressing information security policy violations for personnel and relevant third parties under Control 6.4.

questions.question: How is the disciplinary process communicated to personnel, and what anonymised evidence confirms consistent, fair application when confirmed violations occur?
questions.guidance: Communicate disciplinary expectations clearly through employee handbooks, contracts, and annual security awareness. Maintain confidential HR/legal case logs—summarised in anonymised form for audit or governance review—demonstrating consistent handling of verified breaches (or a formal confirmation if no disciplinary cases occurred during the period).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify staff know policy breaches carry consequences and ask HR for anonymised summary evidence (or nil-incident confirmation) demonstrating the process is operational and consistently applied.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Onboarding packs, employee handbooks, and awareness modules communicate disciplinary expectations clearly. HR maintains confidential investigation records and can provide an anonymised governance summary confirming consistent application—or a documented nil-case statement—for the audit period.
questions.red_flags: Staff unaware that security breaches can attract disciplinary action. Known deliberate policy violations ignored for senior staff while junior personnel are penalised.
questions.nc_pattern: The disciplinary process is not communicated to personnel, or verified serious security breaches are left unaddressed contrary to Control 6.4.

controls.control_name: Responsibilities After Termination or Change of Employment
controls.short_summary: Define, communicate and enforce security duties after role change or departure.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.5 ensures that security duties—such as confidentiality, intellectual property protection, and lawful handling of organisational data—are explicitly defined, communicated, and enforced when employees or contractors leave or change roles. It bridges HR offboarding and transfer workflows with IT access adjustments and asset return.
controls.why_it_matters: Departures and internal moves are peak moments for accidental data retention, privilege creep, or intentional data exfiltration. Explicitly reminding leavers of enduring legal duties and tightening access promptly protects sensitive commercial and customer information.
key_deliverables: Post-Employment and Role-Change Security Procedure
Offboarding and Internal Transfer Checklists
Exit Reminder Letters and Signed Acknowledgements
Secure Knowledge-Transfer and Access-Adjustment Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace sampled leavers and internal transfers from HR notification through exit reminders, asset return, and IT privilege updates. The most common gap is handling departures properly while overlooking internal role transfers, leaving staff with accumulated legacy access and duties.

questions.question: How are enduring post-employment and role-change security responsibilities—including confidentiality, intellectual property, and enforcement mechanisms—defined for employees and contractors?
questions.guidance: Specify in employment contracts, contractor agreements, and HR offboarding policies which information security duties remain valid after termination or role transition—covering ongoing confidentiality, non-use of proprietary data or credentials, and return/deletion of company information. Define legal and HR escalation steps if post-employment breaches are detected.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check that post-employment clauses exist and survive contract end, cover both employees and contractors, and link to a defined enforcement path if a former worker misuses confidential data.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Contracts and HR policies explicitly define surviving confidentiality, intellectual property, and data-return duties for both permanent staff and contractors. Legal escalation procedures specify how suspected post-departure breaches are investigated and enforced.
questions.red_flags: Contracts silent on survival of confidentiality obligations after termination. Contractors departing without defined enduring security duties or enforcement mechanisms.
questions.nc_pattern: Information security responsibilities and duties remaining valid after termination or change of employment are not defined or enforceable under Control 6.5.

questions.question: What operational records confirm that departing and transferring personnel are formally reminded of ongoing obligations, complete secure knowledge transfer, and have access adjusted promptly?
questions.guidance: Embed security steps into HR exit and internal-transfer workflows: issue written reminders of enduring confidentiality duties during exit interviews or offboarding emails, manage handover of files and shared accounts securely (without sharing personal passwords), and trigger IT and facilities tickets to revoke or re-scope physical and logical access.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample recent leavers and internal movers, checking exit checklists, written reminder acknowledgements, handover records, and timestamps showing access was removed or adjusted in line with policy.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Completed offboarding and internal-transfer checklists exist for sampled personnel, recording exit reminders of enduring obligations, secure handover of business records, asset return, and timely removal or re-scoping of logical and physical access.
questions.red_flags: Departing staff leave with no written reminder of continuing confidentiality obligations. Internal transfers retain previous department privileges indefinitely. Knowledge transfer performed by emailing credentials or copying files to personal drives.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to communicate enduring security responsibilities upon termination or change of employment, or failure to manage role transitions and offboarding security duties consistently under Control 6.5.

controls.short_summary: Identify, execute, track and periodically review confidentiality and NDA agreements.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.6 requires confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) tailored to the organisation's information protection needs to be executed with employees, contractors, suppliers, and other external parties before sensitive information is shared, and reviewed periodically so terms remain legally sound.
controls.why_it_matters: Sharing commercial roadmaps, architecture diagrams, source code, or customer datasets without an executed, enforceable NDA strips away contractual remedies if information leaks. Unreviewed legacy NDAs can also conflict with modern privacy laws, regulatory reporting rights, or statutory whistleblower protections.
key_deliverables: Standard One-Way and Mutual NDA Templates
Signed NDA Register and Document Repository
Periodic Legal Review Records for NDA Templates
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample recently onboarded suppliers, consultants, and prospective partners who accessed confidential information to confirm an NDA was signed before disclosure, and check when NDA templates were last legally reviewed.

questions.question: How are confidentiality and NDA requirements defined—including mutual NDAs where appropriate—to reflect organisational protection needs for personnel and external parties?
questions.guidance: Define clear criteria specifying when confidentiality clauses within employment/master agreements suffice versus when standalone one-way or mutual NDAs are required (for example, pre-contract vendor RFPs, penetration testers, M&A advisers, or strategic partners). Ensure templates specify what constitutes confidential information, permitted use, duration, return/destruction duties, and lawful carve-outs (such as regulatory or statutory disclosures).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors examine NDA templates and procurement/sales workflows to verify protection scope aligns with the organisation's classification scheme and clearly requires execution before sharing confidential data.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Legally approved one-way and mutual NDA templates cover information definitions, handling duties, duration, data return/destruction, and statutory carve-outs. Procurement, sales, and HR procedures mandate executed confidentiality terms prior to disclosing non-public information.
questions.red_flags: Ad-hoc NDAs downloaded from random websites without legal review. Confidential architecture or customer data shared during vendor demos before any NDA is executed. Templates lacking clear return or destruction obligations.
questions.nc_pattern: Confidentiality or non-disclosure requirements reflecting the organisation's needs for protecting information are not identified, documented, or required prior to disclosure under Control 6.6.

questions.question: Is a central register of executed NDAs maintained, and are NDA templates and standing agreements reviewed and updated regularly?
questions.guidance: Track executed external NDAs (and employment/supplier agreements containing confidentiality schedules) in a searchable register recording counterparty, effective date, term/expiry, and storage link. Review NDA templates periodically (for example, annually or upon legislative/business changes) so terms stay aligned with Australian privacy, IP, and regulatory developments.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample external parties from the supplier or visitor register to verify signed NDAs can be produced promptly, and check legal review dates on NDA templates.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintained contract/NDA register enables instant retrieval of executed agreements with effective and expiry dates. Dated legal review logs confirm NDA templates are checked periodically and updated when business models or laws change.
questions.red_flags: Executed NDAs scattered across individual sales or manager inboxes and unable to be located during audit. Expired NDAs still relied upon for ongoing data sharing. Templates unreviewed for several years.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to retain evidence of signed confidentiality agreements for relevant parties or failure to regularly review confidentiality requirements and templates under Control 6.6.

controls.short_summary: Protect information accessed, processed or stored outside corporate premises.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.7 requires security measures whenever personnel work outside corporate offices—whether from home, client sites, transit, or overseas. It combines clear policy rules, technical endpoint and network protections, and practical workspace safeguards to prevent eavesdropping, shoulder-surfing, theft, or interception.
controls.why_it_matters: Hybrid and remote work permanently expanded the corporate perimeter into home Wi-Fi networks, shared households, cafes, and public transport. Without consistent endpoint encryption, MFA, physical privacy discipline, and overseas-work controls, remote work becomes an easy entry point for data loss and credential theft.
key_deliverables: Remote and Hybrid Working Security Policy
Endpoint and Remote-Access Technical Standards (MDM, Encryption, VPN/ZTNA, MFA)
Remote-Worker Security Guidance and Awareness Records
Remote Workspace Self-Assessment and Overseas-Work Approval Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify both policy rules and live technical enforcement (checking MDM encryption, screen lock, and MFA configs), and test how organisations govern public-space work or temporary overseas remote working.

questions.question: Does a documented Remote Working Security Policy define physical workspace, network, device, and data-handling requirements for working outside corporate premises?
questions.guidance: Establish clear rules covering acceptable remote locations, visual and audio privacy (protecting screens and confidential calls in shared spaces), approved corporate versus BYOD devices, home router hygiene, prohibition of unencrypted local storage or insecure public Wi-Fi without VPN/ZTNA, and handling of printed confidential material at home.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check that the policy reflects how the workforce actually works (including hybrid, travelling, and interstate/overseas scenarios) and defines unambiguous rules rather than generic advice.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved Remote Working Security Policy sets clear requirements for endpoint hardening, encrypted remote access, physical workspace security, public-space conduct, paper-document handling, and reporting of lost or stolen equipment.
questions.red_flags: No remote working policy despite a predominantly hybrid workforce. Policy fails to address public Wi-Fi, shared living spaces, or personal/BYOD device boundaries.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to define security measures protecting information accessed, processed, or stored at remote working locations as required by Control 6.7.

questions.question: What technical controls and user training records verify that remote working devices, connections, and data are protected in day-to-day operations?
questions.guidance: Enforce technical safeguards across remote endpoints—full-disk encryption, managed EDR/anti-malware, automatic screen locking, MFA-enforced SSO/VPN or ZTNA, and conditional access blocking unmanaged devices where policy prohibits BYOD—and ensure remote workers receive practical security guidance during onboarding and refresher training.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect live MDM, IdP conditional-access, and VPN/ZTNA console configurations alongside remote-worker training records to verify policy rules are technically enforced rather than honour-system only.
questions.what_good_looks_like: MDM and identity-provider reports confirm full-disk encryption, automatic screen lock, patched OS baselines, EDR coverage, and phishing-resistant or strong MFA for remote access. Awareness records confirm remote workers are trained on home and travel security obligations.
questions.red_flags: Remote access permitted from unencrypted or unmanaged personal laptops without compensating controls. VPN or cloud apps accessible with passwords alone. Remote workers never briefed on physical or travel data protection.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of implemented technical or procedural safeguards protecting remote endpoints, remote access connections, or data processed off-premises under Control 6.7.

questions.question: How are remote working environments periodically assessed for security suitability, including formal risk approval for high-risk or overseas remote working arrangements?
questions.guidance: Use periodic remote-workspace security self-assessments (often paired with WHS home-office checks) to verify physical privacy, lockable storage where needed, and secure home Wi-Fi practices. Require advance security and legal approval before personnel work remotely from overseas jurisdictions (accounting for geopolitical risk, cross-border privacy obligations, and conditional-access geo-blocking).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect completed remote-workspace assessment records and ask how temporary overseas remote work requests are risk-assessed and approved.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Remote workers complete periodic workspace security checklists tracked to closure, covering physical privacy and home-network hygiene. An explicit travel/overseas remote-work approval workflow reviews country risk, data-sovereignty rules, and geo-access exceptions before departure.
questions.red_flags: Zero visibility into remote workspace conditions or staff routinely working from high-risk overseas destinations without approval or security review.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to assess or manage material physical, environmental, or jurisdictional risks associated with remote working arrangements under Control 6.7.

controls.short_summary: Provide a clear, blame-free channel for prompt staff reporting of security events.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 6.8 requires a simple, widely understood mechanism so personnel can promptly report observed or suspected information security events—including phishing emails, lost devices, misdirected data, or physical tailgating—without fear of retaliation. Rapid human reporting is often the earliest detection signal available.
controls.why_it_matters: When staff hesitate to report a clicked phishing link or misaddressed email out of fear of blame, minutes turn into days and containable events escalate into major data breaches. Fast, friction-free reporting directly supports timely containment and regulatory notification deadlines.
key_deliverables: Information Security Event Reporting Procedure and Escalation Guide
Dedicated Reporting Channels (e.g., Security Hotline, Email, Ticket Portal, Report-Phish Button)
Non-Retaliation / Blame-Free Reporting Commitment
Event Reporting Logs and Triage Timestamps
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors ask randomly sampled employees how they would report a lost laptop or suspicious email right now, then inspect the security ticket queue to verify real reports are logged and triaged promptly.

questions.question: Is a clear, accessible reporting mechanism defined—specifying what events must be reported, expected reporting timeframes, and protection for good-faith reporters?
questions.guidance: Document an intuitive reporting procedure defining reportable events (suspected phishing, malware, lost/stolen devices, unauthorised disclosures, misdirected emails, system anomalies, and physical security weaknesses), clear channels (such as a monitored security email, portal, phone line, or email report button), expected urgency (immediate / as soon as detected), and explicit non-retaliation protections for good-faith reporting.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review the reporting procedure for clarity on reportable event types, urgency expectations, out-of-hours escalation, and explicit protection against retaliation for honest reporters.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A plain-English reporting guide defines concrete examples of reportable events and weaknesses, specifies immediate reporting expectations via monitored channels, and includes an explicit blame-free commitment protecting good-faith reporters.
questions.red_flags: Buried or complex reporting instructions requiring staff to locate an obscure form. No clear guidance on reporting weaknesses or near-misses. Fear-based culture discouraging prompt disclosure of honest mistakes.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of a defined mechanism enabling personnel to report observed or suspected information security events through appropriate channels in a timely manner under Control 6.8.

questions.question: What evidence confirms personnel know how to use the reporting channels and that reported events are logged and triaged promptly into incident management?
questions.guidance: Promote reporting channels repeatedly during onboarding, annual awareness, intranet banners, and after phishing exercises. Retain event intake logs showing reports submitted by personnel, acknowledgement/triage timestamps, and escalation into formal incident response (and statutory or APRA notification assessment where thresholds are met).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors interview staff across non-IT departments to test real recall of reporting channels, then sample recent staff-submitted tickets to verify timely triage and hand-off to Control 5.25/5.26.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Sampled employees across business teams immediately name how to report a security event. Ticket or SIEM intake logs show regular staff-submitted reports (including near-misses and suspicious emails) triaged promptly within target SLAs and escalated cleanly when warranted.
questions.red_flags: Zero staff-reported security events logged across an entire year (a strong indicator of under-reporting rather than zero risk). Reported suspicious emails sitting unread in a shared mailbox for days.
questions.nc_pattern: Personnel are unaware of how to report information security events, or reported events are not captured and triaged in a timely manner as required by Control 6.8.

controls.short_summary: Define layered physical boundaries around sensitive areas and facilities.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.1 requires clearly defined physical barriers—such as building shells, swipe-controlled office floors, locked server rooms, and secured emergency exits—to protect areas containing information and processing facilities. Layered perimeters match physical strength to the sensitivity of the assets inside.
controls.why_it_matters: Logical security controls can be bypassed rapidly if an intruder walks straight into an unlocked comms room or slips through a propped-open fire exit. Clear perimeters also help cloud-first organisations document where their physical boundary ends and a landlord or data-centre provider's responsibility begins.
key_deliverables: Physical Security Policy and Zone Classification
Annotated Floor Plans Showing Security Perimeters and Barriers
Emergency Exit Security and Safety Specifications
Periodic Physical Perimeter Inspection Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors walk the site (or review landlord/colocation evidence for hosted environments) checking door locks, perimeter walls, ground-floor windows, and fire exits. The #1 trap is propped-open rear doors or shared-tenancy office suites with no clear separation from public hallways.

questions.question: How are physical security perimeters, security zones, and emergency exit safeguards defined and documented across in-scope facilities?
questions.guidance: Map layered physical zones (public reception, general office, restricted server/comms rooms) on current floor plans and define barrier requirements—solid doors, card readers, tamper-resistant locks, and alarmed push-bar emergency exits that preserve WHS life safety while preventing unauthorised external entry. For fully cloud-hosted infrastructure, document the reliance boundary with cloud or colocation providers.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review annotated floor plans against physical walkthrough observations, inspecting perimeter door construction, emergency exit alarms, and landlord/co-working boundary controls.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Current floor plans demarcate public, general, and secure zones with defined physical barriers aligned to asset sensitivity. Emergency exits allow immediate egress for safety while remaining locked from outside and alarmed on activation. Hosted facility boundaries are explicitly documented.
questions.red_flags: No floor plans or defined perimeter boundaries. Fire exits propped open for ventilation or lacking external locks and alarms. Shared co-working spaces housing sensitive operations without lockable private suites.
questions.nc_pattern: Physical security perimeters protecting areas containing in-scope information or processing facilities are not defined or lack adequate physical barriers under Control 7.1.

questions.question: What evidence confirms that physical security perimeters are periodically inspected for vulnerabilities and maintained effectively?
questions.guidance: Conduct scheduled physical security walkthroughs (at least annually and after office fit-outs or relocations) to check door closers, lock hardware, perimeter glazing, ceiling/underfloor voids around secure rooms, and alarm operation, tracking any physical defects to prompt remediation.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect recent facility inspection checklists and maintenance tickets alongside their own physical walkthrough findings to confirm perimeter integrity is actively maintained.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Dated physical security inspection reports document checks across all perimeter doors, windows, locks, and secure-room walls, with identified defects logged and remediated promptly.
questions.red_flags: Broken magnetic locks, faulty door closers, or unpatched wall penetrations left unaddressed. Zero physical inspection records since office occupancy began.
questions.nc_pattern: Physical perimeter barriers are degraded or unmaintained, creating unmitigated unauthorised entry paths contrary to Control 7.1.

controls.short_summary: Restrict physical access to authorised personnel and supervise all visitors.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.2 ensures secure areas are protected by entry controls that authenticate authorised personnel, enforce least-privilege physical access, promptly revoke badges when people leave, and strictly control visitor and delivery access through sign-in logs, identification, and escorting.
controls.why_it_matters: Tailgating, unreturned access cards, and unescorted visitors allow attackers to bypass expensive perimeter hardware effortlessly. Tight entry logging also provides essential audit trails if equipment disappears or tampering is suspected.
key_deliverables: Physical Access Control Procedure and Badge Provisioning Matrix
Electronic Access Control Logs and Periodic Physical Access Reviews
Visitor and Contractor Sign-In Register
Badge Revocation Records Tied to HR Offboarding
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors reconcile active building/server-room swipe cards against the current HR leaver list and inspect the visitor sign-in log for missing sign-out times or unescorted entries. The #1 trap is revoking IT accounts on termination while leaving physical access cards active for months.

questions.question: How is physical entry to offices and secure areas restricted to authorised personnel, reviewed periodically, and revoked promptly upon termination or role change?
questions.guidance: Authenticate entry via individual swipe cards, mobile credentials, or biometrics (never shared PIN codes for secure rooms), restrict high-security areas such as server rooms to named authorised staff, review active access lists periodically, and integrate physical badge deactivation directly into HR offboarding workflows.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors pull the active physical access roster, compare it against recent HR terminations and role changes, and verify entry logs are retained and protected.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Individual access credentials are issued only upon approved requests, with server-room access limited to named operational staff. Periodic physical access reviews and HR-linked revocation records confirm leavers' badges are disabled on their final day.
questions.red_flags: Shared keypad PINs unchanged for years. Active swipe cards still assigned to former employees or unnamed generic 'spare' cards left untracked at reception.
questions.nc_pattern: Unrestricted or unauthenticated entry to secure areas, failure to revoke physical access promptly upon termination, or absence of periodic physical access reviews under Control 7.2.

questions.question: How are visitors, contractors, and deliveries authenticated, logged, escorted, and separated from secure areas?
questions.guidance: Require visitors and third-party contractors to register at reception with date, name, organisation, host, and entry/exit timestamps; issue visually distinct temporary passes; enforce continuous host escorting inside restricted zones; and isolate loading docks or courier drop-off points from internal office and server areas.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review the visitor register for completeness (including sign-out times and host names), observe reception handling during the audit visit, and check how couriers and cleaners are managed.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An electronic or bound visitor register captures identity, purpose, host, and entry/exit times while protecting visitor privacy from casual viewing. Temporary badges are issued and collected on departure, hosts escort visitors inside controlled areas, and deliveries remain segregated from secure zones.
questions.red_flags: Open paper sign-in sheet exposing prior visitors' personal details, missing sign-out times, or contractors wandering through offices and comms closets unescorted.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to log, authorise, and supervise visitors or third-party personnel entering secure areas as required by Control 7.2.

controls.short_summary: Secure offices, meeting spaces and server rooms against unauthorised access.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.3 focuses on the physical security of internal rooms and facilities—including offices, boardrooms, print areas, and dedicated server or communications rooms. Sensitive facilities must be discreetly located, properly locked when unattended, and shielded from visual or acoustic eavesdropping.
controls.why_it_matters: Even inside an office perimeter, unlocked server closets, glass-walled boardrooms facing public lobbies, or shared print stations allow visitors and unauthorised staff to observe or steal sensitive information.
key_deliverables: Office and Server-Room Physical Security Standards
Key and Lock Management Register
Server-Room / Comms-Closet Inspection and Access Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check whether server rooms and network patch closets are locked and unmarked on public directories, test key control registers, and look for exposed confidential whiteboards or glass-front executive rooms.

questions.question: How are offices, meeting rooms, shared print areas, and sensitive rooms designed and secured to prevent unauthorised access, visual observation, or eavesdropping?
questions.guidance: Site sensitive rooms away from public walkways, avoid labelling server or security rooms on public building directories, use frosting or blinds on glass meeting rooms handling confidential discussions, lock unoccupied offices holding sensitive material, and apply pull-printing or physical controls to shared printers.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors walk through general offices, shared spaces, and meeting rooms observing glazing privacy, door locks, printer placement, and public directory signage.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Facility guidelines define room-level security covering discreet placement of sensitive rooms, visual/acoustic privacy in meeting areas, lockable storage for print/mail rooms, and controlled key management. Physical walkthroughs match documented standards.
questions.red_flags: Public lobby directory pointing directly to 'Main Server Room'. Confidential HR or executive rooms with transparent glazing facing public waiting areas. Uncontrolled spare keys hanging in unlocked cupboards.
questions.nc_pattern: Offices, meeting rooms, or sensitive facilities lack appropriate physical security design or locking controls against unauthorised access or observation under Control 7.3.

questions.question: What operating evidence confirms that server rooms, communications closets, and high-security rooms remain locked and restricted to authorised personnel?
questions.guidance: Keep server rooms, MDF/IDF network cabinets, and archive rooms continuously locked with individualised access control or strictly logged key custody. Review entry logs and perform periodic spot checks confirming racks are closed, doors are not wedged open, and no combustible storage or clutter accumulates inside equipment rooms.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors physically inspect comms closets and server rooms (or review colocation/cloud SOC 2 physical controls where on-premises servers do not exist) and check key registers and access logs.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Server and network rooms remain locked with logged, least-privilege access, clean cable/rack housekeeping, and tracked key custody. For cloud-hosted workloads, current provider ISO 27001 or SOC 2 assurance reports verify equivalent facility security.
questions.red_flags: Network switch rack located in an unlocked cleaner's cupboard or open office corridor. Server-room door wedged open for cooling. No record of who holds physical override keys.
questions.nc_pattern: Server rooms, communications closets, or sensitive rooms are left unlocked or accessible to unauthorised personnel, breaching Control 7.3.

controls.short_summary: Continuously monitor premises for unauthorised access and respond to alerts.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.4 (a 2022 new control) requires continuous physical monitoring of premises—using tools such as intrusion alarms, CCTV, and door-forced sensors—backed by tested alert response procedures and secure retention of monitoring records. Where workloads live in cloud or colocation facilities, organisations must obtain assurance over the provider's physical monitoring.
controls.why_it_matters: Preventive locks alone cannot stop a determined intruder if nobody detects a forced door or after-hours entry until Monday morning. Reliable monitoring and verified response close the detection gap while supplying forensic evidence when incidents occur.
key_deliverables: Physical Monitoring Architecture (CCTV, Intrusion Alarms, Door Sensors)
Alarm Monitoring Contract and Incident Response Runbook
Monitoring Uptime, Maintenance and Alert-Testing Records
CCTV/Log Retention Policy and Cloud/Colocation Assurance Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that cameras and alarms actually work (not dead recorders), test how after-hours alerts are answered, check footage retention and privacy compliance, and verify cloud/colocation assurance reports for hosted systems.

questions.question: How is continuous physical security monitoring implemented for organisational premises, and how is physical monitoring verified for cloud or colocation facilities?
questions.guidance: Deploy risk-appropriate physical monitoring—intrusion detection, door-ajar/forced-entry alarms, and CCTV covering entry/exit points and secure rooms—linked to a 24/7 monitoring centre or building security desk. For cloud or colocation environments, review and record annual provider assurance artefacts (such as ISO/IEC 27001 certificates or SOC 2 Type II reports) covering physical monitoring.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify camera and sensor placement against entry points and secure rooms, confirm 24/7 monitoring coverage, and inspect reviewed cloud/colocation assurance reports.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented monitoring coverage maps CCTV cameras, motion sensors, and door alarms across all perimeter entrances and secure rooms, backed by a 24/7 monitoring arrangement. Cloud and colocation vendor reviews explicitly verify physical monitoring controls annually.
questions.red_flags: Blind spots at rear entrances or server-room doors. Reliance on building landlord CCTV without verifying coverage or access to footage. Cloud provider physical security assumed without reviewing SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports.
questions.nc_pattern: Premises containing in-scope assets are not continuously monitored for unauthorised physical access, or physical monitoring assurance is unverified for hosted facilities under Control 7.4.

questions.question: What evidence confirms that physical monitoring systems operate continuously and that detected alerts trigger timely, tested response?
questions.guidance: Protect monitoring panels and recorders with backup power and tamper detection, conduct periodic health checks and alarm-trigger tests, and maintain documented response procedures defining escalation paths, security-patrol dispatch, and hand-off into the information security incident response process.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review alarm test logs, recorder uptime/health records, and recent alarm or tailgating alert tickets to confirm alerts are genuinely monitored and acted upon.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Routine alarm and CCTV health checks confirm continuous recording, tamper protection, and backup power. Tested response runbooks and alert-handling logs show physical security triggers are investigated promptly and escalated to incident management when warranted.
questions.red_flags: CCTV NVR failed months ago unnoticed. Frequent false alarms ignored or silenced without investigation. No documented response procedure for after-hours intrusion alerts.
questions.nc_pattern: Physical monitoring systems are not maintained in continuous operation, or there is no effective response capability for detected physical security alerts under Control 7.4.

questions.question: How are physical monitoring recordings and access logs protected against tampering, restricted to authorised reviewers, and retained in compliance with privacy laws?
questions.guidance: Store CCTV footage and access logs securely (tamper-resistant local NVR inside a locked room or encrypted cloud storage) with role-based access and audit trails of viewing/exports. Define retention periods aligned with business need and Australian workplace surveillance and privacy laws, including clear workplace CCTV signage.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify who can access or delete CCTV footage, inspect retention settings, and check compliance with state/territory workplace surveillance notice requirements.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Monitoring systems enforce encrypted storage, role-based access, and defined retention windows (for example, 30–90 days) with automatic purge. Workplace surveillance notices are displayed appropriately, and footage access is logged.
questions.red_flags: CCTV recorder sitting unlocked under reception desk with default admin password. Unbounded indefinite footage retention or unrestricted viewing by general staff. Missing workplace surveillance notices.
questions.nc_pattern: Physical monitoring data is unprotected against unauthorised access or tampering, or lacks defined retention and legal compliance controls under Control 7.4.

controls.control_name: Protecting Against Physical and Environmental Threats
controls.short_summary: Assess and mitigate fire, flood, weather and environmental threats to facilities.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.5 requires organisations to identify physical and environmental threats—including fire, flood, bushfire, extreme heat, storms, and civil disruption—and implement proportionate protective measures across offices and hosted facilities to safeguard personnel and information assets.
controls.why_it_matters: Australian facilities face real environmental hazards from severe storms, bushfire smoke, and urban flooding alongside everyday server-room fires or burst pipes. Proactive environmental risk assessment and tested fire/water safeguards directly protect availability and link cleanly to Amendment 1:2024 climate considerations.
key_deliverables: Physical and Environmental Threat Risk Assessment
Fire Detection, Suppression and Environmental Monitoring Specifications
Annual Fire-Safety and Environmental Equipment Inspection Certificates
Hosted Data-Centre Environmental Assurance Reviews
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check that environmental risks have been formally assessed for each site and inspect current fire-equipment service tags, water/temperature sensors, and hosted facility certifications.

questions.question: How are physical and environmental threats—including fire, flood, extreme weather, and site-specific hazards—assessed and reviewed across organisational and hosted facilities?
questions.guidance: Conduct and periodically review a physical and environmental threat assessment for each in-scope location (covering natural disasters, bushfire/flood zoning, neighbouring hazardous occupancy, and building infrastructure risks), feeding relevant findings into the main risk register and business continuity plans.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify site-specific environmental threats were evaluated—aligning with Clause 4.1 climate determinations—rather than assuming urban office buildings have zero environmental exposure.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented site environmental risk assessment evaluates fire, water ingress, extreme weather, power/cooling failure, and local hazards for each facility, linked to business continuity scenarios and reviewed annually or upon site change.
questions.red_flags: No environmental risk assessment exists for on-premises server rooms or regional offices. Site relocations completed without assessing flood, fire, or climate risks.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to identify and assess physical and environmental threats affecting in-scope facilities as required by Control 7.5.

questions.question: What protective controls and maintenance records verify ongoing protection against fire, water, temperature, and other environmental threats?
questions.guidance: Implement appropriate safeguards—smoke/fire detection, suitable suppression (clean-agent systems or dry extinguishers appropriate for electrical equipment), water-leak detection, HVAC/temperature alerting in equipment rooms, and prohibition of combustible materials near racks—and retain statutory fire-safety and maintenance inspection certificates (plus provider reports for cloud/colocation sites).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors check fire extinguisher service tags (AS 1851 compliance in Australia), fire-panel inspection certificates, server-room environmental alerts, and hosted provider assurance reports.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Current inspection certificates confirm fire detection, suppression, and HVAC systems are serviced on schedule. Server/comms rooms have active temperature/water alerting, clean housekeeping free of cardboard storage, and verified environmental assurance for hosted data centres.
questions.red_flags: Expired fire extinguisher service tags, cardboard boxes stacked beside server racks, disabled temperature alarms, or water-based sprinklers over unprotected live racks with no mitigation.
questions.nc_pattern: Physical and environmental protective measures are absent, unmaintained, or ineffective against identified threats under Control 7.5.

controls.short_summary: Enforce behavioural rules, supervision and recording restrictions in secure areas.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.6 establishes strict operating rules for anyone working inside high-security areas such as server rooms, data centres, network operations centres, or restricted processing zones. It restricts knowledge of secure areas to a need-to-know basis, requires supervision of third parties and lone workers where warranted, and controls cameras or recording devices.
controls.why_it_matters: A single smartphone photo of rack wiring, asset tags, or monitoring screens—or an unsupervised cleaner or technician in a server room—can expose sensitive architecture or enable physical tampering.
key_deliverables: Secure Area Working Rules and Signage
Photography and Recording Device Restriction Policy
Escort, Supervision and Access Logs for Secure Areas
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect secure area rules, verify how cleaners, facilities staff, and external technicians are supervised inside server rooms, and check whether unauthorised photography or recording is explicitly controlled.

questions.question: Are operating rules defined and communicated for working in secure areas—including need-to-know restrictions and controls over photography, video, and recording equipment?
questions.guidance: Publish clear rules for secure zones covering authorised activities, prohibition of food/drink or unattended work where inappropriate, locking rooms whenever vacant, limiting awareness of secure-area existence to need-to-know staff, and restricting personal cameras, phones, or audio/video recording devices unless explicitly authorised.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify documented secure-area rules exist, check visible signage or briefings for authorised personnel, and confirm recording-device restrictions are enforceable.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented secure-area rules explicitly cover permitted activities, vacant-room locking, need-to-know discretion, and restrictions on photographic, video, and audio recording devices. Personnel authorised for secure areas acknowledge these rules.
questions.red_flags: No written rules governing conduct inside server rooms or restricted work zones. Routine unapproved photos of server racks or restricted operations posted in public chats or social media.
questions.nc_pattern: Security measures and working rules for personnel operating in secure areas—including controls over recording equipment—are not designed or implemented under Control 7.6.

questions.question: How is work inside secure areas supervised and verified, particularly for third-party technicians, cleaners, and maintenance staff?
questions.guidance: Require continuous accompaniment by an authorised staff member whenever third-party technicians, facilities workers, or cleaners enter secure rooms, log entry/exit times and work performed, and perform post-visit checks confirming doors are locked and nothing unauthorised was left behind.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect server-room escort logs and interview facilities or IT staff to confirm third-party maintenance and cleaning personnel are never left unsupervised inside secure rooms.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Escort logs record every third-party entry into secure areas with named internal host, purpose, and entry/exit timestamps. Routine checks verify vacant secure areas remain locked and free of unauthorised items.
questions.red_flags: After-hours cleaning staff holding master keys to server rooms with no supervision. External network technicians left alone inside comms closets without logs or verification.
questions.nc_pattern: Unsupervised third-party access or lack of operational enforcement of secure-area working controls under Control 7.6.

controls.short_summary: Protect papers, removable media and unattended screens from casual exposure.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.7 requires clear desk rules for papers and removable storage media alongside clear screen rules for computers and mobile devices. Workspaces must be cleared when unattended, lockable storage provided where paper is used, and endpoint screens locked automatically after short inactivity.
controls.why_it_matters: Confidential printouts left on desks or printers and unlocked laptops in open-plan offices, hot-desking hubs, or remote homes remain an effortless source of accidental data disclosure and credential hijack.
key_deliverables: Clear Desk and Clear Screen Policy
MDM / Group Policy Automated Screen-Lock Configuration
Lockable Physical Storage and Secure-Print Arrangements
Periodic Walkthrough Compliance Check Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors perform live office walkthroughs looking for sticky-note passwords, unattended confidential printouts, or unlocked screens, and check MDM/GPO enforcement of automatic screen-lock timeouts.

questions.question: Are clear desk and clear screen rules defined, supported by lockable physical storage and technical automatic screen-lock enforcement?
questions.guidance: Establish clear rules requiring personnel to lock screens manually when stepping away, enforce automated inactivity screen locks via MDM/GPO (typically 5–15 minutes), store sensitive paper records and removable media in locked drawers or cabinets when unattended, clear meeting-room whiteboards, and retrieve printouts promptly (ideally using pull-printing).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify policy clarity, inspect MDM/GPO screen-lock settings across corporate endpoints (including Windows, macOS, and mobile devices), and check that lockable storage or shred bins are provided where paper is handled.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved Clear Desk and Clear Screen Policy covers offices, shared spaces, and remote workspaces, reinforced by MDM/GPO policies enforcing automatic screen locks and password/biometric re-authentication. Lockable cabinets, secure-print release, and locked shred bins are readily available.
questions.red_flags: Screen-lock timeouts disabled or left to user discretion. Sensitive hard-copy files handled by finance or HR with no lockable cabinets or cross-cut shredding facilities provided.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined clear desk and clear screen rules, or failure to provide necessary physical storage and screen-locking controls under Control 7.7.

questions.question: What evidence verifies ongoing compliance with clear desk and clear screen rules across offices and managed endpoints?
questions.guidance: Verify compliance through periodic unannounced or scheduled office walkthroughs (recording findings and coaching follow-ups) alongside automated MDM compliance reports confirming screen-lock policies are active across the endpoint fleet.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors combine their own on-site walkthrough observations with MDM screen-lock compliance dashboards and periodic internal inspection logs.
