questions.what_good_looks_like: MDM compliance reports confirm screen-lock enforcement across managed endpoints, while periodic office walkthrough logs record spot checks of desks, printers, and whiteboards with prompt follow-up on any exceptions.
questions.red_flags: Passwords written on sticky notes, sensitive HR/client files left overnight on open desks, or MDM reports showing widespread screen-lock exemptions.
questions.nc_pattern: Clear desk and clear screen rules are not enforced or verified in practice, resulting in exposed unattended documents or unlocked endpoints contrary to Control 7.7.

controls.short_summary: Site and shield hardware to reduce environmental damage and unauthorised viewing.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.8 requires information processing equipment—such as servers, network gear, workstations, and printers—to be physically positioned and protected to minimise environmental hazards, accidental physical damage, electromagnetic interference, and unauthorised shoulder-surfing.
controls.why_it_matters: Placing network switches beneath overhead water pipes, positioning reception monitors toward public visitors, or allowing drinks beside hardware racks creates preventable outages and data leaks.
key_deliverables: Equipment Siting and Protection Standards
Server-Room and Workstation Physical Layout Reviews
Privacy Screen and Environmental-Siting Inspection Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors visually inspect server racks, network closets, reception desks, and shared printers during walkthroughs for overhead water risks, overheating, cable trip hazards, and exposed screens.

questions.question: How are siting criteria established to protect equipment from environmental hazards, physical damage, and unauthorised visual observation?
questions.guidance: Define physical siting rules requiring critical equipment to be mounted off the floor in locked ventilated racks away from water pipes, windows, direct sunlight, and dust; banning food and drink near server racks; and angling monitors or fitting privacy filters for screens visible to reception areas, windows, or public walkways.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify documented siting rules address both environmental/physical resilience and visual privacy (such as reception or ground-floor workstations).
questions.what_good_looks_like: Facility and IT standards specify rack elevation, airflow, separation from plumbing and hazard zones, food/drink bans in equipment rooms, and screen positioning or privacy-filter requirements for exposed desks.
questions.red_flags: Servers sitting directly on carpet in basement areas prone to leaks. Reception or customer-service screens facing public seating with no angling or privacy filters.
questions.nc_pattern: Equipment siting criteria fail to address environmental hazards, physical damage, or unauthorised viewing risks under Control 7.8.

questions.question: What inspection evidence confirms that equipment is sited and physically protected in practice across organisational sites?
questions.guidance: Perform periodic physical checks of comms rooms, racks, printers, and high-visibility workstations to confirm protective conditions remain intact (and review hosted provider physical infrastructure reports where infrastructure is outsourced).
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors corroborate inspection logs with live walkthroughs of office floors, print hubs, and comms cabinets.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Periodic site inspection records confirm equipment racks are elevated, cooled, locked, and clear of liquids or hazards, and high-visibility monitors use proper positioning or privacy filters. Hosted facilities are backed by current provider assurance reports.
questions.red_flags: Coffee cups resting on network switches, blocked rack vents causing overheating, or ground-floor monitors displaying customer records directly facing a public street.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope equipment is sited in a manner that exposes it to avoidable environmental damage, tampering, or unauthorised observation contrary to Control 7.8.

controls.short_summary: Authorise, track and protect organisational equipment and data taken off-site.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.9 protects laptops, mobile devices, portable media, and documents taken outside organisational premises—whether during business travel, client visits, home working, or courier transit. Assets must be authorised for off-site removal, tracked accurately, protected from theft or exposure, and remotely lockable or wipeable if lost.
controls.why_it_matters: Stolen laptops from cars, lost phones at airports, and untracked demo equipment remain frequent triggers for notifiable data breaches. Strong encryption paired with tight asset tracking turns a physical theft into a minor hardware replacement rather than a regulatory crisis.
key_deliverables: Off-Premises Asset Security Policy and Travel Guidance
Asset Assignment and Off-Premises Tracking Register
MDM Encryption and Remote-Wipe Capability Evidence
Lost/Stolen Asset Incident and Return Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors trace assigned laptops and mobile devices in the asset register to confirm encryption, MDM tracking, and off-site authorisation rules, and check how lost or stolen devices were handled.

questions.question: How are off-premises asset authorisation, physical handling, transit protection, and technical safeguards (such as encryption and remote wipe) defined and communicated?
questions.guidance: Define policy and practical user guidance covering which assets may leave premises, rules against leaving devices unattended in vehicles or public spaces, carrying laptops as cabin luggage during air travel, disguising corporate branding where risk warrants, encrypting all portable devices, and immediately reporting loss or theft.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review off-premises handling rules, check alignment with remote-working and acceptable-use policies, and verify users receive clear guidance on travel and physical protection.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Approved off-premises and travel security guidance specifies authorisation rules, never-leave-unattended physical care, secure transit packaging, full-disk encryption, remote-wipe readiness, and immediate theft-reporting channels. Personnel acknowledge these rules during onboarding and awareness training.
questions.red_flags: No rules governing removal of corporate laptops, backup drives, or physical files from offices. Staff routinely storing unencrypted work laptops in unattended car boots overnight.
questions.nc_pattern: Off-site assets are not covered by defined physical and technical security requirements or user protection guidance under Control 7.9.

questions.question: How are assets removed from premises tracked throughout their custody, and what evidence verifies prompt response if an off-site asset is lost or stolen?
questions.guidance: Maintain an accurate asset register linking every portable laptop, phone, and loan device to a named custodian (augmented by MDM check-in telemetry), require formal sign-out/return tracking for shared or pool equipment, and retain incident tickets showing remote lock/wipe execution and credential revocation whenever a device is reported lost or stolen.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample off-site devices in the asset register to confirm custodian ownership and MDM encryption status, inspect loan-pool logs, and review any lost-device incident tickets.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A reconciled asset register paired with MDM telemetry maps every off-premises laptop or mobile device to an active custodian with verified encryption and remote-wipe capability. Shared equipment uses signed checkout logs, while lost-device tickets prove rapid remote wipe alongside session revocation.
questions.red_flags: Untracked pool laptops or devices still assigned to departed staff. Unable to confirm whether a recently lost laptop was encrypted or remotely wiped.
questions.nc_pattern: Assets removed from premises are not tracked to accountable custodians or lack verifiable protection against loss or theft under Control 7.9.

controls.short_summary: Control storage media across acquisition, encrypted use, transport and disposal.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.10 governs the entire lifecycle of physical storage media—such as USB drives, external hard disks, SD cards, and backup tapes—from acquisition and encrypted usage through secure physical storage, authorised transport, and verified erasure or destruction at end of life.
controls.why_it_matters: Uncontrolled USB sticks are both a primary malware vector and an effortless data-exfiltration route. Even in cloud-native businesses, organisations must prove removable media is either technically blocked or strictly controlled, encrypted, and securely destroyed.
key_deliverables: Storage Media Handling and Removable-Media Policy
Endpoint USB/Removable-Media Restriction Configuration (DLP/MDM/EDR)
Removable Media Inventory (where permitted)
Verified Media Erasure and Destruction Certificates
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors test whether USB mass storage is actually blocked (or encryption-enforced) on endpoints via MDM/EDR, and inspect destruction certificates for any retired hard drives, backup tapes, or removable media.

questions.question: How is storage media—including removable media such as USB drives and external disks—governed and technically controlled across acquisition, encrypted use, storage, and transport?
questions.guidance: Either prohibit removable storage media technically via MDM/EDR device-control policies (with formal time-bound exceptions) or mandate organisation-issued, hardware-encrypted media tracked in an asset register. Define physical storage rules (locked cabinets aligned to classification) and secure tamper-evident courier procedures if physical media is ever transported.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect endpoint device-control rules in MDM/EDR consoles to verify USB blocking or mandatory encryption is enforced, and review any approved exception registers.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A clear media-handling policy paired with active MDM/EDR device-control policies blocks unauthorised USB mass storage across endpoints (or enforces mandatory encryption for approved business cases). Any authorised media is inventoried, stored securely, and transported via tracked, encrypted methods.
questions.red_flags: Policy bans USB drives on paper while every corporate laptop allows unrestricted read/write to personal flash drives. Unencrypted external hard drives used for ad-hoc backups and kept in unlocked drawers.
questions.nc_pattern: Storage media is not managed across its lifecycle in accordance with classification and handling rules, or removable-media restrictions are unenforced under Control 7.10.

questions.question: How is storage media securely erased or physically destroyed when no longer required, and what verifiable disposal records are retained?
questions.guidance: Define sanitisation and destruction methods matched to information classification (such as cryptographic erasure, NIST SP 800-88 / ISM-aligned overwriting, degaussing, or physical shredding/crushing) using vetted destruction vendors where outsourced. Retain serialised destruction certificates and erasure logs cross-referenced to the asset register.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample retired drives, tapes, or removable media from the asset register and trace each item to a dated erasure log or third-party certificate of destruction.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Disposal procedures mandate classification-aligned sanitisation or physical destruction before media leaves organisational control. Serialised certificates of destruction or verified erasure logs are retained and reconciled back to asset retirement records.
questions.red_flags: Old hard drives or USB sticks tossed in general e-waste bins or piled indefinitely in an unlocked storeroom. Missing serial numbers on vendor destruction certificates.
questions.nc_pattern: Storage media containing organisational information is disposed of without verified secure erasure or physical destruction, or without retaining auditable disposal records under Control 7.10.

controls.short_summary: Protect, monitor and test power, cooling and telecom utilities supporting facilities.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.11 protects information processing facilities from power failures, surges, cooling loss, and telecommunications outages through resilient utility design (such as UPS units, generators, redundant ISP links, and HVAC), continuous fault monitoring, and regular maintenance and failover testing.
controls.why_it_matters: Unplanned power cuts, dead UPS batteries, or failed server-room air conditioning cause abrupt data corruption and prolonged downtime. For cloud-first firms, demonstrating due diligence over cloud or colocation utility resilience is equally vital to availability commitments.
key_deliverables: Supporting Utilities Architecture and Resilience Specifications
Utility Monitoring and Fault-Alerting Configurations
UPS, Generator and HVAC Maintenance and Failover Test Records
Cloud/Colocation Provider Resilience Assurance Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect UPS health, generator and HVAC test logs, and redundant telecom feeds (or review Tier/SOC 2 availability evidence for cloud and colocation providers). The classic failure is installing a UPS years ago and never testing or replacing its expired batteries.

questions.question: How are supporting utilities—including power, UPS/generators, cooling, and telecommunications—protected and designed with redundancy commensurate with availability requirements?
questions.guidance: Match utility resilience to business continuity targets: deploy surge protection and UPS battery backup for orderly shutdown or generator cutover, dual-carrier telecommunications where office connectivity is critical, adequate HVAC for equipment rooms, and physical protection of utility intake switches. For cloud or colocation workloads, verify multi-zone redundancy and provider facility certifications.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify utility resilience aligns with documented RTO/availability targets and check physical protection of power/utility distribution boards and hosted provider assurance reports.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Utility specifications document UPS capacity, generator backup (where required), HVAC redundancy, and diverse telecom links aligned with availability targets, with utility panels secured against tampering. Cloud and colocation resilience is verified via current provider assurance reports.
questions.red_flags: Critical on-premises servers or network gear plugged directly into unprotected wall sockets with no UPS. Single-point-of-failure office internet with no failover despite real-time operational dependency.
questions.nc_pattern: Information processing facilities are not protected against failures or disruptions in supporting utilities commensurate with availability requirements under Control 7.11.

questions.question: How are supporting utilities monitored for faults, capacity degradation, or outages, and how are alerts escalated?
questions.guidance: Configure automated monitoring and alerting on UPS battery health, power failovers, server-room temperature/humidity, and WAN link availability so operations teams receive immediate warnings before equipment shuts down or overheats.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect live monitoring dashboards or alerting rules for UPS, HVAC, and telecom links and verify alert recipients and escalation workflows are current.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated SNMP/NMS or building-management alerts monitor UPS load, battery health, power transitions, HVAC temperatures, and primary/secondary network links, routing alerts immediately to on-call operations staff.
questions.red_flags: UPS beeping with a red battery-fault light inside a comms room with no automated alerting configured. Utility alerts routed to a former employee's email address.
questions.nc_pattern: Supporting utilities lack operational monitoring or effective fault escalation capable of detecting failures before service impact under Control 7.11.

questions.question: What inspection, maintenance, and testing records confirm that backup utilities and failover mechanisms work reliably under load?
questions.guidance: Schedule periodic vendor servicing and functional testing—UPS battery load tests, generator start/transfer tests, HVAC servicing, and redundant ISP failover drills—and retain dated test reports along with remediation records for any failed checks.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors review dated maintenance certificates and failover test logs from the past 12 months, verifying batteries and generators are actually tested rather than assumed operational.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Annual or semi-annual maintenance logs and failover test reports confirm UPS batteries, generators, cooling units, and backup telecom circuits perform within specification, with worn components replaced proactively.
questions.red_flags: UPS batteries well past manufacturer replacement life with zero test records. Generator or WAN failover never tested since installation.
questions.nc_pattern: Supporting utilities are not regularly inspected, maintained, or tested in accordance with manufacturer specifications and availability requirements under Control 7.11.

controls.short_summary: Protect power and data cables from interception, interference or physical damage.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.12 requires power and telecommunications cables carrying data or supporting critical services to be physically protected against interception, electromagnetic interference, and accidental or deliberate damage—using locked conduits, segregated power and data runs, secured patch panels, and accurate cable documentation.
controls.why_it_matters: Exposed network cables in public lobbies or unlocked wall ports enable physical network tapping or rogue device attachment, while undocumented 'spaghetti' patch cabinets lead to accidental outages during maintenance.
key_deliverables: Physical Cabling Protection Standards
Patch Panel and Cabling Labelling / Port-Mapping Records
Comms-Rack and Cabling Inspection Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check comms racks, under-floor/overhead conduits, unused wall ports in public reception or meeting rooms, and cable labelling during physical walkthroughs.

questions.question: How are power and telecommunications cables protected from interception, electromagnetic interference, and physical damage?
questions.guidance: Route power and network cables underground, in enclosed conduits, or through secured risers; separate power and data cabling to prevent interference; terminate patch panels inside locked cabinets or comms rooms; disable or apply NAC/802.1X to exposed wall ethernet ports in reception or visitor meeting rooms; and encrypt network traffic where physical pathways traverse shared building risers.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect exposed cabling paths, locked patch cabinets, visitor-area wall ports, and compensating network encryption or port-security controls.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Power and data cabling run in segregated, protected conduits terminating inside locked comms cabinets. Unused wall ports in public or shared areas are patched out or protected via port security/802.1X, and sensitive traffic traverses encrypted links.
questions.red_flags: Live corporate ethernet jacks accessible in public reception waiting areas. Loose power and data cables trailing across walkways or hanging out of unlocked hallway cabinets.
questions.nc_pattern: Power or telecommunications cables carrying in-scope data or supporting services are left exposed to avoidable damage, tampering, or interception under Control 7.12.

questions.question: How is network and power cabling documented, labelled, and periodically inspected to prevent misconnection or tampering?
questions.guidance: Maintain clear labelling on patch panels, key trunk cables, and power feeds alongside up-to-date port/cabling diagrams so technicians can trace circuits safely without disrupting live services or overlooking unauthorised inline taps.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect comms racks for structured labelling and ask to see current patch-panel or cabling documentation matched to physical ports.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Structured cabling diagrams and patch-panel schedules match neatly labelled physical cables inside locked racks. Periodic rack inspections verify cabling neatness, port accuracy, and absence of unauthorised connections.
questions.red_flags: Unlabelled tangle of patch cables in an unlocked rack where nobody knows which port feeds critical firewalls or uplinks.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of cabling documentation, labelling, or inspection controls creating unmanaged outage or tampering risk under Control 7.12.

controls.short_summary: Maintain hardware per vendor specs using authorised technicians and logged controls.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.13 ensures information processing equipment is serviced according to manufacturer intervals and specifications to preserve availability, integrity, and confidentiality. Maintenance must be performed only by authorised personnel, with strict access supervision, data protection before off-site repairs, and complete maintenance logs.
controls.why_it_matters: Neglected hardware degrades into unexpected outages, while unsupervised third-party repair visits or sending faulty drives off-site without wiping or contract protections exposes sensitive data directly.
key_deliverables: Equipment Maintenance Schedule and Vendor Support Contracts
Authorised Maintenance Personnel / Vendor Register
Maintenance Service Logs and Off-Site Repair Sanitisation Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check maintenance schedules for critical hardware (UPS, firewalls, servers, HVAC), verify vendor authorisation and escort logs, and ask what happens to sensitive data when a laptop or server disk is sent away for warranty repair.

questions.question: How is equipment maintained in accordance with manufacturer specifications using only authorised maintenance personnel and approved support agreements?
questions.guidance: Maintain an inventory of critical hardware (servers, network appliances, UPS units, environmental systems) with defined preventive maintenance intervals, active vendor support/warranty agreements, and an approved list of authorised internal or third-party maintenance technicians.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify maintenance schedules exist for critical physical equipment, check that vendor support contracts are current, and confirm only authorised, vetted technicians perform servicing.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintenance schedule tracks manufacturer-recommended service intervals and active support contracts for critical hardware. Only vetted, contractually authorised vendors or qualified internal staff are permitted to perform repairs or servicing.
questions.red_flags: Critical hardware running past end-of-support with no maintenance plan. Unvetted ad-hoc local repair shops handed corporate laptops or network gear without authorisation or confidentiality agreements.
questions.nc_pattern: Equipment is not maintained in accordance with recommended service intervals and specifications, or maintenance is performed by unauthorised personnel contrary to Control 7.13.

questions.question: How are on-site maintenance access, off-site repair data protection, and post-maintenance verification controlled and logged?
questions.guidance: Escort external maintenance technicians on-site, log all suspected faults and completed preventive or corrective work, wipe or remove storage media (or enforce encrypted media plus vendor drive-retention clauses) before sending hardware off-site for repair, and verify security controls and configurations are intact before returning serviced equipment to production.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors inspect maintenance service tickets, escort logs, and off-site RMA/warranty repair records to confirm sensitive data was protected and devices were checked before re-entry.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Service logs capture fault descriptions, technician identity, escort details, work performed, and return-to-service checks. Off-site repairs require prior media removal, full-disk encryption verification, or documented vendor confidentiality and drive-retention arrangements.
questions.red_flags: Faulty laptops or server disks couriered to external repair centres with unencrypted data and no wipe or drive-retention record. Maintenance visits performed without logs or post-service verification.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of controlled access, data protection for off-site repairs, or retained maintenance records for in-scope equipment under Control 7.13.

controls.control_name: Secure Disposal or Re-Use of Equipment
controls.short_summary: Verify data sanitisation before equipment is disposed of, returned or re-used.
controls.plain_english_summary: Control 7.14 requires verifying that all sensitive data and licensed software are securely erased or destroyed before any item of equipment containing storage media is disposed of, returned under lease, or reassigned for internal or external re-use. It also covers stripping organisational labels and asset identifiers that could reveal sensitive metadata.
controls.why_it_matters: Residual customer data left on a donated laptop, a returned photocopier hard drive, or a reissued employee workstation causes preventable privacy breaches and software-licensing violations. Both end-of-life disposal and routine internal re-use require verifiable sanitisation, never a simple file delete or quick format.
key_deliverables: Equipment Disposal and Re-Use Sanitisation Procedure
Serialised Third-Party E-Waste Destruction Certificates
Internal Equipment Wipe and Re-Issue Verification Logs
Asset Register Decommissioning and Reassignment Audit Trail
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample both retired assets (demanding serialised destruction certificates matched to the asset register) and reissued laptops or leased printers (verifying full cryptographic wipe/OS re-imaging before re-use). The #1 trap is tracking e-waste disposal certificates while forgetting internal laptop re-use or leased multifunction printers.

questions.question: Does a documented procedure govern both secure disposal and equipment re-use—specifying approved sanitisation standards, verification steps, and removal of organisational identifiers?
questions.guidance: Establish clear lifecycle rules covering all equipment containing storage media (laptops, mobiles, servers, network gear, and multifunction printers) across both retirement/disposal and internal or external re-use. Specify approved sanitisation methods (such as Australian ISM / NIST SP 800-88 Purge or Destroy, verified cryptographic erasure, or physical destruction), require removal of licensed software and company asset stickers where appropriate, and define chain-of-custody controls.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors verify the procedure explicitly covers both disposal AND re-use (including leased equipment returns and non-obvious storage like copiers), rather than only e-waste disposal.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved decommissioning and re-use procedure specifies classification-aligned sanitisation methods (ISM/NIST SP 800-88), explicitly addresses servers, endpoints, mobile devices, and multifunction printers, mandates removal of asset/organisational labels prior to external disposal, and defines verification sign-off requirements.
questions.red_flags: Procedure covers only end-of-life e-waste disposal with no rules for internal laptop re-use or leased copier returns. Relying on simple OS file deletion or quick formatting instead of verified sanitisation.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined verification and sanitisation procedures governing both secure disposal and re-use of equipment containing storage media under Control 7.14.

questions.question: What verifiable records confirm that retired or disposed equipment (including vendor-managed e-waste and returned leased hardware) was securely sanitised or destroyed with full chain of custody?
questions.guidance: Store retired equipment securely while awaiting collection, use vetted e-waste/destruction vendors under contract, reconcile serial numbers before handover, and retain dated certificates of destruction or sanitisation verification reports cross-referenced to asset retirement entries in the asset register.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors select retired assets from the asset register or finance depreciation schedule and trace each serial number to its corresponding destruction certificate or verified wipe log.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Retired hardware awaits disposal in locked storage with logged custody handover. Serialised destruction or sanitisation certificates from vetted disposal vendors reconcile cleanly against decommissioned entries in the asset register, including leased printers and networking hardware.
questions.red_flags: Generic bulk weight receipts ('150 kg e-waste') with no asset serial numbers. Retired laptops donated to schools or sold to staff without verified sanitisation logs. Leased multifunction printers returned without wiping internal drives.
questions.nc_pattern: Equipment containing storage media is disposed of or returned without verifying and documenting secure removal or destruction of sensitive data and licensed software under Control 7.14.

questions.question: What operating records verify that equipment designated for internal or external re-use is securely sanitised, stripped of prior user data and unlicensed software, and verified before reassignment?
questions.guidance: Whenever a laptop, mobile device, or server is returned by a departing or upgrading user for reassignment, execute a documented full cryptographic wipe / MDM factory reset and clean OS rebuild (verifying prior user profiles, local caches, keys, and unnecessary licensed software are completely removed) and log completion in the IT service ticket and asset register before reissuing the device.
questions.auditor_focus: Auditors sample reissued laptops or mobiles from recent onboarding tickets and verify wipe/re-imaging records exist between the previous owner's offboarding date and the new custodian's issue date.
questions.what_good_looks_like: ITSM tickets paired with MDM wipe logs verify that every returned laptop or mobile device undergoes cryptographic erasure before clean re-provisioning. Technician sign-off confirms prior user data plus unneeded licensed software are removed prior to asset reassignment.
questions.red_flags: Returned laptops handed straight to new hires after simply creating a second local Windows/macOS user account. No wipe verification recorded between custodians.
questions.nc_pattern: Equipment containing storage media is re-used or reassigned without verifying that previous sensitive data and licensed software have been securely removed or overwritten under Control 7.14.

controls.short_summary: Harden, encrypt, enrol and manage all laptops, mobiles and workstations.
controls.plain_english_summary: Every laptop, desktop, tablet and mobile device that accesses or stores organisational information must be managed against a documented security baseline. This requires full-disk encryption, automated screen locking, controlled removable media use, endpoint security tooling and reliable remote-wipe procedures for lost or stolen hardware.
controls.why_it_matters: Unprotected endpoints are the most common entry point for ransomware, credential theft and accidental data exposure during travel or remote work. Without central management and encryption, a single lost laptop can trigger a notifiable data breach under the Australian Privacy Act or APRA CPS 234.
key_deliverables: Endpoint Security Policy and Hardening Standard
MDM/UEM Enrolment and Compliance Dashboard Export
Full-Disk Encryption Status and Key Escrow Report
Lost, Stolen and Decommissioned Device Response Procedure
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors first reconcile your asset register and identity directory against MDM/UEM enrolment and encryption telemetry. The most common trap is unmanaged contractor, executive or BYOD devices authenticating to corporate cloud apps outside policy controls.

questions.question: How are endpoint security baselines, screen locks and removable media restrictions defined and technically enforced across corporate and BYOD devices?
questions.guidance: Provide your endpoint security policy and mobile device management (MDM/UEM) configuration profiles showing enforced idle screen locks, host firewalls, OS update baselines and USB/removable storage controls. Clearly state whether BYOD is permitted and, if so, what containerisation or conditional access controls restrict local data storage.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that documented policy settings (such as idle lock timeouts and USB restrictions) actually match live MDM/UEM or Group Policy configurations across Windows, macOS, iOS and Android fleets.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved endpoint security policy defines mandatory controls for corporate and permitted BYOD endpoints, including idle screen locks of 5 to 15 minutes, local administrator removal and USB mass-storage blocking. Technical profiles in Intune, Jamf or Group Policy enforce these settings automatically, with exceptions recorded and approved by risk owners.
questions.red_flags: Policy mandates screen locks or USB blocking, but users can manually disable them or retain permanent local administrator privileges without oversight.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of documented endpoint security rules or systematic failure to enforce baseline protections on in-scope user endpoints accessing organisational information.

questions.question: How do you verify that full-disk encryption and endpoint protection controls are active across all in-scope user devices?
questions.guidance: Supply current compliance exports from your MDM/UEM platform showing encryption status (such as BitLocker or FileVault with escrowed recovery keys) and active host security agents reconciled against the asset register and identity sign-in logs.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check active user count in the identity provider against managed encrypted devices to spot shadow laptops, newly imaged machines or offline endpoints missing encryption.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated MDM compliance reports demonstrate 100% full-disk encryption across managed laptops and mobile devices, with recovery keys securely escrowed. Non-compliant devices are automatically flagged, blocked via conditional access and remediated within defined timeframes.
questions.red_flags: Encryption relies on manual setup checklists with no central verification, recovery keys are not escrowed, or more than a small tracked exception cohort appears unencrypted.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope endpoints storing or accessing confidential organisational data operate without encryption or without verifiable evidence of protection coverage.

questions.question: What procedures and technical capabilities govern lost, stolen or compromised user endpoints from initial report through remote wipe and credential revocation?
questions.guidance: Provide your lost or stolen device response procedure along with sample ticket records or test evidence showing session revocation, remote lock/wipe commands and asset register updates.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that helpdesk and security staff can promptly revoke active authentication tokens and issue a remote wipe, and check whether past device-loss incidents were closed with documented verification.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented runbook requires immediate reporting of lost or stolen endpoints to IT and Security, triggering token revocation, account credential reset and remote device lock or wipe within defined SLAs. Completed tickets record timestamps for each containment step and confirm whether any sensitive data exposure requires privacy or regulatory assessment.
questions.red_flags: No remote-wipe capability exists on corporate laptops or mobiles, or lost devices are simply replaced without revoking active SSO sessions or assessing breach impact.
questions.nc_pattern: No defined or operational mechanism to protect organisational information when user endpoints are lost, stolen or retired.

controls.short_summary: Strictly restrict, approve, authenticate and review elevated admin privileges.
controls.plain_english_summary: Administrative, root, cloud-owner and emergency break-glass accounts carry disproportionate blast radius and must be tightly controlled. Organisations must separate privileged identities from day-to-day user accounts, restrict allocation to verified business need, enforce strong authentication and review privileged memberships frequently.
controls.why_it_matters: Compromised privileged credentials allow attackers to disable logging, destroy backups and move laterally across the entire estate in minutes. Weak privilege hygiene is one of the fastest paths to a Major Nonconformity in ISO 27001 audits and heightened APRA CPS 234 scrutiny.
key_deliverables: Privileged Account and Service Identity Register
Privileged Access Provisioning and Break-Glass Procedure
Periodic Privileged Access Review Sign-Off Records
MFA and Privileged Activity Logging Configuration Evidence
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect live lists of Domain Admins, cloud Global Administrators and database superusers directly from consoles and compare them to approved registers. The top trap is standing admin rights attached to everyday email-enabled accounts or orphaned service accounts.

questions.question: How are all privileged accounts, roles and emergency break-glass identities inventoried, separated from standard user accounts and restricted to least privilege?
questions.guidance: Provide your privileged access register covering infrastructure, cloud tenants, databases, SaaS administrators, high-privilege service accounts and break-glass accounts. Explain how administrative identities are separated from standard email and web-browsing accounts, and note any vaulting or just-in-time (JIT) elevation practices used.
questions.auditor_focus: Pull live high-privilege group memberships (e.g., Entra ID Global Admin, AWS IAM Admin, Domain Admins) and reconcile every single identity against the register, verifying no shared generic admin accounts are used without attribution.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A current privileged access register inventories all human admin accounts, break-glass credentials and privileged service identities with named owners and scope boundaries. Administrators use dedicated, non-mail-enabled accounts for elevated tasks, and commercial PAM or cloud-native JIT elevation is used where proportionate to risk.
questions.red_flags: Users perform daily email and browsing with standing Global Admin privileges, break-glass credentials are shared informally, or service accounts hold wildcard administrative permissions without documented ownership.
questions.nc_pattern: Uncontrolled, uninventoried or excessive allocation of privileged access rights without enforcement of least privilege or separation from routine user duties.

questions.question: How is privileged access formally approved, provisioned (including time-bound or break-glass use) and periodically reviewed for ongoing need?
questions.guidance: Provide your privileged access provisioning workflow, sample approval tickets, and the most recent privileged access review records showing management sign-off and timely revocation of unneeded privileges.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent admin additions and role changes to confirm independent approval before elevation, then inspect review records to verify that identified stale privileges were actually removed rather than merely noted.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Privileged access requests require documented business justification and independent asset-owner approval before provisioning, with temporary elevation used for ad-hoc maintenance. Formal privileged access reviews occur at least quarterly (or more frequently for critical systems), with documented sign-off and prompt revocation of terminated or changed-role accounts.
questions.red_flags: Administrators can self-approve elevated roles, access reviews are rubber-stamped without comparing against HR leaver lists, or former staff retain administrative access.
questions.nc_pattern: Privileged access rights are granted without formal authorisation or are not reviewed and revoked when roles change or employment ends.

questions.question: How are privileged accounts protected by strong multi-factor authentication and monitored through tamper-resistant activity logging?
questions.guidance: Provide conditional access or authentication configurations enforcing phishing-resistant or strong MFA on all privileged consoles, alongside evidence that privileged actions (including break-glass logins) generate high-priority audit logs and alerts.
questions.auditor_focus: Test whether any privileged account, legacy protocol or break-glass login bypasses MFA without documented compensating controls, and verify that privileged activities are captured in logs outside the administrator's ability to alter.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Strong MFA (preferably FIDO2/hardware token or managed authenticator) is technically enforced on every privileged account across identity providers, cloud consoles, hypervisors and network gear. All privileged logins, privilege escalations and break-glass activations are logged centrally and trigger automated alerts reviewed by an independent party; PAM session recording is adopted as good practice for high-risk systems.
questions.red_flags: MFA is optional or excluded for service-desk admins, break-glass usage does not raise an immediate alert, or local administrators can clear their own audit logs.
questions.nc_pattern: Privileged accounts lack strong authentication protections appropriate to risk, or privileged administrative activities are not logged and overseen.

controls.short_summary: Enforce need-to-know and classification-based access across apps and data.
controls.plain_english_summary: Access to information and application functions must be technically restricted in accordance with your access control policy and information classification scheme. Rather than relying on trust or open shared drives, systems must enforce least privilege across folders, cloud repositories, business applications and underlying databases.
controls.why_it_matters: Over-permissioned SharePoint sites, cloud storage buckets and production databases turn routine phishing compromises or insider mistakes into organisation-wide breaches. Demonstrable technical enforcement proves that your classification and access policies operate in reality, not just on paper.
key_deliverables: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) or Permission Matrix
Application and Database Access Control Configuration Evidence
Data Classification and Repository Permission Audit Report
Bulk Export and Sensitive Data Extraction Control Settings
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample a restricted dataset (such as HR payroll, customer PII or board papers) and trace who can read, modify or export it at both the application and database layers. The #1 trap is broad 'Everyone' or 'All Staff' read links on cloud document repositories.

questions.question: How are need-to-know and classification-based access restrictions technically enforced across business applications, document repositories and databases?
questions.guidance: Provide your RBAC or access permission matrix alongside live configuration screenshots from key applications, cloud file stores and databases demonstrating least-privilege separation by role and data classification.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect actual group permissions on sensitive repositories and production databases to confirm that non-authorised staff, developers or generic service accounts cannot bypass application-layer controls.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Access to applications, cloud workspaces and databases is mapped to defined job roles and classification tiers using RBAC or attribute-based controls, with default-deny permissions for restricted data. Direct production database access is tightly limited to authorised DBAs or controlled break-glass workflows, preventing staff from bypassing application access checks.
questions.red_flags: Sensitive HR, finance or customer folders are accessible to 'All Authenticated Users', developers hold standing read/write access to production databases, or permissions are assigned ad hoc to individuals rather than roles.
questions.nc_pattern: Technical access restrictions do not enforce the organisation's access control policy, allowing unauthorised users to view or modify restricted information.

questions.question: How are bulk data extraction, external sharing and sensitive query activities restricted and verified as auditable?
questions.guidance: Explain how sensitive systems restrict bulk downloads, CSV exports, API scraping and external link sharing, and provide sample audit logs or access-restriction verification reports demonstrating traceability.
questions.auditor_focus: Check whether ordinary users can export entire customer tables or share restricted files externally via anonymous links, and verify that denied access attempts and sensitive exports are recorded for review.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Applications restrict bulk export, printing and external sharing of confidential datasets to explicitly authorised roles, backed by technical settings such as disabled anonymous sharing links and scoped API tokens. Access grants, permission changes and high-volume data extractions generate immutable audit logs that are periodically reviewed.
questions.red_flags: Any standard user can download full client registers without logging or approval, or access control changes on critical repositories leave no audit trail.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of proportionate technical controls or auditability over extraction and sharing of restricted information, enabling undetected unauthorised disclosure.

controls.short_summary: Protect source code, build pipelines and deployment tools from unauthorised change.
controls.plain_english_summary: Read and write access to application source code, infrastructure templates, build pipelines and software libraries must be tightly managed to prevent unauthorised tampering or theft of intellectual property. Production code branches and release pipelines must enforce separation of duties so no single individual can silently inject malicious changes into production.
controls.why_it_matters: Compromised repositories or CI/CD pipelines allow attackers to poison software builds and reach every customer or internal system downstream. Auditors treat unreviewed direct commits to production branches as a major integrity and segregation failure.
key_deliverables: Source Code Repository Access and Branch Protection Configuration
CI/CD Pipeline Permission and Deployment Approval Matrix
Sample Pull Request Approval and Signed Commit Audit Trail
Private Package Registry and Dependency Governance Record
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect live Git repository settings (branch protection, required reviewers, admin bypass rules) and trace a recent production release back to its approved pull request. The #1 trap is developers holding repository admin rights that let them override branch protection and merge their own code.

questions.question: How is read and write access to source code repositories, production branches and build/deployment pipelines restricted and segregated?
questions.guidance: Provide repository membership exports, branch protection rules (such as blocked direct pushes and mandatory pull request approvals) and CI/CD pipeline permissions demonstrating segregation between code authors and production deployment controls.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify live settings on main/production branches to confirm force-pushes are disabled, repository administrators are strictly minimised and former contractors have been removed from Git and CI/CD platforms.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Source code repositories enforce SSO and MFA with least-privilege team roles so staff only access repositories required for their role. Protected main and release branches block direct pushes, require independent peer review before merging, and restrict production deployment pipelines and signing keys to authorised release workflows rather than individual developer workstations.
questions.red_flags: Developers can push directly to main or deploy straight to production without independent approval, repositories are inadvertently set to public visibility, or ex-contractors still retain SSH keys or personal access tokens.
questions.nc_pattern: Unrestricted read or write access to source code or build pipelines, or absence of controls preventing unilateral unauthorised changes to production code.

questions.question: How are all source code modifications, third-party libraries and software packages tracked, attributed and protected against unauthorised tampering?
questions.guidance: Provide sample commit and pull-request audit logs showing individual attribution and approval history, alongside controls governing internal package registries, pinned dependency lockfiles and write access to shared libraries.
questions.auditor_focus: Trace two or three recent production releases from deployed artefact back to attributed commits and approved pull requests, checking for unreviewed merges or uncontrolled third-party library injection.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every code change is uniquely attributed to an authenticated user through immutable version control history, linked to an approved change ticket or pull request, and optionally cryptographically signed. Third-party dependencies and internal libraries are pinned via lockfiles, pulled through controlled or scanned package registries and protected against unauthorised modification.
questions.red_flags: Commits use shared service identities or unverified author emails, audit logs of repository access are not retained, or unvetted external packages can be silently substituted during builds.
questions.nc_pattern: Inability to trace and attribute source code or build-library changes to authorised individuals and approved change records.

controls.short_summary: Enforce MFA, strong technical auth protocols and credential-attack defences.
controls.plain_english_summary: Authentication systems must technically verify user and service identities in proportion to the sensitivity of the systems accessed. Distinct from credential lifecycle rules in 5.17, this control covers the technical mechanisms—such as SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, secure password verification, session timeouts and brute-force lockouts—that stop unauthorised logins.
controls.why_it_matters: Stolen passwords, adversary-in-the-middle phishing and credential stuffing remain leading causes of Australian cyber incidents. Weak or bypassable authentication lets attackers walk straight through the front door as legitimate users.
key_deliverables: Identity Provider and SSO Conditional Access Configuration
MFA Enrolment and Enforcement Coverage Report
Password Policy, Breach-Check and Legacy-Protocol Block Settings
Account Lockout, Rate-Limiting and Credential-Attack Protection Evidence
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect live identity provider policies for MFA exclusions, legacy authentication protocols (IMAP/POP/SMTP/Basic Auth) and weak lockout settings. The #1 trap is claiming 'MFA everywhere' while leaving VPNs, legacy SaaS apps or exclusion groups unprotected.

questions.question: What authentication architecture is implemented, and how is multi-factor authentication (MFA) technically enforced across remote access, cloud services and internal systems?
questions.guidance: Provide your identity provider (IdP) conditional access policies and MFA enrolment reports demonstrating coverage across corporate SSO applications, VPN/remote access, email and standalone systems. Detail any exceptions and their compensating controls.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect IdP conditional access exclusion lists and standalone non-SSO applications to confirm MFA is technically mandatory rather than user-optional, and check whether legacy single-factor protocols are blocked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Centralised SSO using SAML 2.0 or OIDC governs access to corporate applications, with technical MFA enforced for all remote access, cloud services and high-risk internal systems. Legacy basic authentication protocols are disabled, MFA enrolment coverage approaches 100% and any rare technical exclusion is formally risk-accepted with compensating network or device restrictions.
questions.red_flags: MFA is enabled only for administrators while general staff use passwords alone for webmail or VPN, legacy protocols remain open, or undocumented accounts sit in permanent MFA-bypass groups.
questions.nc_pattern: Authentication mechanisms are not commensurate with information classification and risk, or required MFA controls are absent or bypassable on in-scope systems.

questions.question: How do authentication systems technically enforce credential strength, prohibit default or compromised passwords and protect credentials in transit and storage?
questions.guidance: Supply technical configuration screenshots from Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta or application authentication modules showing minimum password length/complexity, banned or breached-password filtering, secure hashing and encrypted transmission (TLS).
questions.auditor_focus: Check that authentication systems reject default vendor credentials and known compromised passwords, mask credential entry on screen, avoid plaintext storage and enforce idle session expiration.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Authentication platforms enforce modern passphrase length (such as 12 to 14+ characters) and block common or known breached passwords automatically. Credentials are transmitted exclusively over encrypted channels, stored using strong salted adaptive hashing (such as Argon2 or bcrypt) and paired with bounded session lifetimes.
questions.red_flags: Applications still accept vendor default passwords, store passwords reversibly or with weak hashes, permit 6-character passwords or leave web sessions valid indefinitely without re-authentication.
questions.nc_pattern: Systems fail to technically enforce defined authentication strength requirements or transmit/store authentication secrets insecurely.

questions.question: How do systems handle repeated authentication failures and technically defend against brute-force, password-spraying and credential-stuffing attacks?
questions.guidance: Provide configuration evidence for progressive lockout or throttling, smart lockout, IP/bot rate limiting, impossible-travel or anomalous sign-in detection and generic authentication error messages that avoid account enumeration.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that login endpoints throttle or lock repeated failed attempts without creating trivial denial-of-service risks, log all failures centrally and alert security teams to spraying or stuffing spikes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Identity providers and public login portals enforce smart lockout, progressive delays and WAF rate limiting against brute-force and password-spraying attempts while returning generic failure messages. High-risk sign-ins (such as impossible travel, anonymised IPs or leaked-credential detections) automatically trigger step-up authentication, session blocking and security alerts.
questions.red_flags: Unlimited login attempts are permitted on external portals or APIs, error messages reveal whether a username exists, or mass authentication failures generate no operational alerts.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of technical controls to limit and detect repeated failed authentication attempts or automated credential attacks on exposed authentication interfaces.

controls.short_summary: Monitor resource utilisation, forecast demand and scale capacity ahead of limits.
controls.plain_english_summary: Computing, storage, network bandwidth and cloud service quotas must be continuously monitored and forecast against business growth and seasonal peaks. Distinct from architectural redundancy in 8.14, capacity management prevents performance degradation and availability outages caused by exhausted resources.
controls.why_it_matters: Full disks halt security logging and corrupt databases, while exhausted compute or bandwidth cripples critical customer services and can mask denial-of-service attacks. Under APRA CPS 230, unchecked capacity bottlenecks directly threaten board-approved service tolerances.
key_deliverables: Infrastructure and Cloud Capacity Monitoring Dashboards
Threshold Alerting Configuration and Escalation Runbook
Periodic Capacity Review and Demand Forecast Report
Auto-Scaling or Resource Expansion Procedure
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors look for active utilisation alerts (CPU, memory, disk, database connections, cloud quotas) and evidence of proactive capacity reviews—not just firefighting after an outage. The #1 trap is assuming 'we are in the cloud' eliminates capacity limits while ignoring service quotas, IP exhaustion or database tier ceilings.

questions.question: How is resource utilisation monitored across compute, storage, network and cloud quotas, and what threshold alerts trigger proactive intervention?
questions.guidance: Provide screenshots or exports from your infrastructure monitoring tools showing tracked metrics (CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, log-ingestion volumes and cloud service limits), warning/critical thresholds and sample ticket responses when thresholds were breached.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that alerting thresholds leave sufficient lead time to act before exhaustion, and verify that recent capacity alerts resulted in tracked remediation rather than being ignored.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated monitoring tracks CPU, memory, disk space, network throughput, database connections and cloud API quotas across production systems and security infrastructure. Staged warning and critical alerts (for example, at 75% and 85% utilisation) route to on-call operations teams with clear runbooks before user impact or logging loss occurs.
questions.red_flags: Disk or quota exhaustion is only discovered after an application crashes or stops writing logs, or monitoring alerts flood an unmonitored inbox.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of ongoing monitoring and alerting for resource utilisation across in-scope information processing facilities, exposing availability to preventable exhaustion.

questions.question: How are future capacity requirements forecast against business growth and peak events, and how is capacity scaled when demand increases?
questions.guidance: Provide your capacity planning reviews, trend analyses or load-test projections covering expected business growth, seasonal peaks and major releases, alongside documented manual or automated scaling procedures (including cloud auto-scaling bounds and cost/quota guardrails).
questions.auditor_focus: Look for forward-looking trend data and evidence that capacity planning informs infrastructure procurement or cloud scaling limits prior to peak trading or major product launches.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Operations and engineering teams conduct periodic capacity reviews combining historical utilisation trends with upcoming business initiatives and seasonal peaks. Documented scaling procedures—including tested cloud auto-scaling policies, database tier upgrades and pre-approved quota increases—ensure capacity expands smoothly within operational tolerance levels.
questions.red_flags: No forward capacity forecasting exists, cloud auto-scaling is uncapped or untested against service quotas, or procurement lead times repeatedly cause performance degradation.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of capacity planning and adjustment mechanisms to align resource availability with current and projected operational requirements.

controls.short_summary: Deploy, update, verify and govern anti-malware and EDR across all attack vectors.
controls.plain_english_summary: Workstations, servers, cloud workloads, email gateways and web channels must be protected by coordinated anti-malware and endpoint detection and response (EDR) controls. Effective protection requires verified fleet-wide coverage, timely detection updates, automated quarantine and strict governance over tamper protection and scanning exclusions.
controls.why_it_matters: Modern ransomware and info-stealers specifically target unmonitored servers, stale detection agents and overly broad antivirus exclusions. Gaps in malware defences can rapidly escalate into full operational disruption and reportable APRA or OAIC incidents.
key_deliverables: Anti-Malware / EDR Deployment and Asset Coverage Report
Email Gateway and Web Malware Filtering Configuration
Malware Detection, Quarantine and Containment Playbook
Tamper Protection and Antivirus Exclusion Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors reconcile the EDR console against your asset inventory and check tamper protection and scanning exclusion lists. The #1 trap is leaving servers, Linux/macOS hosts or legacy appliances unprotected while auditing only Windows laptops.

questions.question: How is anti-malware or EDR deployed across all in-scope endpoints, servers and cloud workloads, and how is complete coverage verified against your asset inventory?
questions.guidance: Provide console coverage reports from your anti-malware or EDR platform reconciled against your CMDB/asset register across Windows, macOS, Linux servers and cloud workloads. Explain what compensating controls protect any system that cannot run a standard agent.
questions.auditor_focus: Compare total active hosts in cloud/directory inventories against healthy, recently checking-in EDR agents to identify unmonitored servers, shadow VMs or stale offline endpoints.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Centrally managed anti-malware and EDR agents run across all supported workstations, servers and cloud workloads, with automated daily reconciliation against the asset inventory flagging missing or unhealthy sensors. Systems unable to host an agent (such as network appliances) are explicitly documented with compensating network and hardening controls.
questions.red_flags: Only corporate Windows laptops run EDR while Linux production servers or macOS developer machines are excluded, or dozens of agents have not checked in for months without investigation.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope endpoints or servers lack anti-malware protection or verified deployment coverage without documented, risk-accepted compensating controls.

questions.question: How are malware definitions kept current, how are email and web vectors filtered, and how are malware detections quarantined and investigated?
questions.guidance: Provide configuration evidence showing automated signature/cloud-intelligence updates, email attachment and URL sandboxing/filtering, web-gateway malware blocking, and sample tickets demonstrating containment and root-cause review of past detections (including user reporting supported by awareness under 6.3).
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that email and web malware filters actively block or sandbox malicious payloads, confirm definition update currency across the fleet and review sample detection tickets to see whether alerts are genuinely investigated.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Anti-malware signatures and behavioural detection engines update automatically at least daily (or continuously via cloud intelligence), while email and web gateways scan, sandbox and block malicious attachments, macros and URLs. Detections automatically quarantine files or isolate compromised hosts, triggering a documented security triage workflow with root-cause verification before restoration.
questions.red_flags: Email gateways allow executable or macro-enabled attachments unfiltered, definitions are days or weeks out of date, or quarantined alerts are auto-closed without confirming how the payload arrived.
questions.nc_pattern: Malware detection engines are not kept current, primary delivery vectors (email/web) lack scanning controls, or malware alerts are not acted upon in a timely manner.

questions.question: How are anti-malware controls protected against user or attacker tampering, tested for effectiveness and governed when scanning exclusions are requested?
questions.guidance: Provide EDR policy settings showing tamper protection and uninstall passwords enabled, evidence of periodic control testing (such as EICAR or purple-team validation) and your approved exclusion register showing rationale, scope and periodic review of any excluded paths or processes.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the antivirus/EDR exclusion list for dangerous broad wildcards (such as excluding C:\ or /tmp), verify standard users cannot disable real-time scanning and check for evidence that alerts actually reach responders.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Tamper protection prevents users and unauthorised processes from disabling agents, stopping services or altering policies, with uninstall rights restricted to authorised security administrators. Scanning exclusions are narrowly scoped, require documented security approval with expiry dates, and are reviewed periodically alongside routine detection-path verification tests.
questions.red_flags: Local users can pause or uninstall anti-malware, broad folder or file-extension exclusions exist without documented approval or review, or EDR alerting integration has never been tested.
questions.nc_pattern: Anti-malware protections can be disabled without authorisation, or uncontrolled scanning exclusions materially undermine malware protection without risk oversight.

controls.short_summary: Discover, risk-prioritise, patch and govern technical vulnerabilities.
controls.plain_english_summary: Organisations must systematically obtain timely vulnerability intelligence, scan their full technology estate, prioritise remediation by real-world exploitability and asset criticality, and verify closure against defined SLAs. Where a critical vulnerability cannot be patched within SLA, documented compensating controls, formal risk acceptance and—for APRA-regulated entities—timely regulatory assessment are mandatory.
controls.why_it_matters: Unpatched internet-facing services and outdated libraries are the primary initial access vector in major Australian breaches. Under APRA CPS 234 §36 and CPS 230 §31, unremediated material control weaknesses carry explicit remediation and 10-business-day notification obligations.
key_deliverables: Vulnerability and Patch Management Policy and SLA Matrix
Authenticated Vulnerability Scan and Advisory Intake Reports
Patch Compliance and SLA Remediation Trend Dashboard
Vulnerability Exception, Compensating Control and APRA §36 Escalation Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect recent authenticated scan results, compare open Critical/High CVEs against your stated SLAs and verify whether overdue items have valid compensating controls. The #1 trap is publishing aggressive SLAs (like 48 hours for Critical) that operational teams routinely miss without governance.

questions.question: How do you identify technical vulnerabilities across your infrastructure, endpoints, cloud services and application dependencies through authenticated scanning and security advisories?
questions.guidance: Provide your vulnerability management procedure, scanner scope configuration (showing authenticated internal scans, external perimeter scans and container/dependency scanning), and evidence of subscribed advisory feeds (such as ASD/ACSC alerts, vendor advisories and CISA KEV).
questions.auditor_focus: Check that vulnerability discovery covers the entire in-scope asset inventory—including cloud workloads, third-party libraries and network appliances—and uses authenticated scans rather than surface-level port checks alone.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented vulnerability management programme pairs automated authenticated scanning of servers, endpoints, cloud environments and software dependencies with active monitoring of ACSC, vendor and CISA KEV advisories. Scan coverage is reconciled against the asset register to ensure newly deployed systems are discovered and assessed promptly.
questions.red_flags: Only unauthenticated external scans are run annually, software dependencies and cloud images are omitted from scanning, or no owner monitors emergency zero-day advisories.
questions.nc_pattern: Failure to obtain timely information about technical vulnerabilities affecting in-scope information systems or absence of systematic vulnerability identification.

questions.question: How are identified vulnerabilities prioritised by risk, remediated within defined SLAs and verified as closed?
questions.guidance: Provide your vulnerability prioritisation matrix (combining CVSS, active exploitation/KEV status, internet exposure and asset criticality), patching SLAs by severity tier, and recent compliance reports showing actual remediation performance and re-scan verification.
questions.auditor_focus: Test a sample of recently remediated Critical and High vulnerabilities from scan detection to verified closure, checking whether real-world performance meets documented SLAs and whether end-of-life unsupported software is tracked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Vulnerabilities are triaged using a risk-based framework incorporating exploitability, external exposure and asset criticality, mapped to realistic, approved remediation SLAs (such as urgent timelines for actively exploited internet-facing flaws). Remediation is verified via follow-up authenticated scans or patch telemetry, with monthly compliance metrics reported to security governance.
questions.red_flags: Patching SLAs are routinely breached across dozens of Critical vulnerabilities, remediation is marked 'complete' based solely on verbal confirmation without re-scanning, or unsupported end-of-life operating systems remain in production unaddressed.
questions.nc_pattern: Identified technical vulnerabilities are not evaluated for exposure or remediated in a timely, verifiable manner consistent with organisational risk criteria.

questions.question: How are overdue, unpatchable or end-of-life vulnerabilities governed through compensating controls, time-bound risk acceptance and material-weakness escalation?
questions.guidance: Provide your vulnerability exception register showing business justification, implemented compensating controls (such as virtual patching, WAF rules or network isolation), senior risk-owner approval, expiry dates and escalation triggers—including assessment against APRA CPS 234 §36 (10-business-day notification of unremediated material control weaknesses) and CPS 230 §31 where applicable.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect every overdue Critical or High vulnerability to verify that it either has an active remediation plan with documented compensating controls and senior sign-off, or has been formally escalated as a material control weakness.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Any vulnerability that cannot be patched within SLA requires a time-bound exception documenting why patching is deferred, what technical compensating controls reduce exposure, a target remediation date and risk-owner sign-off. Material control weaknesses that cannot be remediated in a timely manner are escalated to executive risk committees and assessed for APRA CPS 234 §36 notification within 10 business days and CPS 230 §31 remediation tracking.
questions.red_flags: Overdue Critical vulnerabilities sit open indefinitely with no exception record, expired risk acceptances are never re-reviewed, or APRA-regulated entities have no trigger linking severe unpatched weaknesses to CPS 234 §36.
questions.nc_pattern: Unremediated high-risk vulnerabilities persist past defined timeframes without documented risk assessment, compensating controls or formal management escalation.

controls.short_summary: Establish hardened baselines, control changes and monitor configuration drift.
controls.plain_english_summary: Hardware, software, cloud platforms and network devices must be built and maintained against documented security baselines rather than insecure vendor defaults. Organisations must govern changes to those configurations, keep records accurate and routinely detect and remediate unauthorised drift.
controls.why_it_matters: A single misconfigured cloud storage bucket, open security group or default administrative credential can expose entire datasets without any software exploit at all. Consistent baselines also make incident response and vulnerability remediation dramatically faster.
key_deliverables: Hardening Baselines and Build Standards (OS, Cloud, Network, DB)
Configuration Change Approval and Version History Records
Configuration Compliance and Drift Monitoring Report
Baseline Exception and Deviation Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample live production servers, cloud accounts or network devices and compare actual settings against your documented hardening standards. The #1 trap is adopting CIS Benchmarks on paper without ever measuring or enforcing them against live systems.

questions.question: How are security configuration baselines documented across operating systems, cloud platforms, databases and network devices, including removal of insecure defaults?
questions.guidance: Provide your hardening standards (such as tailored CIS Benchmarks, ASD hardening guides or cloud landing-zone baselines) showing mandatory security settings, disabling of unnecessary ports/services and removal of default vendor accounts and settings prior to production use.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that baselines exist for each major technology stack in scope, specify concrete verifiable settings rather than vague aspirations, and are applied as part of system commissioning.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented, version-controlled hardening baselines cover every in-scope platform tier (endpoints, servers, cloud tenants, databases and network equipment), grounded in recognised benchmarks such as CIS or ASD guidance. Commissioning checklists or golden images verify that default credentials, sample applications and unnecessary services are removed before systems enter production.
questions.red_flags: No documented hardening standards exist, cloud services are provisioned using permissive vendor defaults, or default SNMP strings and admin credentials remain active on network devices.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined security configuration baselines or deployment of in-scope production systems with insecure vendor defaults unaddressed.

questions.question: How are configuration records maintained and protected, and how are baseline changes reviewed and approved prior to implementation?
questions.guidance: Describe how current system and security configurations are recorded, backed up and updated through controlled change management. Note any automated configuration management or Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tooling used as good practice to keep deployments repeatable.
questions.auditor_focus: Trace a sample of recent firewall, cloud IAM or server configuration changes back to approved change records, checking that configuration baselines are updated when architecture evolves.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Security configurations are documented or stored in version-controlled repositories with restricted write access, and changes follow formal change management with security impact assessment and approval. Where proportionate to scale, Infrastructure as Code (such as Terraform) or automated configuration management is used as good practice to enforce repeatable builds and peer-reviewed changes.
questions.red_flags: Engineers routinely apply undocumented manual tweaks directly in production consoles, configuration backups are missing, or baseline documents have not been updated for years.
questions.nc_pattern: Security configurations are modified without controlled change authorisation or lack accurate records required to maintain secure system states.

questions.question: How is ongoing configuration compliance monitored to detect, investigate and remediate unauthorised drift from approved baselines?
questions.guidance: Provide outputs from Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), compliance scanners, Group Policy/MDM compliance checks or periodic manual hardening audits showing how configuration drift is identified and corrected.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that drift detection runs continuously or on a defined schedule across production environments and that high-severity misconfigurations (such as public storage buckets or disabled encryption) are remediated promptly.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated posture tools (such as CSPM, CIS benchmark scanners or MDM compliance checks) or scheduled verification reviews continuously compare live systems against approved baselines. Unauthorised configuration drift raises alerts or tickets tracked to remediation, and justified deviations are recorded in a time-bound exception register.
questions.red_flags: Systems are hardened once at build time and never re-checked, CSPM dashboards show hundreds of unresolved critical misconfigurations, or drift alerts have no assigned owner.
questions.nc_pattern: No ongoing verification or review mechanism exists to detect and correct deviations from required security configurations.

controls.short_summary: Securely delete information when no longer needed across live systems and backups.
controls.plain_english_summary: Information stored in systems, cloud services and storage media must be securely deleted once retention periods expire or business and legal purposes end. Effective deletion requires defined retention schedules, approved sanitisation or cryptographic erasure methods, clear handling of backup lifecycles and verifiable disposal records.
controls.why_it_matters: Hoarding expired customer PII and legacy records dramatically expands the fallout of any security breach and breaches Australian Privacy Principle 11.2. Regulators increasingly penalise organisations that fail to delete data they had no lawful reason to keep.
key_deliverables: Information Retention and Secure Deletion Policy
Approved Sanitisation and Cryptographic Erasure Standard
Verified Deletion Logs and Third-Party Destruction Certificates
Privacy and Contractual Erasure Request Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors test whether retention schedules actually trigger deletion in production databases, SaaS platforms and file shares rather than remaining theoretical. The #1 trap is retaining years of expired customer records or unpurged backups with no documented schedule.
