questions.question: How are information deletion requirements, secure sanitisation methods and backup-expiry handling defined and enforced across systems and cloud services?
questions.guidance: Provide your retention and deletion policy, technical standards specifying approved methods (such as cryptographic erasure, NIST SP 800-88/ISM sanitisation or verified cloud purge) and documentation explaining how deleted records age out of immutable backups or are suppressed upon restore.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that deletion schedules align with statutory retention obligations (such as tax, corporate and Privacy Act APP 11.2 rules), specify secure non-recoverable methods for sensitive data and address SaaS and backup repositories.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved retention and deletion policy maps data categories to lawful retention periods and mandates secure deletion methods (including cryptographic erasure or ISM-aligned media sanitisation) once data is no longer required. Automated lifecycle rules purge expired records in cloud and core systems, while backup procedures document bounded retention windows and post-restore suppression checks.
questions.red_flags: Data is retained indefinitely 'just in case', deletion relies only on basic file-system unlinking for decommissioned media, or backup retention rules conflict with stated deletion commitments.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined information deletion rules or failure to securely delete information that is no longer required in line with legal, regulatory and business obligations.

questions.question: How do you verify that scheduled deletions, customer offboarding purges and privacy erasure requests are completed and evidenced?
questions.guidance: Provide sample deletion execution logs, automated purge job records, third-party certificates of destruction or completed privacy/client erasure tickets showing end-to-end verification across primary systems and sub-processors.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent client offboardings, scheduled retention purges or privacy deletion requests to confirm deletion actually occurred across downstream systems and generated auditable completion evidence.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Scheduled purge jobs and ad-hoc deletion requests produce tamper-evident execution logs or signed destruction certificates recording dataset scope, date, method and verifying owner. Privacy and contractual erasure requests are tracked to completion within statutory timeframes, including confirmation from relevant cloud or third-party processors.
questions.red_flags: Deletion requests are handled informally via email with no completion verification, third-party processors are overlooked, or expired datasets remain discoverable in reporting exports or staging tables.
questions.nc_pattern: No verifiable evidence that required information deletions or contractual/regulatory erasure obligations are reliably executed.

controls.short_summary: Mask, pseudonymise or anonymise sensitive fields to minimise unnecessary exposure.
controls.plain_english_summary: Where users, analysts, applications or downstream processes do not need to see raw sensitive values, data masking techniques—such as obfuscation, tokenisation, pseudonymisation and anonymisation—must limit exposure. Distinct from environment separation (8.31) and test-data governance (8.33), this control focuses on the technical masking techniques and rules themselves.
controls.why_it_matters: Exposing raw tax file numbers, payment details or customer identities in UI screens, logs, analytics warehouses or non-production datasets multiplies breach impact and privacy risk. Properly engineered masking preserves analytical or operational utility while removing re-identification risk.
key_deliverables: Data Masking, Pseudonymisation and Anonymisation Standard
Sensitive Field Masking Rule Catalogue
Dynamic/Static Masking Technical Configuration Evidence
Masking Effectiveness and Re-Identification Verification Report
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect masking rules for reversibility and check actual outputs (analytics tables, UI displays, exports or masked extracts) for leaked PII or weak transformations. The #1 trap is using predictable static substitution or unsalted hashes that allow trivial re-identification.

questions.question: Where are data masking, pseudonymisation or anonymisation techniques required, and how are masking rules and methods documented?
questions.guidance: Provide your data masking standard and rule catalogue detailing which sensitive fields (such as PII, TFNs, health records or payment data) must be dynamically or statically masked, tokenised, pseudonymised or anonymised, and how mapping keys or lookup tables are segregated.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that masking techniques match legal, regulatory and classification requirements—distinguishing irreversible anonymisation from reversible pseudonymisation—and that re-identification keys are strictly isolated.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented data masking standard defines approved techniques (dynamic UI masking, format-preserving tokenisation, pseudonymisation and irreversible anonymisation) mapped to classified data elements. Rule catalogues specify exact field transformations, require strict segregation of pseudonymisation lookup keys and align with Privacy Act de-identification expectations.
questions.red_flags: Masking is applied ad hoc by individual developers without documented rules, reversible hashing without salts is treated as 'anonymisation', or pseudonymisation mapping tables sit alongside the masked dataset.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of defined data masking standards or documented rules where risk assessment, privacy or contractual requirements mandate masking of sensitive data.

questions.question: How is data masking technically enforced and periodically verified to ensure sensitive values cannot be reconstructed while preserving required utility?
questions.guidance: Provide technical configuration evidence (such as database dynamic data masking, ETL anonymisation pipelines or API redaction filters) together with verification test records confirming no unmasked sensitive data leaks into permitted downstream datasets, reports or non-production copies.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect a sample of masked outputs or query views as a non-privileged user to verify that underlying sensitive attributes are genuinely hidden and cannot be inferred through free-text columns or indirect joins.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated pipelines and database/UI controls enforce masking consistently across permitted analytical, support and non-production use cases without relying on manual spreadsheet scrubbing. Validation checks verify both technical utility and absence of residual unmasked sensitive fields (including free-text notes), with periodic audits confirming ongoing compliance.
questions.red_flags: Masking scripts break silently after schema changes and expose new PII columns, free-text fields retain raw customer identifiers, or masking effectiveness is never validated after deployment.
questions.nc_pattern: Technical masking controls fail to prevent exposure or re-identification of sensitive information in environments or views where masking is required.

controls.short_summary: Detect and prevent unauthorised sensitive data exfiltration across channels.
controls.plain_english_summary: Data leakage prevention (DLP) combines technical inspection, channel restrictions and alerting to stop sensitive information from leaving the organisation without authorisation. Effective DLP maps to your information classification scheme, covers realistic egress channels—such as email, cloud sharing, web uploads and removable media—and backs alerts with a working triage process.
controls.why_it_matters: Misdirected emails, departing employees copying client lists to personal drives and unauthorised uploads to public AI or file-sharing tools are among the top causes of OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches. Technical guardrails catch both accidental mistakes and deliberate theft before data leaves your perimeter.
key_deliverables: DLP Policy and Sensitive Information Type Rule Set
Egress Channel Coverage and Enforcement Mode Configuration
DLP Alert Triage, Investigation and Escalation Procedure
Periodic DLP Rule Tuning and Incident Review Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors check which egress channels are actually monitored (email, SharePoint/OneDrive, endpoints, web/AI uploads) and inspect recent DLP alerts to confirm someone investigates them. The #1 trap is running DLP permanently in silent 'audit-only' mode with thousands of unread alerts.

questions.question: What data leakage prevention controls are implemented, which sensitive data types and egress channels are covered, and where is blocking versus detection mode enforced?
questions.guidance: Provide your DLP policy configuration showing covered channels (such as email, cloud collaboration, endpoints/USB and web uploads/SaaS), defined sensitive data patterns or sensitivity labels (such as PII, TFNs, credit cards, source code or confidential markings) and rationale for block, warn-with-justification or detect-only modes.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that DLP rules align with your data classification scheme and highest-risk egress paths, and check whether high-confidence exfiltration patterns are actively blocked or gated rather than silently logged.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Risk-proportionate DLP controls monitor and restrict unauthorised egress of classified data across primary channels including email, cloud file sharing, endpoints/USB and web uploads. Policies inspect sensitivity labels and Australian-relevant data patterns (such as TFNs, Medicare numbers and financial identifiers), enforcing active blocking or user-justified overrides on high-confidence rules while tuning lower-confidence rules carefully.
questions.red_flags: DLP covers email only while USB drives and personal cloud uploads remain wide open, rules rely solely on generic US templates rather than Australian data types, or every rule remains permanently in unmonitored audit mode.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of proportionate technical or procedural data leakage controls for systems processing sensitive or confidential information.

questions.question: How are DLP alerts triaged, investigated and escalated, and how are rules tuned to maintain effectiveness?
questions.guidance: Provide your DLP alert-handling procedure, sample closed investigation tickets (showing false-positive handling, user follow-up and incident escalation where confirmed leakage occurred) and records of periodic rule tuning.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the live DLP alert queue for unaddressed backlogs and trace sample high-severity alerts to verify timely investigation and linkage to incident management or HR processes where warranted.
questions.what_good_looks_like: DLP alerts route into a monitored security queue with defined triage SLAs, clear escalation criteria to incident response (5.24) and privacy/legal notification teams, and documented closure outcomes. Security teams review false-positive trends regularly to refine policies and reduce alert fatigue.
questions.red_flags: Thousands of unreviewed DLP alerts accumulate in the console, confirmed data exfiltration triggers no incident ticket, or business users routinely bypass warning prompts without review.
questions.nc_pattern: DLP alerts are not monitored, investigated or escalated in a timely manner, rendering detection controls ineffective.

controls.short_summary: Maintain immutable, segregated backups aligned to RPO/RTO and test restores.
controls.plain_english_summary: Critical data, system configurations and application code must be backed up on a schedule aligned with business recovery objectives and stored securely away from the primary environment. Backups must be protected against ransomware tampering—using encryption, segregated credentials and immutability—and periodically restored to prove they actually work.
controls.why_it_matters: An untested backup is merely an assumption, and ransomware operators routinely target online backup consoles before encrypting production systems. Reliable, immutable and verified backups underpin operational resilience under both ISO 27001 and APRA CPS 230.
key_deliverables: Backup and Recovery Policy Aligned to RPO/RTO
Automated Backup Job Completion and Failure-Alert Logs
Backup Encryption, Immutability and Off-Site Replication Configuration
Periodic Backup Restoration Test Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors demand dated restoration test logs—not just green backup-job dashboards—and verify that a compromised domain admin cannot delete backup snapshots. The #1 trap is backing up data reliably for years without ever verifying whether a full restore succeeds within RTO.

questions.question: How does your backup policy define scope, frequency and retention aligned to business RPO/RTO, and how is scheduled backup execution verified?
questions.guidance: Provide your backup policy mapping critical systems, databases, SaaS data and configurations to RPO/RTO and CPS 230 data-loss tolerances, alongside recent backup job completion reports and failure-remediation tickets.
questions.auditor_focus: Cross-check critical systems in the asset inventory and BIA against active backup jobs to ensure nothing—especially SaaS platforms, configuration stores or newly launched databases—is missed, and confirm failed jobs are promptly re-run.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved backup policy defines scope, schedule and retention for all critical data, configurations and SaaS repositories in alignment with BIA RPO/RTO and operational tolerance levels. Automated monitoring tracks daily job outcomes, immediately alerts operations on failures and logs timely re-runs until verified complete.
questions.red_flags: Key cloud SaaS data or infrastructure configurations are excluded from backups, repeated job failures sit unresolved for days, or backup schedules do not match stated RPO commitments.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope information or system configurations lack scheduled backups consistent with defined recovery requirements, or backup failures are not monitored and remediated.

questions.question: How are backups encrypted, stored in geographically separate locations and protected from unauthorised modification or ransomware deletion?
questions.guidance: Provide technical evidence of backup encryption at rest and in transit, geographically separate or cross-region replication, logical isolation (separate identity/MFA plane) and immutability or WORM/object-lock protections.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify whether a compromised primary domain or cloud production administrator can delete or shorten retention on backup repositories, and confirm geographic separation addresses regional physical or environmental hazards.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Backups are encrypted in transit and at rest with segregated key management, replicated to a geographically distinct region or off-site facility, and protected by immutability (such as WORM object lock or offline/air-gapped copies). Administrative access to backup consoles is isolated from primary production directories and guarded by dedicated MFA and multi-party approval for deletion.
questions.red_flags: Backups reside on the same storage array or cloud account using the same admin credentials as production, immutability is disabled, or encryption keys are stored inside the backup itself without segregation.
questions.nc_pattern: Backups lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, physical/geographic separation or tamper-protection controls commensurate with threat and resilience risks.

questions.question: How frequently are backup restorations tested, and how are restore integrity, recovery duration and identified defects documented and resolved?
questions.guidance: Provide dated backup restoration test reports from the last 12 months showing systems tested, restore scope, actual recovery time achieved versus RTO, data integrity verification and remediation tickets for any issues uncovered.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that restoration tests actually restore and validate usable application/database data into an isolated environment—not merely check backup metadata—and verify that lessons learnt lead to tracked fixes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Scheduled restoration tests (at least quarterly or semi-annually for critical systems, and annually across the broader estate) restore backups into isolated environments, verify application and data integrity, and measure elapsed recovery time against RTO and CPS 230 tolerances. Formal test reports capture pass/fail evidence and track any recovery defects to verified closure.
questions.red_flags: No documented restore test has been executed in the past year, tests only check file existence without validating database consistency, or failed restore tests have no follow-up action.
questions.nc_pattern: Backup media and recovery procedures are not regularly tested to confirm that information can be reliably restored within required recovery timeframes.

controls.short_summary: Design resilient failover architecture and verify availability targets.
controls.plain_english_summary: Information processing facilities—spanning compute, storage, networking, power and cloud availability zones—must incorporate architectural redundancy proportionate to business availability requirements. Distinct from capacity forecasting in 8.6, this control eliminates unmanaged single points of failure and verifies through testing that failover and failback operate reliably under disruption.
controls.why_it_matters: Hardware failures, fibre cuts and cloud availability-zone outages happen routinely; without tested redundancy, critical services breach customer SLAs and APRA CPS 230 disruption tolerances. Discovering hidden single points of failure during a live outage turns a manageable fault into a major business crisis.
key_deliverables: High-Availability and Redundancy Architecture Diagrams
Single Point of Failure (SPOF) Assessment and Mitigation Register
Availability Tier and Tolerance Alignment Matrix
Failover and Failback Test Plans and Post-Test Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors compare your Business Impact Analysis (BIA) and CPS 230 critical operation tolerances against actual architecture diagrams and failover test reports. The #1 trap is claiming multi-zone or disaster-recovery redundancy while never testing live failover or overlooking shared dependencies like DNS, identity providers or VPN gateways.

questions.question: How is architectural and geographic redundancy aligned with business availability requirements, and how are single points of failure identified and mitigated?
questions.guidance: Provide architecture diagrams, your availability-tier matrix (linked to BIA and CPS 230 critical operations/tolerances) and single-point-of-failure (SPOF) reviews covering compute, databases, network paths, DNS/identity dependencies and geographic diversity.
questions.auditor_focus: Check that redundancy architecture actually matches documented RTO/availability commitments—and that shared upstream dependencies (such as single WAN links, unclustered firewalls or single-region identity relays) are either eliminated or formally risk-accepted.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Critical systems and supporting infrastructure (network links, firewalls, compute, databases and power/cooling or cloud zones) implement documented redundancy aligned to BIA availability tiers and board-approved CPS 230 tolerance levels. Periodic SPOF assessments identify residual shared dependencies—including third-party and geographic concentration risks—and either remediate them or record formal risk acceptance.
questions.red_flags: Architecture diagrams are outdated, critical customer services depend on a single server or single internet circuit despite high availability targets, or geographic redundancy exists for applications but not their databases or authentication layer.
questions.nc_pattern: Information processing facilities lack redundancy sufficient to meet stated availability requirements, or critical single points of failure remain unassessed and unmanaged.

questions.question: How frequently are failover and failback mechanisms tested under realistic disruption scenarios, and how are test findings tracked to remediation?
questions.guidance: Provide scheduled failover/disaster-recovery test plans, dated test execution reports (including actual switchover times, functional validation and failback verification) and remediation records for gaps identified during testing.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that failover testing goes beyond tabletop exercises for critical systems, validates end-to-end service availability including failback, and occurs at the cadence committed in policy (at least annually for APRA CPS 230 critical operations).
questions.what_good_looks_like: Redundant components and disaster-recovery failover procedures are tested on a defined schedule—at least annually for critical operations under severe-but-plausible disruption scenarios—measuring actual switchover duration, application health and clean failback. Post-test reports document evidence, compare results against RTO and tolerance thresholds, and track every defect to verified closure.
questions.red_flags: Failover has never been tested since initial build, tests cover only individual components without end-to-end user validation, or recurring failover defects remain unfixed across consecutive annual tests.
questions.nc_pattern: Redundancy and failover capabilities are not periodically tested to verify they operate effectively when required.

controls.short_summary: Generate, centralise, protect and retain security logs across all systems.
controls.plain_english_summary: Systems, applications, cloud platforms and security controls must record detailed, attributable logs of security-relevant events—such as authentication, privileged actions, access changes and failures. Logs must be securely aggregated, protected against tampering or premature deletion, and retained long enough to support incident investigation, audits and regulatory enquiries (with timestamp accuracy owned by 8.17).
controls.why_it_matters: Without intact, searchable logs, teams cannot determine when an attacker entered, what data was accessed or whether a breach must be reported to the OAIC or APRA. Attackers routinely delete local logs to cover their tracks, making centralised, tamper-resistant collection essential.
key_deliverables: Security Logging Standard and Event Coverage Matrix
Centralised Log Aggregation / SIEM Ingestion Inventory
Log Access Control and Tamper-Protection Configuration
Log Retention Schedule and Storage Lifecycle Evidence
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample a live system, perform or inspect a recent privileged event and trace it into your central log repository to confirm completeness, immutability and retention. The #1 trap is enabling default SaaS or cloud logs that silently roll off after 7 to 30 days.

questions.question: What security-relevant events and mandatory log fields are defined and captured across infrastructure, applications, databases and cloud platforms?
questions.guidance: Provide your logging standard and event coverage matrix demonstrating capture of user and privileged authentication, permission changes, admin actions, security-tool alerts, system failures and data-access events, containing who, what, when, source and outcome fields (relying on synchronised clocks under 8.17).
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect sample raw log records from key applications, cloud audit trails and identity providers to confirm they record individual user IDs, event outcomes and source identifiers—without leaking passwords or raw payment/PII secrets into logs.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented logging standard defines mandatory security event categories and structured fields (user identity, timestamp, asset/source, action and success/failure outcome) across all in-scope infrastructure, cloud tenants and business applications. Log schemas explicitly exclude plaintext credentials and unnecessary sensitive payload data while ensuring full forensic attribution.
questions.red_flags: Critical business applications or cloud control planes do not log administrative changes or failed logins, logs omit user attribution behind proxies, or plaintext secrets appear in debug logs.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope systems fail to generate logs recording required user activities, exceptions, faults and security-relevant events.

questions.question: How are security logs centrally aggregated and protected against unauthorised access, modification or deletion?
questions.guidance: Provide architecture and configuration evidence showing log forwarding to a centralised repository or SIEM, encrypted log transport, strict role segregation so system administrators cannot alter or delete their own logs, and integrity controls (such as append-only storage or write-once locks).
questions.auditor_focus: Check whether infrastructure or cloud administrators can disable logging silently or delete historical log buckets, and verify that ingestion outages or silent log-source drops are detected.
questions.what_good_looks_like: In-scope log sources forward events over encrypted channels to a centrally managed, access-controlled log platform or segregated immutable archive bucket. Write-once/append-only storage and duty separation ensure system and network administrators cannot modify or delete audit logs, and automated health checks alert if any critical log source stops ingesting.
questions.red_flags: Logs remain solely on local servers where compromised admins can wipe them, logging pipelines fail silently without alerting, or broad IT staff hold delete permissions on the central log archive.
questions.nc_pattern: Logs are not protected against tampering, unauthorised access or premature deletion, compromising auditability and forensic integrity.

questions.question: How are log retention periods aligned with legal, regulatory and forensic needs, and how is retention verified across active and archived storage?
questions.guidance: Provide your log retention policy and live storage lifecycle configurations showing hot/warm searchable retention and cold archive duration across SIEM, cloud audit logs and SaaS platforms.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify live retention settings on cloud tenants (such as Microsoft 365, Entra ID, AWS CloudTrail and key SaaS apps) rather than accepting policy claims alone, confirming older logs can actually be retrieved for investigation.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented retention schedule aligns hot and cold log storage durations (commonly 90 days hot and at least 12 months archived, or longer where required by APRA/ASIC/contractual obligations) with legal, privacy and investigative needs. Live storage configurations enforce these periods automatically and prevent premature rollover, with periodic checks verifying archived logs remain retrievable.
questions.red_flags: Policy claims 12-month log retention while Entra ID or firewall logs overwrite after 30 days due to default licensing or disk limits, or cold archives have never been tested for retrieval.
questions.nc_pattern: Log retention periods are undefined or not technically enforced, leaving insufficient historical evidence for incident investigation or compliance obligations.

controls.short_summary: Continuously monitor networks and systems to detect anomalies and escalate incidents.
controls.plain_english_summary: Collecting logs is useless unless networks, systems and applications are actively monitored for anomalous behaviour and potential security events. Organisations must establish baselines of normal activity, configure actionable alerting rules, triage alerts promptly and periodically review detection effectiveness as threats and infrastructure evolve.
controls.why_it_matters: Attackers often dwell inside environments for days or weeks conducting reconnaissance before launching ransomware or exfiltrating data. Active monitoring and timely alert triage cut dwell time and enable APRA-regulated entities to detect and escalate material incidents promptly under CPS 234 §23 and CPS 230 §32.
key_deliverables: Security Monitoring Architecture and Coverage Matrix
Detection Use-Case and Alerting Rule Catalogue
Alert Triage Runbooks and Sample Investigation Tickets
Periodic Detection Effectiveness and Alert-Tuning Review
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect your live alert queue, triage SLAs and sample closed alerts to verify genuine human investigation rather than rubber-stamped closure. The #1 trap is deploying a SIEM or MDR tool without validating that alerts fire reliably and reach on-call responders.

questions.question: How are networks, systems, cloud services and user activities continuously monitored against baselines to detect anomalous behaviour?
questions.guidance: Describe your monitoring operating model (in-house SOC, managed detection and response (MDR) or security operations workflow), scope of monitored telemetry (endpoints, identity, cloud control plane, network traffic and critical apps) and how behavioural baselines or anomaly detection identify unusual activity.
questions.auditor_focus: Confirm that monitoring covers critical assets across both business hours and out-of-hours windows proportionate to risk, and verify clear ownership if an external MDR or managed SOC provider is used.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Continuous security monitoring ingests telemetry from endpoints, identity providers, cloud control planes, network perimeters and critical applications to detect anomalous behaviour against established baselines. Coverage hours, escalation paths and responsibilities (including MDR/SOC service-level commitments where outsourced) are clearly documented and aligned to asset criticality.
questions.red_flags: Monitoring is purely ad hoc or reactive after user complaints, cloud control planes or identity logs are excluded from behavioural monitoring, or out-of-hours critical alerts wait until Monday morning.
questions.nc_pattern: Absence of ongoing monitoring activities capable of detecting anomalous behaviour and potential information security incidents across in-scope systems.

questions.question: What security alerting and correlation rules are configured, and how are triggered alerts triaged, investigated and escalated into incident response?
questions.guidance: Provide your detection use-case catalogue (such as privileged escalation, impossible travel, malware detection, mass data exfiltration and log-tampering alerts), alert triage playbooks and sample closed investigation records showing response times and escalation hand-offs.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect recent high-severity alerts end-to-end—from trigger timestamp to analyst acknowledgement, investigative notes and incident escalation—checking for ignored queues or unverified 'false positive' closures.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Prioritised detection rules map to key organisational threats—including MITRE ATT&CK techniques, privileged abuse, malware and anomalous data access—generating tiered alerts with defined triage SLAs. Every alert is tracked in a ticketing workflow recording investigative rationale, containment actions and formal escalation to incident response (5.24) when suspicious activity is confirmed.
questions.red_flags: Alert queues contain hundreds of aged untriaged items, alerts are closed as 'false positive' with no investigative justification, or no clear criteria connect security alerts to incident declaration.
questions.nc_pattern: Security alerts are poorly defined, unmonitored or not investigated and escalated within timeframes appropriate to operational risk.

questions.question: How is the effectiveness of security monitoring and alerting rules periodically reviewed, tested and tuned?
questions.guidance: Provide records of periodic detection reviews, alert-noise tuning, purple-team or simulated-attack detection tests, and updates made following incidents, threat intelligence or architecture changes.
questions.auditor_focus: Look for evidence that detection coverage evolves over time—such as updating rules after new cloud services launch, validating that alerts still fire after connector updates, and measuring mean time to detect (MTTD) and respond (MTTR).
questions.what_good_looks_like: Security teams review detection coverage, false-positive rates and triage metrics at least quarterly, validating critical alerting rules through controlled test triggers or adversary simulations. New threat intelligence, post-incident lessons and newly onboarded systems systematically feed updates into the detection rule catalogue.
questions.red_flags: Detection rules have not been updated since initial SIEM deployment, broken log parsers silently blind key rules, or monitoring KPIs are never reported to management.
questions.nc_pattern: Monitoring capabilities and detection rules are not reviewed or maintained to remain effective against changing systems and threats.

controls.short_summary: Synchronise all system clocks to authoritative time sources and monitor time drift.
controls.plain_english_summary: Clocks across all servers, endpoints, network devices, cloud workloads and logging platforms must be synchronised to approved, authoritative time sources using consistent time-zone standards (preferably UTC for logs). Accurate, monitored time synchronisation ensures event logs can be correlated reliably during forensic investigations and keeps cryptographic protocols such as Kerberos and TLS functioning properly.
controls.why_it_matters: Even a few minutes of clock drift across firewalls, identity servers and applications breaks forensic timelines and can undermine the evidential value of logs in regulatory or legal proceedings. Severe time skew also breaks authentication tokens and certificate validation.
key_deliverables: Time Synchronisation Architecture and NTP Configuration Standard
Authoritative NTP / Cloud Time-Service Configuration Evidence
Log Time-Zone Standardisation (UTC) Verification
Clock Drift Monitoring and Alerting Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect live NTP configurations on domain controllers, Linux servers and network appliances and verify that logs record unambiguous UTC timestamps or offsets. The #1 trap is synchronising corporate Windows machines via Active Directory while forgetting firewalls, storage arrays or standalone Linux/OT devices.

questions.question: How are all in-scope systems synchronised to documented, authoritative time sources with consistent time-zone handling?
questions.guidance: Provide your documented time synchronisation configuration showing approved upstream time sources (such as authenticated NTP/NTS pools, National Measurement Institute Australia time servers or native cloud time services), internal time hierarchy and standardisation on UTC (or explicit ISO-8601 time-zone offsets) across systems and logs.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect live NTP/Chrony/w32tm settings across a sample of servers, network devices and cloud workloads to confirm they point to approved authoritative sources and record consistent UTC or offset-tagged timestamps.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented time-synchronisation architecture configures all in-scope servers, endpoints, network gear and cloud workloads to synchronise with redundant, authoritative time sources (such as native cloud time services or authenticated stratum-1/2 NTP servers). All security logs and system timestamps standardise on UTC or include explicit ISO-8601 UTC offsets to prevent daylight-saving ambiguity.
questions.red_flags: Standalone servers or network appliances rely on free-running local hardware clocks, different platforms log local AEST/AEDT without time-zone offsets, or NTP settings are undocumented and ad hoc.
questions.nc_pattern: In-scope information processing systems are not synchronised to approved, accurate time sources, compromising log correlation and forensic integrity.

questions.question: How is clock synchronisation health monitored to detect and correct time drift or failed NTP services?
questions.guidance: Provide monitoring configurations, sample status checks (such as `chronyc tracking`, `w32tm /query /status` or SIEM ingestion-skew checks) and alerting thresholds showing how unsynchronised hosts or NTP failures are identified and remediated.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that operations teams would actually notice if an internal NTP server failed or a firewall drifted by several minutes, rather than discovering the skew only during an incident investigation.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Infrastructure monitoring or SIEM ingestion checks track NTP daemon health and clock offset across critical hosts, raising alerts whenever drift exceeds defined tolerances (such as 1 to 5 seconds). Unsynchronised systems generate operational tickets tracked to prompt correction.
questions.red_flags: NTP services are configured once during build and never monitored, firewall rules silently block outbound UDP/123 without triggering an alert, or SIEM logs show large gaps between event time and ingestion time.
questions.nc_pattern: Lack of monitoring or verification over clock synchronisation, allowing undetected time drift across in-scope systems.

controls.short_summary: Restrict, approve and log utilities able to override system controls
controls.plain_english_summary: Privileged utility programs — such as database editors, packet sniffers, debuggers and low-level disk tools — can bypass normal application and operating system safeguards. Organisations must catalogue these tools, strip unnecessary utilities from production hosts and tightly govern who can run the remainder. Every invocation should be explicitly approved, time-bounded and captured in tamper-resistant audit logs.
controls.why_it_matters: Uncontrolled administrative utilities let insiders or compromised accounts alter financial records, extract raw data or disable security controls without triggering standard application checks. Certification auditors frequently raise nonconformities where powerful tools sit installed across production servers with standing access and no usage audit trail.
key_deliverables: Privileged Utility Program Register
Hardened Server and Endpoint Baseline Standards
Privileged Utility Approval and Checkout Procedure
Centralised Privileged Session and Execution Logs
Periodic Privileged Utility Access Review Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect production hosts and privileged access tooling to verify that unnecessary utilities are removed and remaining tools require ticketed approval. The #1 trap is treating privileged utilities as generic admin access, leaving database clients or scripting tools ungoverned and unlogged.

questions.question: How are privileged utility programs identified, minimised and technically restricted across operational systems?
questions.guidance: Maintain a current inventory of system, database, network and forensic utilities capable of overriding security or application controls. Remove unnecessary compilers, debuggers, packet-capture tools and raw data editors from production builds through hardened baselines, and enforce execution restrictions via OS permissions, application control or privileged access management (PAM).
questions.auditor_focus: Review the privileged utility inventory against a sample of production servers, databases and jump hosts. Verify that non-essential utilities are absent from hardened images and that standard user accounts cannot invoke remaining privileged tools.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A maintained register catalogues all approved privileged utilities, their business purpose, authorised roles and host scope. Production images strip non-essential diagnostic and build tools by default. Technical enforcement via PAM or application control blocks unauthorised execution across servers and endpoints.
questions.red_flags: No inventory of privileged utilities exists. Production servers retain compilers, debuggers or raw database clients by default. Standard operational accounts can execute system-level utilities without restriction.
questions.nc_pattern: Privileged utility programs capable of bypassing system or application controls are unidentified, widely installed on production systems without justification, or technically accessible to unauthorised personnel.

questions.question: How is the use of privileged utility programs authorised, logged and periodically reviewed?
questions.guidance: Require documented, ticketed approval before invoking high-risk utilities in production, using just-in-time elevation rather than standing rights. Capture user identity, command parameters, session recordings and timestamps in centralised immutable logs, and periodically reconcile utility executions against approved change or incident tickets.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent production executions of privileged utilities from SIEM or PAM logs and trace each event back to an authorised change or incident ticket. Inspect recent periodic access and capability reviews for timely revocation of unused rights.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Utility use in production requires time-limited, ticket-linked approval with segregation between requester and approver. PAM or SIEM logs record every invocation with full user attribution. Quarterly reviews reconcile logged executions against tickets and revoke dormant utility permissions.
questions.red_flags: Administrators hold permanent access to privileged utilities without checkout workflows. Execution logs are stored only locally on target hosts or lack individual user attribution. Periodic reviews are skipped or fail to verify actual usage.
questions.nc_pattern: Use of privileged utility programs in operational environments is neither formally authorised nor reliably logged, preventing detection of unauthorised control bypass.

controls.control_name: Installation of software on operational systems
controls.short_summary: Enforce application control, trusted sourcing and managed software deployment
controls.plain_english_summary: Uncontrolled software installation introduces malware, unpatched vulnerabilities and licensing breaches directly into live environments. Organisations must remove local administrative installation rights from standard users, enforce application control and ensure all operational software is vetted, sourced from trusted repositories and deployed through managed tooling. Continuous software inventory and detection controls catch unauthorised binaries before they persist.
controls.why_it_matters: Unauthorised executables and shadow-IT installers are a primary vector for ransomware and credential theft, which is why application control is a cornerstone of the ACSC Essential Eight. Auditors test this control directly on live endpoints and servers rather than trusting policy statements alone.
key_deliverables: Software Installation and Application Control Standard
Endpoint Privilege Management and Allowlisting Policies
Approved Software Catalogue and Vetting Records
Automated Software Inventory and Discovery Reports
Unauthorised Software Detection and Remediation Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect endpoint management consoles and test whether a standard user can install or run an unsigned binary. The #1 trap is relying on an acceptable-use policy prohibiting unauthorised software while leaving users with local administrator privileges.

questions.question: How are software installation rights restricted and application controls enforced on operational endpoints and servers?
questions.guidance: Remove standing local administrator privileges from standard user accounts and block self-service installation of unapproved software. Implement technical application control (such as allowlisting via WDAC, AppLocker, Santa or managed EDR policies) to prevent execution of unapproved binaries, scripts and installers in user-writable directories, with time-bound elevation only where strictly justified.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect MDM, Group Policy or server configuration baselines to confirm standard users lack installation rights. Verify application control enforcement mode (audit versus block) and review approved exception lists for scope and expiry.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Standard users cannot install software or run unapproved executables on corporate endpoints or production servers. Application control rules enforce allowlisting for executables, DLLs and scripts across managed fleets. Any temporary privilege elevation is ticketed, logged and automatically revoked.
questions.red_flags: General staff hold permanent local administrator rights on workstations. Application control runs permanently in audit-only mode with no enforcement plan. Portable executables or browser extensions can be installed freely without technical blocks.
questions.nc_pattern: Operational systems lack effective technical restrictions preventing unauthorised personnel from installing or executing unapproved software.

questions.question: How is operational software vetted, sourced from trusted channels and approved prior to deployment?
questions.guidance: Define a structured software intake workflow requiring security, licensing and compatibility checks before any new package enters the approved software catalogue. Obtain software only from verified vendor channels or signed internal repositories, validate cryptographic signatures or checksums prior to rollout and retain rollback packages in case an update fails.
questions.auditor_focus: Select recently deployed software packages and trace each to its security assessment, business approval, signature/hash verification and managed deployment record. Confirm software is distributed via managed repositories rather than ad-hoc downloads.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All new software undergoes documented security, privacy and licence vetting before addition to the managed catalogue. Packages are sourced from official vendor channels with digital signature verification enforced by deployment pipelines. Previous stable versions are retained to support controlled rollback.
questions.red_flags: Administrators download installers directly from unverified websites onto production hosts. Software is pushed to production without security review or testing in non-production. Open-source or third-party packages lack integrity checks.
questions.nc_pattern: Software is installed on operational systems from untrusted sources or without prior security vetting, integrity verification and management approval.

questions.question: How is installed software tracked in an authoritative inventory and how is unauthorised software detected and removed?
questions.guidance: Use automated endpoint and server management agents to maintain a near-real-time inventory of installed applications, versions and licence allocations. Reconcile discovered software against the approved catalogue, trigger alerts when unauthorised installations or unapproved binaries appear and follow a documented remediation workflow to quarantine or remove them.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect automated software inventory reports and compare them against the approved software list. Review recent alerts or tickets showing detection, investigation and removal of unauthorised software.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated discovery continuously catalogues installed software and versions across workstations, servers and cloud workloads. Discrepancies against the approved catalogue generate alerts routed to IT and security operations. Unauthorised software is removed promptly and root causes are tracked.
questions.red_flags: Software inventory is maintained manually in stale spreadsheets. Discovery covers Windows workstations but omits macOS, Linux servers or cloud instances. Alerts for unapproved applications sit unresolved without removal evidence.
questions.nc_pattern: The organisation lacks an accurate inventory of software installed on operational systems or has no effective mechanism to detect and remove unauthorised software.

controls.short_summary: Harden, filter and continuously monitor networks and wireless infrastructure
controls.plain_english_summary: Networks carry sensitive business traffic and connect critical infrastructure to external services and remote users. Organisations must secure routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers and wireless access points using hardened configurations, least-privilege traffic filtering and strong encryption. Continuous network monitoring and logging enable rapid detection of lateral movement, rogue devices and anomalous flows.
controls.why_it_matters: A single misconfigured firewall rule, unpatched edge appliance or weakly secured Wi-Fi network can expose internal systems to immediate compromise. Auditors routinely sample firewall rulesets, device hardening records and network telemetry to verify that perimeter and internal controls operate in practice.
key_deliverables: Network Architecture Diagrams and Device Inventory
Network Device Hardening and Wireless Security Standards
Firewall and Access Control List (ACL) Review Records
Out-of-Band Management Interface Configuration Evidence
Network Intrusion Detection and Flow Monitoring Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors review current network diagrams, sample firewall rules for overly permissive 'any-any' entries and check whether management interfaces are isolated. The #1 trap is deploying firewalls once and failing to conduct periodic ruleset reviews or disable legacy management protocols.

questions.question: How are network devices, wireless networks and perimeter traffic filtering rules hardened and reviewed?
questions.guidance: Maintain up-to-date network topology diagrams and harden all routers, switches, firewalls and wireless controllers by removing default credentials, disabling unused ports and applying timely firmware updates. Enforce default-deny perimeter firewall policies with periodic ruleset reviews, and secure corporate wireless networks using enterprise authentication (WPA3-Enterprise or WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X) alongside rogue access point detection.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect network diagrams, sample firewall rulesets for overly broad rules and stale entries, and verify evidence of periodic firewall reviews. Check wireless controller settings for enterprise encryption, certificate-based or 802.1X authentication and isolated guest SSIDs.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Current network diagrams accurately reflect on-premises, wireless and cloud perimeters. Firewalls enforce default-deny ingress and controlled egress rules reviewed at least six-monthly. Corporate Wi-Fi requires 802.1X authentication with modern encryption, and network devices run supported, hardened firmware.
questions.red_flags: Firewall rulesets contain undocumented 'any-any' rules or expired temporary exceptions. Corporate wireless networks rely on static shared passphrases distributed to all staff. Edge appliances run end-of-life firmware or retain default vendor accounts.
questions.nc_pattern: Network devices, wireless infrastructure or boundary filtering rules are unhardened, overly permissive or not subject to periodic review, exposing operational networks to unauthorised access.

questions.question: How are network management interfaces, administrative protocols and core network services protected?
questions.guidance: Isolate network device administration onto dedicated out-of-band or restricted management networks accessible only from hardened bastion hosts with multi-factor authentication. Disable insecure protocols such as Telnet, HTTP and SNMPv1/v2c in favour of SSHv2, TLS and SNMPv3, and protect core routing, DNS and DHCP services against spoofing or unauthorised changes.
questions.auditor_focus: Check device configurations to confirm administrative interfaces are never exposed to the public internet or standard user subnets. Verify MFA enforcement on network management consoles and review logs of administrative configuration changes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All network management planes are isolated from user and internet-facing networks and require authenticated bastion access with MFA. Encrypted administrative protocols are enforced universally, and core DNS, DHCP and routing services use signed or authenticated updates.
questions.red_flags: Firewall or router administrative consoles are reachable from the internet or general office VLANs. Network devices use shared local admin logins or unencrypted SNMPv2 community strings. Administrative changes occur without logging or configuration backups.
questions.nc_pattern: Network management interfaces or core network services lack authentication, encryption or network isolation, allowing unauthorised modification or interception of network infrastructure.

questions.question: How is network traffic continuously monitored to detect intrusions, anomalous flows and unauthorised devices?
questions.guidance: Deploy network telemetry — such as firewall logs, VPC flow logs, DNS logs and IDS/IPS or NDR sensors — feeding into a centralised SIEM or security monitoring platform. Define detection rules for suspicious scanning, command-and-control beacons, data exfiltration and unauthorised network connections, supported by clear triage and escalation procedures.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify that firewall, DNS, VPN and cloud flow logs are actively ingested into the monitoring platform. Inspect sample alerts, tuning records and incident tickets demonstrating timely analyst investigation of network anomalies.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Boundary, internal and cloud network telemetry streams continuously into centralised monitoring with automated correlation alerts. IDS/IPS or NDR signatures and threat feeds update automatically. Network alerts are triaged against defined response SLAs with documented outcomes.
questions.red_flags: Network logs remain siloed on individual devices with short retention periods. IDS/IPS sensors generate high-volume alerts that nobody reviews. No visibility exists into east-west traffic or cloud VPC flows.
questions.nc_pattern: Network traffic is not adequately monitored or logged to detect unauthorised network activity, intrusions or anomalous data flows.

controls.short_summary: Specify, contract and monitor security and resilience of network services
controls.plain_english_summary: Organisations rely heavily on managed network services — including WAN links, MPLS, SD-WAN, SASE, DNS, CDN and cloud interconnectivity — delivered either in-house or by external carriers. Security attributes, encryption protocols, service levels and management obligations for every network service must be formally defined in service agreements. Ongoing assurance ensures providers maintain agreed security, availability and redundancy commitments.
controls.why_it_matters: Carrier outages, misconfigured managed firewalls or unencrypted WAN circuits can disrupt critical operations or expose traffic in transit outside the organisation's direct control. Under APRA CPS 230 and ISO 27001, network service providers supporting core operations require explicit security clauses and ongoing performance oversight.
key_deliverables: Network Services Register and Security Requirements Baseline
Network Service Agreements and SLA Schedules
Approved Transport Protocol and Tunnel Encryption Standards
Provider Security and SLA Performance Review Reports
Network Redundancy and Failover Test Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect contracts with ISPs, managed network providers and cloud connectivity vendors to confirm security controls and SLAs are formally specified and reviewed. The #1 trap is signing standard commercial carrier terms with availability SLAs only and zero security, logging or incident-notification obligations.

questions.question: How are security requirements, approved transport protocols and contractual service levels established for internal and third-party network services?
questions.guidance: Identify all internal and externally provided network services (such as WAN, VPN, SD-WAN, managed DNS, CDN and cloud direct-connect circuits) and document required security features including encryption in transit, authentication, DDoS mitigation, log access and incident notification timelines. Embed these obligations into formal service agreements or internal OLAs before onboarding services.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the inventory of network services and sample contracts or SLAs for explicit security clauses, encryption standards, right-to-audit or assurance reporting and breach notification commitments. Verify that network tunnels enforce strong protocols such as TLS 1.2/1.3 or IPsec.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every internal and third-party network service is catalogued with documented security and availability requirements. Provider contracts include binding SLAs, security control commitments, encryption expectations and incident notification timeframes. Unencrypted or deprecated transport protocols are prohibited across all managed links.
questions.red_flags: Network services operate under informal arrangements or standard carrier terms lacking security clauses. Legacy unencrypted protocols remain active over third-party links. No single inventory identifies which external providers carry critical operational traffic.
questions.nc_pattern: Security mechanisms, service levels and management requirements for network services are not formally identified or incorporated into network service agreements.

questions.question: How are network service providers monitored for security compliance, SLA adherence and resilience?
questions.guidance: Track provider SLA attainment, security advisories, independent assurance reports (such as ISO 27001 certificates or SOC 2 Type II reports) and service change notifications on a defined cadence. Design critical connectivity with carrier and path diversity, DDoS protection and tested failover procedures so single-provider failures do not breach operational tolerances.
questions.auditor_focus: Examine periodic vendor review minutes, SLA scorecards and current third-party assurance artefacts for key network providers. Inspect evidence of link redundancy and recent failover testing for critical business connections.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Network service providers undergo scheduled SLA and security assurance reviews backed by current third-party audit reports. Critical sites and cloud uplinks maintain diverse carriers with documented, periodically tested failover. SLA breaches or security incidents trigger formal remediation tracking.
questions.red_flags: Provider assurance certificates are expired or never requested after contract signing. Critical operations depend on a single ISP circuit with untested failover. Managed network changes occur without notification or joint review.
questions.nc_pattern: The security performance, SLA compliance or resilience of network service providers is not monitored or validated on an ongoing basis.

controls.short_summary: Isolate trust zones, critical assets and cloud networks with strict boundary rules
controls.plain_english_summary: Flat networks allow an attacker who compromises a single laptop or public web server to pivot rapidly into core databases and backup systems. Network segregation divides infrastructure into distinct security domains — separating users, guests, IoT devices, DMZs, management planes, non-production and crown-jewel workloads — across both on-premises and cloud environments. Traffic crossing zone boundaries must be explicitly authorised and filtered.
controls.why_it_matters: Effective segmentation contains the blast radius of ransomware and limits compliance scope for regulated datasets such as payment cards or sensitive customer records. Auditors look for proof that logical or physical boundaries actually block unauthorised lateral movement rather than existing only on diagrams.
key_deliverables: Network Segmentation Policy and Zone Architecture Diagram
Inter-Zone Traffic Matrix (Allowed Flows Register)
VLAN, Firewall and NAC Configuration Baselines
Cloud VPC, Subnet and Security Group Architecture
Segmentation Validation and Penetration Test Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors compare zone diagrams against live firewall, VLAN and cloud security group rules to confirm critical systems and guest networks are genuinely isolated. The #1 trap is creating separate VLANs or VPCs while permitting unrestricted routing between them.

questions.question: How are networks segregated into trust zones separating critical systems, user workstations, guest networks and management planes?
questions.guidance: Group information services, users and systems into logical or physical security domains based on asset criticality, data classification and trust level. Isolate internet-facing DMZs, core production databases, backup infrastructure, administrative management networks, IoT/OT devices and guest Wi-Fi onto distinct segments so compromise of a lower-trust zone cannot directly reach critical assets.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the segmentation architecture diagram and verify live VLAN, subnet and routing configurations for critical systems, corporate users and guest Wi-Fi. Confirm guest and BYOD traffic routes directly to the internet with zero access to internal resources.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented trust zones separate internet-facing services, corporate users, guest/BYOD devices, management planes and critical production systems. Guest networks are isolated at the network layer with direct internet egress only. Asset classification drives zone placement consistently across offices and data centres.
questions.red_flags: Servers, workstations, printers and guest devices share a flat network with unrestricted routing. Backup repositories or domain controllers sit on the same unrestricted segment as general user endpoints. Segmentation diagrams do not match production IP addressing.
questions.nc_pattern: Groups of information services, users and information systems are not segregated into distinct network domains commensurate with risk and criticality.

questions.question: How is inter-segment traffic controlled, filtered and periodically verified against least-privilege rules?
questions.guidance: Enforce stateful firewalls, network access control lists or micro-segmentation gateways at every trust-zone boundary using an explicit default-deny stance. Maintain a documented inter-zone traffic matrix justifying permitted ports, protocols and directions, and periodically test segmentation boundaries (such as during penetration tests or automated rule audits) to detect drift.
questions.auditor_focus: Examine boundary ACLs and internal firewall rules between sensitive zones against the approved traffic matrix. Look for independent validation or penetration test results confirming lateral movement between zones is blocked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All traffic crossing security zones passes through inspecting gateways enforcing default-deny policies aligned to a maintained traffic matrix. Administrative protocols such as RDP, SSH and SMB are blocked from user zones to production servers. Periodic segmentation tests confirm boundary controls hold.
questions.red_flags: Separate VLANs exist, but core switches route all inter-VLAN traffic without filtering. Legacy migration rules permit broad subnet-to-subnet access indefinitely. Segmentation has never been technically tested after initial build.
questions.nc_pattern: Traffic between segregated network domains is not filtered on a least-privilege basis or contains unverified, overly broad routing rules that defeat segmentation.

questions.question: How is network segregation designed, automated and governed across cloud and hybrid environments?
questions.guidance: Apply equivalent segregation principles in public and private clouds using separate accounts or subscriptions, isolated VPCs/VNets, public versus private subnets, tight security groups and private service endpoints. Manage cloud network topologies through Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with automated drift detection and guardrails preventing accidental public exposure of private workloads.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect cloud account structure, VPC peering or transit gateway routing tables and sample security groups for `0.0.0.0/0` exposure on sensitive ports. Verify CSPM or IaC policy checks prevent unauthorised changes to cloud network boundaries.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Cloud workloads are segregated by environment and sensitivity across dedicated accounts, VPCs and private subnets with default-deny security groups. Hybrid links into on-premises networks traverse inspected gateways rather than flat peering. Automated CSPM checks alert on public exposure or routing drift.
questions.red_flags: Production and non-production workloads share a single cloud VPC with open internal security groups. Databases or management ports are assigned public IP addresses or `0.0.0.0/0` ingress rules. Cloud network rules are edited manually in consoles without change control.
questions.nc_pattern: Cloud or hybrid network environments lack effective logical isolation, allowing unauthorised reachability across environments or public exposure of internal services.

controls.short_summary: Block malicious and unauthorised websites through risk-based web and DNS filtering
controls.plain_english_summary: Web filtering reduces exposure to phishing pages, drive-by malware, command-and-control domains and unauthorised web categories across managed devices. Organisations should deploy risk-based URL, domain and DNS filtering — on-premises and for remote workers — driven by regularly updated threat intelligence. Clear exception governance and privacy-aware access logging ensure filtering stays effective without obstructing legitimate work.
controls.why_it_matters: A large share of initial compromises begin when a user clicks a phishing link or an endpoint reaches out to a newly registered malicious domain. Web and DNS filtering provides a lightweight preventive barrier that stops many attacks before payloads ever reach the device.
key_deliverables: Web Filtering Policy and Blocked Category Baseline
Secure Web Gateway or Protective DNS Configuration
Web Filtering Exception Register and Approval Records
Centralised Web and DNS Access Logs
Periodic Filtering Rule and Bypass Review Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors verify that web or protective DNS filtering actively blocks known malicious domains and applies consistently to remote endpoints, not only office networks. The #1 trap is leaving remote laptops unprotected off-VPN or granting permanent bypasses that are never reviewed.

questions.question: How is risk-based web and DNS filtering implemented to block access to malicious websites and unauthorised web categories?
questions.guidance: Deploy secure web gateways, protective DNS resolvers or managed browser controls that block known malicious, phishing, command-and-control and high-risk newly registered domains, along with business-defined unauthorised categories. Ensure filtering applies consistently to both on-premises and remote managed devices. Use risk-based domain, URL, SNI or browser-level controls; full SSL/TLS decryption is optional and should only be used where explicitly risk-justified, technically safe and legally compliant.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect active web gateway or protective DNS policies, verify threat-intelligence feed update status and confirm enforcement extends to remote and hybrid endpoints. Test or review evidence showing malicious test domains and restricted categories are blocked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Risk-based web and protective DNS filtering operates across corporate networks and remote managed devices using continuously updated threat feeds. Malicious, phishing and unauthorised categories are blocked consistently, and users receive clear block notices. Filtering methods respect privacy and legal boundaries without relying on unnecessary protocol-breaking interception.
questions.red_flags: Web filtering applies only inside the corporate office while remote staff browse unfiltered. Blocked category lists are undefined or threat-intelligence feeds have stopped updating. Users can easily bypass filtering by altering local DNS settings or using unmanaged proxies.
questions.nc_pattern: Access to external websites is not managed through risk-based web or DNS filtering to reduce exposure to malicious content and unauthorised web resources.

questions.question: How are web filtering exceptions approved and how is web access activity logged while respecting privacy obligations?
questions.guidance: Establish a formal workflow to assess, approve, time-limit and periodically review allowlist overrides or category exceptions so temporary exemptions do not become permanent blind spots. Log blocked and permitted web or DNS events centrally to support security investigations, while configuring retention, access controls and exclusions (such as sensitive personal banking or health domains where applicable) in line with privacy law.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the web filtering exception register for business justification, risk approval and expiry dates. Inspect centralised web or DNS logs for retention, SIEM integration and role-based access restrictions protecting employee privacy.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All filtering exceptions require documented business justification, security sign-off and defined review or expiry dates. Web and DNS access logs stream to the SIEM for incident investigation with strict access controls and defined retention aligned to privacy obligations. Periodic reviews prune stale allowlist entries.
questions.red_flags: Helpdesk staff grant permanent domain or user bypasses via informal chat messages without security review. Web or DNS filtering logs are disabled or inaccessible during phishing investigations. Sensitive browsing logs are viewable by broad IT teams without privacy controls.
questions.nc_pattern: Web filtering exceptions are granted without formal approval and review, or web access events are not logged appropriately to support security monitoring and incident investigation.

controls.short_summary: Enforce modern cryptography standards and full key lifecycle governance
controls.plain_english_summary: Cryptography underpins data confidentiality, integrity and authentication across storage, networks, backups and digital identities, yet weak algorithms or mishandled keys quickly render it ineffective. Organisations must define approved algorithms, minimum key lengths and encryption requirements for data at rest and in transit, while prohibiting deprecated ciphers. Formal key management must cover secure generation, storage, rotation, recovery and destruction.
controls.why_it_matters: Unencrypted databases, exposed TLS keys or legacy ciphers such as TLS 1.0 and SHA-1 routinely lead to severe data breaches and immediate audit findings. Regulators and certification auditors expect proof that cryptographic rules are enforced in live configurations and that key custody is tightly controlled.
key_deliverables: Cryptographic Policy and Approved Algorithm Standard
Data-at-Rest and Data-in-Transit Encryption Inventory
Key Management Lifecycle Procedure
HSM / Cloud KMS Access and Rotation Records
TLS Certificate and Cipher Suite Scan Reports
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect TLS scan outputs, cloud storage encryption settings and KMS/HSM access policies alongside the written cryptographic standard. The #1 trap is publishing a modern policy while legacy servers still negotiate weak TLS ciphers or encryption keys sit alongside the encrypted data.

questions.question: How are cryptographic rules, approved algorithms, minimum key lengths and prohibitions on weak ciphers defined and enforced?
questions.guidance: Maintain a topic-specific cryptographic policy aligned with authoritative guidance (such as the Australian Cyber Security Centre ISM cryptographic standards) specifying approved algorithms, modes and minimum key lengths for encryption, hashing and digital signatures. Explicitly prohibit deprecated ciphers and protocols (such as SSL, TLS 1.0/1.1, DES, 3DES, RC4, MD5 and SHA-1 for security uses) and verify enforcement through automated scanning.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the cryptographic policy for currency, management approval and alignment to recognised standards. Inspect recent vulnerability or TLS scanner outputs confirming deprecated protocols and weak cipher suites are disabled across external and internal endpoints.
questions.what_good_looks_like: An approved cryptographic standard specifies vetted algorithms (such as AES-256, TLS 1.2/1.3 and SHA-256 or stronger) and is reviewed periodically against emerging threats. Automated scans confirm weak protocols and ciphers are disabled across public and internal services. Any legacy exception is formally risk-accepted with a retirement date.
questions.red_flags: No formal cryptographic standard exists or it has not been updated in years. Public websites or internal APIs still accept TLS 1.0/1.1 or weak cipher suites. Applications rely on custom-built encryption routines or unsalted legacy hashes.
questions.nc_pattern: Rules for the effective use of cryptography are undefined, outdated or unenforced, permitting deprecated algorithms or weak cipher configurations in operational systems.

questions.question: How is encryption consistently applied to protect sensitive information at rest and in transit?
questions.guidance: Map encryption requirements directly to information classification so sensitive data is protected at rest across databases, cloud object stores, backups, laptops and removable media, as well as in transit across public, wireless and untrusted internal networks. Use automated compliance checks (such as MDM disk-encryption status and CSPM storage checks) to verify continuous coverage.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect MDM compliance dashboards for full-disk encryption, cloud console or CSPM evidence for encrypted volumes, databases and backups, and sample application traffic configurations confirming end-to-end TLS enforcement.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Encryption at rest is verified via automated tooling across 100% of managed endpoints, production databases, object storage and backups. All external and sensitive internal data flows enforce authenticated TLS or equivalent tunnel encryption. Non-compliant storage resources trigger automated alerts or remediation.
questions.red_flags: Production databases are encrypted but database backups, snapshots or file shares remain unencrypted. Unencrypted HTTP, FTP or cleartext database connections traverse shared networks. Endpoint disk encryption is enabled manually with no central compliance verification.
questions.nc_pattern: Sensitive operational information lacks required cryptographic protection at rest or in transit across production stores, endpoints, backups or network transfers.

questions.question: How is the cryptographic key management lifecycle — including generation, secure storage, rotation, revocation and destruction — governed?
questions.guidance: Manage keys and digital certificates through dedicated Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) or managed Key Management Services (KMS) with strict role separation between key custodians and system administrators. Define documented procedures for random key generation, secure distribution, scheduled rotation, emergency compromise revocation, split-knowledge recovery where needed and secure destruction at end of life.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect KMS/HSM access policies, key rotation schedules, certificate expiry monitoring and audit logs of key administration events. Verify that encryption keys are stored separately from encrypted data and backups.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Keys are generated and stored inside hardened KMS or HSM services with least-privilege access and immutable audit logging. Automated rotation and certificate lifecycle tooling prevent expiry outages and enforce scheduled key turnover. Documented key-compromise revocation and destruction procedures are maintained and tested.
questions.red_flags: Encryption keys sit in plaintext configuration files, source repositories or the same storage bucket as encrypted backups. Master keys have never been rotated and broad admin groups can export raw key material. Expired TLS certificates repeatedly cause service disruptions.
questions.nc_pattern: Cryptographic keys lack structured lifecycle protection, separation of custody, rotation or compromise-revocation controls, undermining the integrity of encrypted data.

controls.short_summary: Embed security governance, reviews and release gates across the SDLC
controls.plain_english_summary: Security must be built into software and systems from initial concept through design, coding, testing, deployment and decommissioning rather than bolted on before go-live. A formal secure development life cycle (SDLC) defines mandatory security checkpoints, role-specific developer training, automated pipeline checks and formal release sign-off. Embedding these controls consistently prevents recurring design flaws from reaching production.
controls.why_it_matters: Fixing a security defect in production costs orders of magnitude more than catching it during design or pull-request review, and unvetted releases are a leading source of exploitable web and API vulnerabilities. Certification auditors trace recent software releases end-to-end to verify the SDLC is actually followed.
key_deliverables: Secure Development Life Cycle (SDLC) Policy and Standard
Role-Based Secure Development Training Records
CI/CD Security Gate and Pipeline Configurations
Peer Security Code Review Records
Pre-Deployment Security Sign-Off and Release Approvals
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors pick 3–5 recent production releases and walk the complete paper trail from requirements and code review through CI/CD test outputs to security sign-off. The #1 trap is maintaining a polished SDLC policy document that agile delivery teams routinely bypass under release pressure.

questions.question: How is the secure development life cycle formally defined, supported by developer security training and embedded across delivery phases?
questions.guidance: Establish and maintain a documented secure SDLC standard covering planning, requirements, design, implementation, verification, deployment and retirement across both bespoke applications and infrastructure-as-code. Provide role-specific secure development training to engineers, architects and testers at onboarding and periodically thereafter so teams understand threat classes and required checkpoints.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the secure SDLC documentation for completeness across all lifecycle phases and inspect developer training completion records for the past 12 months. Verify that project templates or sprint workflows actively incorporate security checkpoints.
