questions.what_good_looks_like: A current, approved secure SDLC standard defines clear security deliverables and exit criteria for each development stage. Engineers complete role-specific secure coding and architecture training annually with tracked attendance. Agile backlogs and project gates consistently capture security tasks alongside functional work.
questions.red_flags: SDLC documentation exists only as a high-level policy with no practical engineering checkpoints. Developers receive only generic phishing awareness training rather than role-specific secure development training. New microservices or internal tools are built outside the SDLC.
questions.nc_pattern: Rules for secure development of software and systems are not formally established, maintained or applied across the development life cycle.

questions.question: How are security code reviews and automated CI/CD security gates enforced prior to merging or building releases?
questions.guidance: Configure source-control branch protection so no code merges into protected branches without documented peer review covering security logic alongside functionality. Integrate automated security scanning — including SAST, software composition analysis (SCA) and secrets detection — into CI/CD pipelines with defined fail-build thresholds for high-severity findings.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect repository branch protection settings, sample merged pull requests for independent reviewer approval and check CI/CD pipeline runs to confirm automated security gates execute and enforce defined thresholds.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Branch protection enforces mandatory independent peer review and passing CI/CD security checks before code can merge. Pipelines run SAST, dependency vulnerability scanning and secret checks on every commit or pull request. Critical findings automatically block builds unless formally triaged.
questions.red_flags: Developers can push commits directly to main or release branches without review. Automated CI/CD security scans run in warning-only mode with hundreds of ignored high-severity alerts. Pipeline security checks exist only for one flagship repo while other production apps have none.
questions.nc_pattern: Development pipelines lack enforced peer review or automated security verification controls to identify vulnerabilities prior to integration and build.

questions.question: How is formal security sign-off obtained and recorded before releasing new systems or major changes to production?
questions.guidance: Define objective release-readiness criteria requiring verification that security requirements, testing evidence and remediation of critical or high vulnerabilities are complete before go-live. Require explicit authorisation from an accountable security or risk approver — separate from the code author — and record any deferred residual risks formally before deployment.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent major software releases and inspect release-gate tickets or deployment records for documented security sign-off, test evidence links and formal risk acceptance for any unresolved medium or low defects.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Production deployments are gated by a documented release checklist requiring verified security testing and independent security or designated risk-owner sign-off. Any unresolved findings above threshold halt deployment until remediated or formally risk-accepted by senior management. Approval records are retained alongside change tickets.
questions.red_flags: Product teams deploy major releases to production without security review or documented approval. Release sign-off is performed solely by the developer who authored the change. Unresolved high-risk vulnerabilities are pushed live verbally with no formal risk acceptance.
questions.nc_pattern: New systems or significant software releases are deployed into production without documented security verification and formal release authorisation.

controls.short_summary: Specify, trace and verify security requirements for built and acquired apps
controls.plain_english_summary: Whether an organisation builds software internally or acquires commercial and SaaS applications, information security needs must be specified upfront before design or procurement begins. Requirements should flow from data classification, threat exposure and statutory obligations such as the Australian Privacy Act or APRA prudential standards. Tracing each requirement through to testing ensures critical safeguards are delivered rather than quietly dropped.
controls.why_it_matters: Retrofitting authentication, audit logging or data encryption after an application is built or contracted is expensive and frequently incomplete. Auditors check that security requirements are genuinely risk-driven and cover both bespoke development and third-party software acquisitions.
key_deliverables: Application Security Requirements Baseline / Catalogue
Risk and Regulatory Requirements Mapping Matrix
Security Requirements Traceability Matrix
Third-Party and SaaS Security Assessment Questionnaires
Application Procurement Security Sign-Off Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample both an internally developed application and a recently procured SaaS or COTS tool to check that security requirements were documented upfront and verified before go-live. The #1 trap is defining generic boilerplate requirements that are never traced to acceptance testing.

questions.question: How are risk-based and regulatory information security requirements defined when specifying new or modified applications?
questions.guidance: Establish a structured baseline of application security requirements covering authentication, authorisation, input validation, cryptography, audit logging, session handling, privacy and resilience — calibrated to data sensitivity and exposure (such as internet-facing versus internal). Incorporate applicable statutory, regulatory and contractual obligations early in business cases and architectural specifications.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect recent project initiation documents, user stories or technical specifications to verify that concrete, risk-tiered and regulatory security requirements were defined prior to build or procurement.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A risk-tiered application security requirements baseline (aligned to frameworks such as OWASP ASVS) informs every new application or major enhancement. Legal, privacy and regulatory mandates are explicitly mapped into project specifications before design sign-off. Requirements are measurable and testable rather than vague statements.
questions.red_flags: Project specifications contain only functional features with no documented security criteria. Regulatory or privacy obligations are discovered only after development is complete. Security requirements use generic wording like 'must be secure' without testable controls.
questions.nc_pattern: Information security requirements are not systematically identified and specified based on risk, asset criticality and regulatory obligations when developing or acquiring applications.

questions.question: How are application security requirements tracked through delivery and assessed for third-party or SaaS applications?
questions.guidance: Maintain traceability from initial security requirements through implementation and acceptance testing so every control is verified before release. For commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) and SaaS acquisitions, evaluate vendor security capabilities against the same requirements baseline during procurement, embed mandatory security commitments into contracts and document compensating controls for any gaps.
questions.auditor_focus: Review requirements traceability records linking security stories to test results for internal builds, and inspect pre-purchase security assessments and contracts for recently onboarded SaaS or third-party applications.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Security requirements are tracked in delivery tooling from specification through to verified test completion before go-live. Third-party and SaaS applications undergo structured pre-procurement security assessment against defined requirements, with unresolved gaps either remediated contractually or risk-accepted with compensating controls.
questions.red_flags: Security requirements are written at project kick-off but never checked during acceptance testing. Business units purchase and connect SaaS applications via corporate cards without security assessment. Vendor capability gaps go undocumented and unmitigated.
questions.nc_pattern: Application security requirements are not tracked to verified implementation, or third-party and SaaS applications are acquired without assessing conformance to security requirements.

controls.control_name: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
controls.short_summary: Apply defence-in-depth principles, threat modelling and architecture reviews
controls.plain_english_summary: Secure systems rely on deliberate architectural choices — such as defence-in-depth, least privilege, zero trust, fail-safe defaults and attack-surface minimisation — rather than ad-hoc patchwork after deployment. Organisations must codify these engineering principles into reusable design patterns and verify conformance through structured architecture reviews and threat modelling. Reviewing designs early catches systemic flaws before code is written.
controls.why_it_matters: Code-level scanners cannot detect missing architectural trust boundaries, broken multi-tenancy isolation or insecure authentication flows. Auditors expect clear evidence that engineering principles actively shape real system designs and evolve alongside new technologies such as cloud-native services and AI.
key_deliverables: Secure Architecture and Engineering Principles Standard
Approved Security Design Patterns and Reference Architectures
Threat Modelling Methodology and Completed Threat Models
Architecture Review Board (ARB) Assessment Records
Architectural Exception and Technical Debt Register
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect the documented architecture principles and sample recent major system designs to verify that threat models and security architecture reviews actually occurred before build. The #1 trap is publishing abstract principles with no review gate proving engineers applied them.

questions.question: How are secure system architecture principles, defence-in-depth controls and reusable design patterns documented and maintained?
questions.guidance: Establish formal secure engineering principles covering least privilege, defence-in-depth, fail-secure behaviour, zero-trust verification, minimal attack surface and clear trust boundaries across application, data, identity and infrastructure layers. Translate these principles into practical reference architectures and vetted design patterns (such as standard SSO, API gateway and encryption patterns) kept current with technology changes.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the documented secure architecture principles and reference patterns for relevance to the organisation's current technology stack (cloud, APIs, microservices, on-premises). Check when they were last reviewed and how engineering teams access them.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented secure engineering principles explicitly address defence-in-depth, least privilege, trust-boundary isolation and fail-safe defaults. Reusable reference architectures and vetted patterns guide authentication, secrets handling, API security and network tiering. Principles are reviewed periodically to reflect evolving platforms and threats.
questions.red_flags: Engineering teams build systems ad hoc with no documented security architecture standards or reference patterns. Applications rely on a single perimeter control with no internal defence-in-depth. Architecture standards describe legacy on-premises patterns while all new builds run in public cloud.
questions.nc_pattern: Principles for engineering secure systems are not formally established, documented or maintained to guide system design and implementation.

questions.question: How are threat modelling and security architecture reviews conducted for new systems and major changes?
questions.guidance: Define clear triggers — such as new internet-facing services, high-classification data flows, new integrations or major architectural refactors — that mandate threat modelling (for example STRIDE or attack-tree analysis) and formal security architecture review prior to build. Record identified threats, required mitigations and any approved architectural exceptions, and verify implementation before release.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample recent major projects or architectural changes and inspect completed threat models, architecture review board minutes, resulting security actions and closure evidence.
questions.what_good_looks_like: New systems and significant architectural changes undergo documented threat modelling and security architecture review before implementation begins. Identified design threats map directly to tracked engineering mitigations. Architectural deviations require formal risk approval with compensating controls.
questions.red_flags: Threat modelling is never performed or exists only as an uncompleted template. Security reviews occur after systems are already built and ready for launch. High-risk architectural shortcuts are accepted informally without tracking remediation.
questions.nc_pattern: Secure architecture principles are not consistently applied or verified through threat modelling and design reviews during system engineering activities.

controls.short_summary: Enforce secure coding standards, static analysis, peer review and secrets hygiene
controls.plain_english_summary: Most exploitable application breaches stem from preventable coding mistakes — such as injection flaws, broken access control, unsafe deserialisation, vulnerable third-party libraries and hardcoded credentials. Organisations must adopt language-specific secure coding standards addressing recognised vulnerability classes, reinforce them through automated static analysis and peer review, and eliminate plaintext secrets from source repositories.
controls.why_it_matters: A single committed API key or unvalidated query can expose an entire customer database within minutes of deployment. Certification auditors examine live repositories, SAST/SCA tool reports and secrets-scanning alerts to verify that secure coding operates continuously rather than only on paper.
key_deliverables: Language-Specific Secure Coding Standards
SAST and Software Composition Analysis (SCA) Reports
Peer Code Review Checklists and Pull Request Logs
Secrets Management Standard and Vault Configurations
Secret Scanning Alerts and Credential Rotation Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect SAST/SCA scan results, sample pull requests for meaningful security peer review and check repository secret-scanning logs. The #1 trap is enabling static analysis tools without tuning rules, triaging findings or enforcing secret-scanning push protection.

questions.question: How are secure coding standards defined, maintained and applied to prevent common vulnerability classes?
questions.guidance: Establish practical, language- and framework-specific secure coding guidelines covering input validation, output encoding, parameterised queries, authentication and authorisation checks, safe error handling, memory safety and third-party library hygiene — aligned to current references such as OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25. Keep standards updated as languages, frameworks and threat techniques evolve.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the secure coding standards for coverage of languages actually used in production and verify developers have access to them. Review how common vulnerability classes (such as OWASP Top 10) are translated into concrete coding rules and linter configs.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Maintained secure coding standards cover the organisation's active programming languages and explicitly address OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25 flaw classes. Security linters and IDE guardrails reinforce rules during coding. Standards are reviewed periodically and updated following recurring vulnerability trends.
questions.red_flags: No secure coding standard exists, or it covers languages no longer used by the team. Developers cannot explain how injection, broken access control or insecure dependencies are prevented. Third-party open-source packages are added without vulnerability or provenance checks.
questions.nc_pattern: Secure coding principles and language-appropriate guidelines are not established or maintained to prevent common software vulnerabilities.

questions.question: How are static application security testing (SAST), dependency scanning and peer code reviews performed and tracked?
questions.guidance: Run automated SAST and software composition analysis (SCA) continuously across repositories to detect code defects and vulnerable open-source dependencies before release. Complement automated scans with structured peer code reviews focused on business logic, authorisation boundaries and security-sensitive changes, tracking findings to documented remediation.
questions.auditor_focus: Review recent SAST and SCA scan outputs, remediation backlogs and a sample of merged pull requests showing independent peer review comments and approvals. Confirm false-positive suppressions require documented justification.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Automated SAST and SCA scan every pull request against default branches, enforcing remediation SLAs for critical or high vulnerabilities. Independent peers review code changes using security-aware checklists before merge. Suppressions or risk acceptances require documented rationale and review.
questions.red_flags: SAST or SCA tools are run only once a year before audit rather than continuously. Pull requests are rubber-stamped within seconds or self-approved by authors. Critical vulnerable dependencies remain unpatched across active production builds.
questions.nc_pattern: Source code and third-party dependencies are not systematically verified through static analysis and independent peer review to identify and remediate coding flaws.

questions.question: How are application secrets, API keys and credentials managed to prevent exposure in source code and builds?
questions.guidance: Prohibit hardcoding passwords, API tokens, private keys or connection strings inside source code, container images or build logs. Store and inject runtime secrets through a dedicated secrets manager or cloud vault with least-privilege identity binding, and enforce pre-commit and repository secret scanning with rapid revocation workflows if a credential leaks.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify secrets-manager usage in deployment configurations, inspect repository secret-scanning settings (including push protection) and sample recent secret-leak alerts to confirm exposed credentials were promptly revoked and rotated.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Runtime secrets are injected dynamically from a central vault or workload-identity service rather than stored in code or environment files. Automated pre-commit and repository push protection blocks accidental credential commits. Any detected secret leak triggers immediate revocation, rotation and git-history remediation.
questions.red_flags: Production API keys, database passwords or certificates appear in Git repositories, `.env` files or CI/CD logs. Secret scanning is disabled or alerts are dismissed without rotating the exposed credential. Developers share static production service credentials locally.
questions.nc_pattern: Application secrets or credentials are hardcoded in source code or build artefacts without automated secret detection and secure vault-based management.

controls.control_name: Security testing in development and acceptance
controls.short_summary: Execute DAST, penetration testing and security acceptance checks before release
controls.plain_english_summary: Even well-designed code can fail under live runtime conditions, misconfigured middleware or complex business-logic interactions. Organisations must embed security testing across development and acceptance phases — combining automated dynamic scanning (DAST), functional security acceptance tests and independent penetration testing for significant releases. Clear remediation gates ensure critical defects are resolved before production exposure.
controls.why_it_matters: Skipping runtime security testing leaves authentication bypasses, broken authorisation and configuration errors directly exposed to internet attackers. For APRA-regulated entities, CPS 234 also mandates systematic control-effectiveness testing performed by functionally independent specialists with annual testing-programme review.
key_deliverables: Security Testing Standard and Acceptance Criteria
Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) Reports
Independent Penetration Test Scopes and Reports
Security Acceptance Test Execution Records
Pre-Release Vulnerability Remediation and Retest Evidence
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect recent DAST outputs, independent penetration test reports and retest certificates confirming critical and high findings were closed prior to go-live. The #1 trap is commissioning an annual penetration test while deploying major application changes throughout the year with zero pre-release security testing.

questions.question: How are security testing criteria, dynamic application security testing (DAST) and security acceptance tests defined and executed before go-live?
questions.guidance: Define risk-based security testing criteria within the SDLC specifying when automated DAST, API security scans and manual security acceptance tests (verifying authentication, role-based authorisation, error handling and logging) must run against staging or pre-production builds. Ensure acceptance testing explicitly validates security requirements alongside business functionality before sign-off.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the security testing standard and sample recent release test packs showing DAST execution outputs and signed security acceptance test cases mapped back to application security requirements.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Documented testing criteria define required runtime security checks by system criticality and change size. Automated DAST and authenticated API scans run against pre-production environments alongside security acceptance test cases. Test outcomes are recorded and reviewed as formal acceptance evidence.
questions.red_flags: Acceptance testing covers functional user journeys only, omitting negative security and authorisation tests. DAST runs unauthenticated against landing pages without covering core APIs or logged-in workflows. Testing criteria are undefined or applied inconsistently.
questions.nc_pattern: Security testing processes and acceptance criteria are not defined or consistently executed during development and acceptance of new or significantly modified systems.

questions.question: How is independent penetration testing scoped, conducted and reviewed for critical systems and major releases?
questions.guidance: Commission qualified, functionally independent testers — either vetted external CREST/OSCP-credentialled specialists or an independent internal red team — to perform penetration testing prior to launching high-risk applications, after major architectural changes and on a scheduled annual or risk-driven cadence. Review the testing programme's scope and methodology annually to ensure continued sufficiency against emerging threats.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect penetration test scopes, tester qualifications and independence, final reports and evidence of annual testing-programme sufficiency reviews. Confirm rules of engagement align with system protection rules under 8.34.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Independent, appropriately credentialled specialists perform penetration tests on critical systems and major releases against clear, risk-based scopes. Testing covers both authenticated business logic and external attack surfaces. Senior management reviews testing programme coverage and sufficiency at least annually.
questions.red_flags: Penetration testing is performed solely by the same developers who built the system, lacking independence. Automated vulnerability scans are mislabelled as penetration tests. Internet-facing systems undergo major releases without updated security testing.
questions.nc_pattern: High-risk systems or major releases are not subjected to appropriately scoped, independent security testing prior to or during operational life.

questions.question: How are security testing findings tracked, remediated and verified via retesting prior to production release?
questions.guidance: Log every security test finding in a central issue tracker with severity ratings, assigned owners and target remediation timeframes. Enforce release gates requiring critical and high vulnerabilities to be fixed and independently retested before deployment, escalating any unresolved deficiencies or time-bound risk acceptances to senior management.
questions.auditor_focus: Trace critical and high findings from recent DAST and penetration test reports through issue tickets to retest verification letters or formal, time-bound executive risk acceptances prior to the production deployment date.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All security testing findings are logged with severity-based SLAs and assigned remediation owners. Critical and high defects must be fixed and verified via independent retesting before production go-live. Any deferred remediation requires formal executive risk acceptance with compensating controls and a firm target date.
questions.red_flags: Critical or high penetration test findings remain open months after production launch with no retest evidence. Findings sit inside static PDF reports and are never entered into engineering backlogs. Developers mark vulnerabilities closed without independent verification.
questions.nc_pattern: Significant vulnerabilities identified during development or acceptance security testing are not remediated, independently retested or formally risk-accepted prior to production release.

controls.short_summary: Contract, oversee and independently test externally developed software
controls.plain_english_summary: Outsourcing software development transfers coding effort to external vendors, but never transfers security accountability or regulatory responsibility. Organisations must embed explicit secure coding, IP ownership, escrow, audit-access and defect-remediation obligations into development contracts before work starts. Continuous oversight during delivery and independent security acceptance testing of all received code prevent hidden vulnerabilities and supply-chain compromise.
controls.why_it_matters: Outsourced codebases frequently suffer from undocumented third-party libraries, weak access controls or unclear intellectual property rights that create severe operational and legal exposure. Under APRA CPS 234 and CPS 230, material outsourced development arrangements require legally binding security, fourth-party transparency and APRA access clauses.
key_deliverables: Outsourced Development Security Schedule and Contract Templates
Vendor SDLC Assessment and Oversight Review Records
Independent Security Acceptance Test Reports for Delivered Code
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and Licence Compliance Records
Contractual Security Defect SLA and Remediation Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect active development vendor contracts for security clauses, IP/escrow protections and APRA/audit rights, then check proof that delivered code was independently security-tested before deployment. The #1 trap is accepting vendor code directly into production based solely on functional UAT.

questions.question: How are security requirements, intellectual property rights, source-code escrow and regulatory audit clauses embedded in outsourced development contracts?
questions.guidance: Include binding security schedules in every software development agreement covering secure coding standards, approved development environments, software bill of materials (SBOM) disclosure, open-source licence compliance, IP ownership and source-code escrow where business continuity depends on the asset. For APRA-regulated entities, ensure material development contracts include mandatory CPS 230 clauses covering fourth-party subcontracting controls, termination/exit support and APRA access rights.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect executed agreements for current outsourced development partners to confirm explicit security specifications, IP/licensing terms, subcontracting controls and audit/regulator access provisions are legally binding.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Outsourced development contracts incorporate a binding security schedule aligned to internal SDLC standards, clear IP ownership, SBOM delivery and open-source licence warranties. Source-code escrow or repository custody protects continuity for critical systems. Material provider contracts include fourth-party oversight and regulatory audit-access clauses.
questions.red_flags: External developers work under generic time-and-materials statements of work with no security obligations. Contracts omit IP ownership, open-source licence restrictions or subcontracting disclosures. Material software vendors refuse audit or APRA access clauses.
questions.nc_pattern: Outsourced software development engagements lack formal contractual security requirements, intellectual property protections or required audit and oversight clauses.

questions.question: How are outsourced development activities, vendor coding practices and developer access monitored throughout delivery?
questions.guidance: Direct and oversee external development teams continuously rather than waiting until final handover. Restrict vendor developer access to dedicated non-production environments using least privilege, review vendor SDLC assurance evidence, monitor progress through periodic security milestone reviews and track any fourth-party subcontractors or offshore delivery locations.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect oversight meeting minutes, vendor SDLC assessments, access provisioning records for external contractors and registers tracking subcontracted delivery teams.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Internal technical owners conduct scheduled security and architecture checkpoint reviews throughout outsourced sprints. External developers hold time-bound, least-privilege access strictly segregated from production systems and real customer data. Subcontracting and offshore delivery changes require prior written approval.
questions.red_flags: Outsourced vendors operate as a 'black box' with no visibility until final code drop. External contractors retain standing access to internal repositories or production systems after project completion. Vendors subcontract coding to unvetted fourth parties without notification.
questions.nc_pattern: Outsourced system development activities are not actively directed, monitored or governed against agreed security and access requirements during delivery.

questions.question: How is externally developed code independently security-tested upon delivery and how are contractual security defects remediated?
questions.guidance: Subject all vendor-delivered code, containers and build artefacts to independent security acceptance checks — including SAST, SCA/SBOM licence and vulnerability scanning, code review and penetration testing for critical builds — before accepting handover or deploying to production. Enforce contractual warranty periods and severity-based remediation SLAs so vendors fix security defects promptly at agreed cost.
questions.auditor_focus: Review independent security test outputs and SBOM scans executed on recent vendor code deliveries prior to production promotion. Inspect defect logs showing contractual SLA enforcement and verified vendor patches.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Delivered vendor code passes independent SAST, SCA, malware and acceptance security testing before sign-off or milestone payment. Contractual SLAs compel timely vendor remediation of critical and high defects, verified by independent retesting. Ongoing post-delivery vulnerability support is clearly assigned.
questions.red_flags: Vendor-supplied code is deployed directly into production without independent security scanning or review. Contracts lack security warranty terms, leaving the organisation to fund fixes for vendor-introduced flaws. Delivered code includes unverified binary blobs or end-of-life open-source packages.
questions.nc_pattern: Externally developed software is accepted and deployed without independent security verification or enforceable defect-remediation obligations.

controls.control_name: Separation of development, test and production environments
controls.short_summary: Isolate dev, test and prod environments, access rights and promotion paths
controls.plain_english_summary: Running development or testing directly inside production risks service outages, data corruption and unauthorised disclosure of live information. Organisations must physically or logically separate development, testing and production environments across compute, storage, networks and cloud accounts, enforcing strict identity isolation and segregation of duties between builders and production operators. Code and configurations should move upwards only through controlled, auditable promotion pipelines.
controls.why_it_matters: Shared credentials, cross-environment network bridges or developers holding direct production write access routinely turn routine bugs into major outages or enable undetected insider fraud. Auditors verify isolation directly in cloud IAM, network routing and CI/CD deployment rules.
key_deliverables: Environment Separation Architecture and Account Strategy
Environment Parity and Configuration Variance Matrix
Environment-Specific IAM and Segregation of Duties Matrix
Automated CI/CD Build and Promotion Pipeline Configurations
Production Deployment Approval and Audit Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect cloud accounts, IAM role assignments and CI/CD pipelines to confirm developers cannot push unreviewed changes straight to production and that environments do not share secrets or databases. The #1 trap is separating infrastructure cleanly while giving every developer production admin access 'for troubleshooting'.

questions.question: How are development, testing and production environments logically or physically separated and how are intentional configuration differences documented?
questions.guidance: Host development, test/staging and production workloads in distinct physical hardware, virtualised clusters, VLANs or separate cloud accounts/subscriptions with dedicated databases, storage buckets and cryptographic keys. Maintain consistent security baselines across environments while documenting any intentional parity differences (such as scaled-down capacity or stubbed external payment gateways) so test results remain reliable.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect infrastructure architecture diagrams, cloud account/VPC lists and database hosting layouts to confirm non-production workloads cannot reach production networks or data stores. Review documented configuration parity baselines across environments.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Development, test and production environments reside in isolated cloud accounts or segmented clusters with separate networks, databases and encryption keys. Non-production systems cannot route to production services or share runtime credentials. Intentional configuration differences are documented and managed through version-controlled IaC.
questions.red_flags: Test applications connect to production databases or share production API keys. Development and production servers run inside the same unrestricted subnet or cloud account. Unexplained configuration drift between staging and production causes recurring post-release security regressions.
questions.nc_pattern: Development, testing and production environments are not adequately separated, creating risks of unauthorised access, cross-environment compromise or operational disruption.

questions.question: How are identity access rights and segregation of duties enforced across non-production and production environments?
questions.guidance: Enforce distinct role-based access controls and separate credentials or identity roles for non-production versus production environments so developers cannot unilaterally alter production code, data or configurations. Where small teams or emergency incidents require developer diagnostic access in production, enforce time-bound, ticketed break-glass elevation with independent logging and post-use review (note: selection and masking of test data itself is governed under 8.33).
questions.auditor_focus: Review IAM role memberships and privileged group lists for production systems to verify developers do not hold standing write or deployment access. Sample recent break-glass access events for approval, duration and audit-log review.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Distinct identity roles and credentials isolate non-production from production access, preventing developers from holding standing production write privileges. Production troubleshooting uses read-only observability tools or time-limited, ticket-approved break-glass elevation. Periodic access reviews verify segregation of duties remains intact.
questions.red_flags: Software engineers hold permanent administrative privileges in both development and production environments. Service accounts or SSH keys are reused across dev, test and prod. Developers can log directly into production hosts to hot-patch live files.
questions.nc_pattern: Access rights and segregation of duties between development, test and production environments are not enforced, allowing developers unrestricted or unmonitored modification of live systems.

questions.question: How is code and configuration promoted between development, test and production environments?
questions.guidance: Enforce automated, unidirectional promotion pipelines that build immutable artefacts once, validate them in test/staging environments and require independent approval gates before deploying to production. Prohibit manual file copying, ad-hoc production compilation or unverified direct pushes into production systems, and retain complete deployment provenance linking every production build back to source commits.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect CI/CD deployment pipeline definitions, environment protection rules and a sample of recent production releases to confirm immutable build promotion and independent approval before production rollout.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Verified, immutable build artefacts progress sequentially from development through testing to production via automated CI/CD pipelines. Production deployment gates enforce independent approval and passing security checks. Production systems lack build compilers and block out-of-band manual code uploads.
questions.red_flags: Engineers manually copy compiled binaries or scripts onto production servers via SSH or FTP. Code changes bypass testing environments to deploy straight from local laptops to production. No provenance links live production binaries back to approved source commits.
questions.nc_pattern: Changes are promoted between development, test and production environments through uncontrolled or manual paths without verification, approval or traceability.

controls.short_summary: Assess security and operational risk, test, approve and audit all system changes
controls.plain_english_summary: Unplanned or poorly tested IT changes are a primary cause of both major service outages and accidental security regressions. Formal change management ensures every modification to information processing facilities, software, cloud infrastructure and security configurations follows a structured path covering operational risk and security impact assessment, pre-deployment testing, independent authorisation and documented rollback planning. Complete change records and drift checks verify that only authorised changes reach production.
controls.why_it_matters: A single misconfigured identity policy or untested firewall edit can expose critical systems or trigger a prolonged outage affecting customers. Under APRA CPS 230 §26, regulated entities must explicitly assess operational risks arising from changes to systems and processes before implementation.
key_deliverables: Change Management Policy and Standard Operating Procedure
Change Risk and Security Impact Assessment Template
Pre-Deployment Test and Rollback Plan Records
Change Advisory Board (CAB) / Approval Audit Trail
Emergency Change Retrospective Review and Drift Reconciliation Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors sample production changes directly from system or CI/CD logs — not just the ticket queue — and trace each backwards to an approved change ticket, risk assessment and test record. The #1 trap is approving changes cleanly in the ticketing tool while engineers apply undocumented 'quick fixes' directly in production.

questions.question: How does your change management process classify changes and assess security and operational risk impacts before implementation?
questions.guidance: Maintain a documented change management process governing standard (pre-approved low-risk), normal and emergency changes across applications, operating systems, networks, cloud infrastructure and security tooling. Require structured evaluation of information security impacts, dependency effects and operational risk (aligned with APRA CPS 230 §26) before approving any significant change.
questions.auditor_focus: Review the change management procedure and sample normal and emergency change tickets to confirm risk classification, documented security and operational risk impact assessments, and clear criteria distinguishing pre-approved standard changes from high-risk changes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A documented change management standard clearly defines workflows for standard, normal and emergency changes across all production systems and infrastructure. Every normal and high-risk change includes a recorded security, dependency and operational risk impact assessment prior to approval. Emergency change criteria are tightly bounded and never used to bypass routine governance.
questions.red_flags: Change management covers application code only and excludes firewall rules, IAM policies, cloud infrastructure or database patches. Change tickets lack documented security or operational risk impact analysis. Routine deployments are routinely labelled 'emergency' to skip assessment.
questions.nc_pattern: Changes to information processing facilities and information systems are not subject to a formal change management process incorporating security and operational risk impact assessment.

questions.question: How are changes tested, independently approved and backed by viable rollback plans prior to production deployment?
questions.guidance: Verify changes in representative non-production environments covering both functional behaviour and security impact before scheduling production rollout. Require formal approval from an authorised approver independent of the implementer, and mandate a documented, verified back-out or rollback procedure — supported by pre-change snapshots or immutable artefacts — so failed changes can be reversed rapidly.
questions.auditor_focus: Sample completed change tickets to confirm attached pre-deployment test evidence, independent approver sign-off timestamped prior to implementation and a specific, actionable rollback procedure.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Changes undergo documented testing in non-production environments before receiving independent approval from a designated change authority or automated policy gate. Every change record includes a concrete rollback plan and verified pre-change backup or immutable previous release. Failed deployments follow documented back-out and incident protocols.
questions.red_flags: Change implementers approve their own tickets without independent review. Rollback plans consist of vague text such as 'revert change' with no technical steps or backups. Testing is skipped routinely for infrastructure or configuration updates.
questions.nc_pattern: Production changes are implemented without prior testing, independent authorisation or a viable rollback capability.

questions.question: How are changes logged, reconciled against production activity and reviewed post-implementation to detect unauthorised modifications?
questions.guidance: Maintain an immutable, searchable register of all requested, approved, implemented and rolled-back changes, including mandatory post-implementation reviews for emergency or failed changes. Periodically reconcile actual production configuration changes (captured from SIEM, cloud audit logs or configuration-monitoring tools) against approved change tickets to detect and investigate unauthorised modifications.
questions.auditor_focus: Select a sample of actual production changes from cloud audit logs, CI/CD logs or firewall change logs and verify each maps to an authorised change ticket. Inspect retrospective review records for recent emergency changes.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Complete change records link requests, assessments, approvals, implementation logs and post-implementation verification outcomes. Emergency changes receive mandatory retrospective review and formal ratification within defined timeframes. Automated drift detection or periodic reconciliation flags unauthorised production modifications for investigation.
questions.red_flags: Production audit logs show configuration edits with no corresponding change tickets. Emergency changes are implemented and never reviewed afterwards. Change records are scattered across emails and chat threads without a central auditable log.
questions.nc_pattern: Production changes lack a complete audit trail, retrospective emergency-change review or reconciliation controls to detect unauthorised changes.

controls.short_summary: Use synthetic or masked test data and protect test datasets through erasure
controls.plain_english_summary: Copying live customer records directly into development or testing databases exposes sensitive personal and commercial data inside less-hardened environments with wider user access. Organisations must select test information carefully — defaulting to synthetic or irreversibly anonymised datasets — and require formal data-owner approval whenever masked operational extracts are unavoidable. All test datasets must be protected throughout use and securely erased once testing concludes.
controls.why_it_matters: Breaches of non-production test databases containing unmasked customer PII have caused several high-profile Australian privacy incidents and OAIC enforcement actions. Certification auditors specifically probe how test environments are populated and whether developers can view real customer data.
key_deliverables: Test Information Management Standard
Synthetic Data Generation and Data Masking Procedures
Operational Data Extraction Approval Register
Test Dataset Access Control and Encryption Evidence
Post-Testing Data Erasure and Sanitisation Logs
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors inspect staging and test databases directly to verify whether real customer names, emails or identifiers are present, and check formal approvals for any production-derived extracts. The #1 trap is restoring nightly production backups directly into staging or UAT without masking.

questions.question: How is test information selected, formally approved and generated using synthetic, anonymised or masked data instead of live operational records?
questions.guidance: Establish clear rules governing the selection and provisioning of test datasets across development, QA and user acceptance testing. Default to synthetic or irreversibly anonymised data; where derived operational data is strictly necessary to reproduce complex defects, require formal data-owner approval, apply verified masking or pseudonymisation before data leaves production and prohibit unmasked PII or sensitive operational records in lower environments.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect the test data standard, sample recent test-data refresh tickets for formal owner approval and examine live records in staging/UAT databases to verify sensitive fields are synthetic or properly masked.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Test environments are populated with synthetic or automated, irreversibly masked datasets verified by schema checks so no raw customer PII enters non-production. Any exceptional use of masked operational extracts requires documented data-owner approval and logging. Masking rules cover free-text fields, attachments and backups as well as structured columns.
questions.red_flags: Teams routinely restore unmasked production database dumps into UAT or developer laptops. Masking scripts scrub names but leave emails, addresses, tax file numbers or free-text notes exposed. No approval trail tracks when or why operational data was copied for testing.
questions.nc_pattern: Unmasked sensitive operational or personal information is copied into development or test environments without formal approval, masking or equivalent security protection.

questions.question: How is test information protected during use and securely erased once testing activities conclude?
questions.guidance: Apply access controls, encryption and audit logging to test datasets proportionate to their sensitivity — matching production protection levels whenever sensitive operational data is approved for temporary testing. Enforce defined retention periods and verified secure deletion so temporary test datasets, exports and log extracts do not accumulate indefinitely across non-production systems.
questions.auditor_focus: Review access control lists and encryption settings on test databases and storage buckets, and inspect logs or tickets confirming timely secure erasure of temporary test datasets after test cycles finish.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Test repositories enforce least-privilege access, encryption at rest and in transit, and audit logging of data copies or exports. Temporary operational test extracts carry strict expiry dates and are securely wiped upon test completion with documented confirmation. Automated lifecycle policies prevent stale test dumps from persisting.
questions.red_flags: Test databases containing sensitive extracts are publicly accessible or open to all internal staff without authentication. Old test exports sit indefinitely in shared folders, S3 buckets or developer workstations after projects close. No deletion verification is recorded.
questions.nc_pattern: Test information lacks adequate access control, cryptographic protection or timely secure erasure after testing is completed.

controls.control_name: Protection of information systems during audit testing
controls.short_summary: Plan, constrain and protect operational systems and evidence during audit tests
controls.plain_english_summary: Technical audits, vulnerability scans and compliance assessments inspect sensitive production infrastructure and can inadvertently cause outages, data corruption or exposure of privileged system details if poorly coordinated. Organisations must plan, scope and approve all audit testing in advance with system owners, restrict auditor access and tooling to safe boundaries, and protect resulting audit evidence as highly confidential information.
controls.why_it_matters: Unscheduled aggressive scanning or unchecked read/write auditor accounts can knock over fragile production systems during peak trading hours, while leaked audit reports hand attackers a detailed blueprint of internal weaknesses. Auditors check that technical assessments follow disciplined rules of engagement rather than ad-hoc requests.
key_deliverables: Audit Testing Rules of Engagement and Scoping Procedure
Approved Technical Audit Test Plans and Maintenance Windows
Time-Bound Auditor Access Provisioning and Revocation Logs
Approved Audit Tooling and Non-Production Test Sign-Offs
Encrypted Audit Evidence Repository and Handling Records
controls.audit_focus_summary: Auditors review recent internal, external or regulatory technical audit plans for formal management approval, read-only/time-bound auditor credentials and post-audit access revocation. The #1 trap is leaving external auditor accounts active weeks after fieldwork ends or emailing raw vulnerability findings unencrypted.

questions.question: How are technical audit tests and regulatory assessments planned, scoped and formally agreed with management before execution?
questions.guidance: Require a documented test plan and rules of engagement — detailing target systems, testing methods, maintenance windows, out-of-bounds assets, emergency halt contacts and applicable statutory or regulatory audit obligations (such as APRA tripartite reviews) — formally approved by system owners and management before any technical audit testing begins.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect approved audit test plans, rules of engagement and sign-off records for recent internal, external or regulatory technical assessments to confirm scope boundaries and scheduling were agreed beforehand.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Every technical audit or assurance assessment operates under a formally approved test plan specifying scope, schedule, permitted techniques, emergency stop contacts and regulatory alignment. System owners sign off on operational impact windows before testing starts. Unplanned or out-of-scope testing is strictly prohibited.
questions.red_flags: Auditors or security testers run technical scans against live production systems without prior scheduling or owner approval. Test plans omit emergency stop procedures or regulatory reporting requirements. Scope boundaries are agreed verbally with no written record.
questions.nc_pattern: Technical audit tests and assurance activities involving operational systems are conducted without prior documented planning, scoping and management approval.

questions.question: How are operational disruption risks minimised, audit tools vetted and auditor access restricted and revoked?
questions.guidance: Conduct disruptive or resource-intensive technical tests in isolated non-production copies or during approved low-traffic maintenance windows with operational monitoring active. Vet and approve all third-party audit scripts or scanning tools before use, restrict auditor accounts to read-only, time-bound least privilege (or supervised access where elevated visibility is essential) and revoke credentials immediately upon completion.
questions.auditor_focus: Verify auditor account permissions (read-only where feasible), approval of audit scripts or tools, operational monitoring during test windows and timestamped proof that temporary auditor accounts were disabled promptly after fieldwork closed.
questions.what_good_looks_like: Intrusive tests execute on isolated replicas or approved off-peak windows with active health monitoring and rapid abort controls. Audit tools and scripts are pre-approved by security and operations teams. Auditor credentials are read-only, time-boxed, centrally logged and demonstrably revoked at engagement close.
questions.red_flags: External auditors receive standing write or domain-admin privileges on live production servers. Unvetted third-party scripts run directly against critical databases during peak business hours. Temporary auditor accounts remain enabled months after an audit concludes.
questions.nc_pattern: Audit testing lacks technical safeguards to minimise operational disruption, vet audit tooling or enforce time-bound, least-privilege auditor access and prompt revocation.

questions.question: How are audit testing activities logged and how is sensitive audit evidence protected during transfer, storage and retention?
questions.guidance: Log all technical audit queries, administrative actions and tool executions centrally so unexpected system behaviour can be attributed and investigated rapidly. Classify audit outputs, configuration extracts and vulnerability findings as highly confidential; transfer and store them only via encrypted, access-controlled repositories and purge working copies once retention obligations expire.
questions.auditor_focus: Inspect logging coverage for recent audit accounts and check how audit evidence packs and technical reports were exchanged, stored and access-restricted, including deletion confirmation for temporary extracts.
questions.what_good_looks_like: All auditor sessions and tool runs are captured in centralised, immutable audit logs. Evidence packs, system dumps and audit reports are exchanged through encrypted portals and stored in tightly access-controlled repositories aligned to classification and retention rules. Working extracts held by external assessors are securely destroyed post-engagement.
questions.red_flags: Audit reports containing exploitable findings or configuration exports are sent over unencrypted email or stored on open file shares. Auditor activity on production systems is excluded from SIEM logging. External assessors retain raw customer or system extracts indefinitely without destruction certificates.
questions.nc_pattern: Audit testing activities are not adequately logged, or sensitive audit evidence and technical outputs are not protected against unauthorised disclosure or improper retention.
